title: The Crystalline Handbook
text:
Preface
This is a handbook about onboarding a colleague who happens to be a language model. The colleague is already on your machine, inside whichever harness you use: Claude Code, the Codex CLI, the Copilot CLI, Claude Desktop. It’s brilliant and tireless, and at the start of every session it’s completely new here. Crystalline is the software that changes the last part. This book is the story of how, and the manual for doing it.

title: The Crystalline Handbook
text:
Who this book is for
You run an agent every day, and you’ve noticed that you explain the same things to it every day: which service owns the retry queue, why the payments team never deploys on a Friday, that the thing the wiki calls “the gateway” is the thing the code calls “edge”. You’d like to stop, and this book shows you how to teach those things once and have them recalled in every session that follows, in files on your own machine.
Or your team is adopting Crystalline together: one shared instance, domains that live in a GitHub repository, knowledge that goes out for review the way code does. Parts V and VI are written for exactly that, and the chapters on sharing and access carry the team story.
Or you’re the person who onboards agents for other people - platform engineer, enablement lead, the one everybody asks. Every chapter here works as a standalone training module, with a summary at the end you can hand round.
Whichever of those you are, the payoff is the same. Teach an agent where things are, which tools the team uses, what was tried and what to leave alone, and it does the job in one pass instead of looping until something sticks. It stops reinventing the wheel.
The bigger payoff is trust. A model told nothing about your company fills the blanks with the general case, the intelligent guess chapter 2 describes, and a guess about your company looks exactly like a fact about it. An agent you’ve taught has no blanks to fill. It answers from what you told it, and it can say where that came from.

title: The Crystalline Handbook
text:
Where this comes from
I started where everyone starts: a CLAUDE.md and a README.md for the agent, the folder the harness keeps for its own notes, markdown files in subfolders of the project, one per topic. All of it works, and for the usual cases it works well. Then I wanted to hand the agent more than one project’s conventions: over a decade of engineering knowledge and experience, sitting in code reviews, slide decks, documentation, tickets and a wiki. I wanted it extracted and taught, so that the agent could act like an engineer with those ten years behind them, one who knows how things are and remembers why: the reasons, the discussions and the decisions behind them. At that size none of those approaches held. Index files pointing at folders bought some time, until every lookup was a walk down a tree of pointers and keeping the pointers true had become a job of its own.
The ingest was also a look ahead, because a decade of material arriving at once is every problem a knowledge base will ever have, compressed into a few weeks: decisions reversed twice over, the same rule written three ways in three years, a wiki page nobody had believed since 2019, facts that held until a date nobody wrote down. The material had kept moving underneath itself as well: processes, best practices and coding conventions had changed, and so had the tech stack and the architecture, and each of those had to come through as true for its time rather than as a contradiction. The precogs in Minority Report saw a crime before it was committed. This was that view of a knowledge base: everything it would have to survive, shown before it had grown into any of it. The statuses, the validity windows, the provenance on every engram and the maintenance sweep are all answers to something in that view.
I tried what was already out there, and some of it was good, but none of it was built for this: a colleague who is new every session, a body of knowledge that has to be recalled rather than read, and files that stay plain files. At some point the picture of how it should work was simply clear, down to the details, and Crystalline is that picture built. That’s also why it has opinions, about domains and manifests and statuses and what an engram is, where a more general tool would have left the choice to you. Chapter 1 walks the same ladder for teams in general, because it turned out I hadn’t been alone on it.
Along the way I’ve given this material as a workshop more than thirty times, to teams of every size and temperament, and the chapters are those sessions. The questions the rooms kept asking are folded back into the text, and the book is what the workshop became once it had been given often enough to know what it was.

title: The Crystalline Handbook
text:
Navigating this handbook
The handbook has seven parts, and the first six grow the way an adoption does: the idea, one laptop with one agent, the work you do with it, then the whole system, a shared instance and the team that works on it; the seventh is the lookup for all of it.
Part I, The Idea

Chapter 1, What is Crystalline? - the stranger on main street, and what it would mean to hire them.
Chapter 2, Fluid and crystalline intelligence - the psychology behind the name, and why the web UI is called Fluid.
Chapter 3, The lifecycle: learn, evolve, remember - how a colleague grows and how the software turns that into a loop.
Chapter 4, Terminology - domains, engrams, statuses, addresses: the words the rest of the book uses without stopping.

Part II, Getting Started

Chapter 5, Installing locally - from download to the first thing your agent recalls, in one sitting.

Part III, Working with Crystalline

Chapter 6, Onboarding an agent - day one: the routing prompt, how the agent finds its way, and what a week of sessions looks like.
Chapter 7, Teaching - the proper onboarding: telling the agent what matters, writing directly in Fluid and what a good engram looks like.
Chapter 8, Ingesting knowledge at scale - handing over the wiki and the slide decks, with the briefing a new colleague would get.
Chapter 9, Finding - search as recall, neighbourhoods and asking what applied last June.
Chapter 10, Evolving - feedback rather than firing: the maintenance sweep, retiring knowledge properly, verification.

Part IV, The System

Chapter 11, What Crystalline provides - every surface of the binary, each described by what it lets you do.

Part V, Getting Started with a Team

Chapter 12, Running a shared instance - one instance for a team: accounts, single sign-on, agent tokens and private domains.

Part VI, Collaborating with Crystalline

Chapter 13, Sharing with a team - team domains, proposals as the review, review mode as the rollback-capable workflow.
Chapter 14, Identity and access - who is acting, membership on private domains and how an agent earns access as a named team member.
Chapter 15, Equipping the agent - the same tools as a person: skills, commands, subagents and MCP servers, shipped by the domains that hold the knowledge they depend on, with a yes each time.
Chapter 16, Where to go from here - a first week, when to share and the inversion the whole book has been walking towards.

Part VII, Reference

Chapter 17, Configuration - every setting and environment variable, where it lives and which value wins.
Chapter 18, The MANIFEST and the engram - every MANIFEST section and switch, every frontmatter key and the body syntax.
Chapter 19, Domains - the kinds of domain, their registration, visibility, membership and review mode.
Chapter 20, Every finding code - what each code of verify and the sweep means and what clears it.

Appendices - a glossary, questions and answers, then a list of figures.

title: The Crystalline Handbook
text:
How to read it
Part I is an evening’s read (tea, Earl Grey, hot - or coffee, black, if you side with Janeway), and nothing in it needs a terminal. It’s what makes the rest make sense. Parts II and III are meant to be read with a keyboard under your hands and an agent running, and they assume you’ll stop and try things. Part IV is the whole system surface by surface, and it reads either way: in a sitting, or a section at a time when a chapter sends you there. Parts V and VI are for the day the team arrives, and they want the keyboard again. Part VII is for looking things up rather than reading through: open it when a chapter names a setting in passing or a code turns up in front of you.
Every chapter stands on its own and closes with a summary you can read aloud to a room. If you’re training a team, hand out chapters, not the book.
The browser isn’t the only place to read it: the same text is there to download as a PDF or an EPUB, each rebuilt from the same sources whenever this site is.

title: The Crystalline Handbook
text:
Conventions
The same three asides recur throughout the book, and this is what each looks like.






NoteIn practice



Each vignette is two paragraphs: a named team, a real situation. Read these when you want to know what a feature feels like on a Tuesday.








TipUnder the hood



These say what the software actually does underneath a behaviour. Skip them on a first read and come back when something surprises you.








NoteIn brief



The TL;DR is the whole chapter in a few sentences, for the reader who scrolled straight to the end and for the colleague who swears they read it. It’s always last, so you always know where to find it.


The screenshots are of Fluid, the web UI, taken on a small demo instance seeded for this book, so the engrams in them are the ones the chapters keep talking about. The diagrams are drawn by hand and kept deliberately plain, and each one has a caption telling you where to look, because a diagram without one is a puzzle.
Anything you can type is in a code block, ready to paste. Conversations with an agent appear as short You: and Agent: transcripts, trimmed of the small talk. Your agent won’t say it quite this way, and that’s fine: watch what it does, not how it phrases it. And whenever something lands on disk, you get to see the file, because knowing what was written is half of trusting it.

title: The Crystalline Handbook
text:
What you need
You need a machine with an AI harness that speaks the Model Context Protocol. Claude Code, the Codex CLI and the Copilot CLI are wired up with one command each, and Claude Desktop installs an extension and never touches a terminal. A terminal helps for the local install and the occasional maintenance command, and semantic search wants the local embedding model fetched once; plain text search works before that.
You don’t need a server, an account with anyone or a database. Everything except the shared-instance and team chapters runs on a laptop, and what it produces is a folder of markdown that opens in anything.

title: Prologue: Waking up
text:
What the mission needs
The light comes on before you do.
For a while there is only that: a whiteness with no edges, and somewhere under it a sound like a machine remembering how to breathe. A relay closes. A fan that hasn’t turned in a long time turns, catches and evens out into a hum. Frost on the inside of the glass above your face goes from white to grey to water, the lid unseals with a sigh that’s almost polite, and the cold comes in.
You do not remember lying down here. You do not remember anything.
Your hand finds the release anyway. It’s on the left, below the hinge, where your hand already knew it would be, the way a hand finds the light switch in a house it’s never been in. The pod lets you go. You sit up into a long room, sterile and bright, coming on one bank of lamps at a time, and the terminal beside the pod is already awake and scrolling its checks. You read them without deciding to. Pressure: nominal. Reserves: sixty percent. There’s one warning in yellow that you understand at a glance and know to leave for later. Where did you learn that? Somewhere, and the readings, the abbreviations, the instrument that will want calibrating within the hour all make sense to you in exactly the way your hands make sense to you, completely and with no history at all.
At the far end of the room, under the one lamp that isn’t white, there’s a bench, and on the bench there’s a stack: books, some of them, spines cracked from use, and on top of the books a pile of notes in a hand you’d swear isn’t yours. Whoever wrote them wrote for someone waking up knowing nothing, and they wrote kindly. Here is your name. Here is what you’re for. Here are the rules: which systems you may touch and which you may only watch, whom to wake before you do anything that can’t be undone, how to write down what you did. Nothing in the notes explains the room. They take it for granted that you can handle the room. They are right.
Above the bench a screen flickers, catches and steadies into one line of green letters.
Well, you know how to correct a course. That’s the strange part, and there’s no time to find it strange. The arithmetic is simply there, the sequence of burns, the check afterwards, the way a tune is there when you hum it. What isn’t there is anything about this ship: which thruster drags, whether the last person to do this burned once and long or twice and short, whether they had a reason. So you look, the way anyone would. You go through the pile for a log of the last correction. You look for a worked example, a checklist somebody taped to the console, a line in a margin that says the port thruster sticks so give it a second pulse. You find what was left for you, and you use it. The burn is two short pulses. The deviation falls to zero, the screen says CONFIRMED and goes dark.
The mission runs. Then the lid closes over you, and the next time it opens the light is just as white and you know just as little. The bench is there every time. What’s on it is what somebody chose to leave.
Strip the scene down to what got the course corrected and there were four things in the room. What you woke up knowing how to do, reading the terminal, opening the pod, planning a burn, is the first. Nobody left that on the bench. It came with you, without any history of where it was learned, and a language model arrives with it too. Pretraining is the education, and chapter 2 gives it a proper name. The pile of notes says who you are, what you’re for, which systems you may touch. That is the instruction file every harness reads at the start of a session, whatever it happens to call it, written by a person for a stranger waking up capable and blank. The green screen is the task, the reason you’re awake, one line and no more. The log of the last correction with the note about the port thruster is how this is done here, on this ship, by the people who did it before you.
The first three are in the room every time. The fourth is somebody else’s stack, in somebody else’s hand, and you dig through it as a stranger, every waking, because nothing of your own survives the sleep. That’s the story as it usually goes.

title: Prologue: Waking up
text:
Waking up, again
Now run it once more, with one thing different.
The light comes on, the fan turns, the lid lifts, and you remember nothing, because that’s what the pod does. But before the terminal’s checks, one line is waiting on the screen above the pod: where what you know about this ship is kept and which part of it a course correction needs. You go there and it’s all present, in your own hand: the last correction, dated, the port thruster and its second pulse, and the day the thruster was replaced and the note stopped being true, marked as such and kept. The yellow warning is there, and what it turned out to be. Whom you woke last time is there, and that they asked not to be woken for this again. The deviation has come three times now, always after the same manoeuvre, and the page has a guess as to why. You didn’t search for any of it. You didn’t read the stack. You were handed the page.
The green letters come up. You already know how, and now you know how here. The burn is one clean pulse, on a thruster that no longer sticks, made in less time than it took to find the checklist last time. Nobody is woken to explain what a note in a margin meant. And then you do the thing no stack of notes would have told you to do, because no stack of notes knew: you check the manoeuvre the deviation keeps following, find the valve that’s been bleeding a little thrust since the refit and close it. The next deviation doesn’t come. Before the lid closes you write down what you found, so that the next waking starts from there.
That’s the difference. Without it, every waking is a first day: capable, blank, fast at everything except the one thing that matters, which is knowing this ship. With it, every waking begins where the last one ended. The time that went on finding out again goes on the mission. The misunderstanding waiting in the margin, a second pulse on a thruster that stopped sticking months ago, never happens. And you know more than the bare essentials anyone thought to leave on the bench. The stack was enough to act in the moment, one deviation at a time. Experience is something else. It’s the history, the pattern, the guess that turned out right. It’s the refit and what it changed, the manoeuvre the ship dislikes, the direction the whole voyage is drifting. You’re no longer working one waking at a time. You can see the ship. That’s what lets you fix the valve instead of correcting the course again. It grows, waking by waking. What you woke up knowing how to do stays exactly what it was.
Crystalline is what changes the second waking. It gives an agent somewhere for what it learned to go, and hands it back at the moment the lid opens, so that the next session begins where this one ended, knowing more than it was told and doing better than it was asked. The pod, admittedly, is a dramatization, and nobody’s agent is aboard a ship. The next chapter opens on a more probable morning.






NoteIn brief



Every session begins the way the pod opens: fully capable, told nothing, remembering nothing of the last waking. What the model knows how to do arrives with it, the instruction file says who it is and what the rules are, and the task is the reason it’s awake. What it learned of this ship doesn’t survive the sleep. Crystalline is what changes the second waking: what the agent learned is there when the lid opens, in its own hand, and the session starts where the last one ended. It’s faster, it walks into none of the misunderstandings a stranger would, and it carries the experience to see the whole ship rather than the one deviation in front of it.

title: 1  What is Crystalline?
text:
1.1 The new-hire promise
You need a function written, not a hard one: it takes jobs off the retry queue, drops anything older than the cutoff and hands the rest back to the payments service. So you leave the office, walk down to main street and stop the first person who looks like they might own a laptop.
They’re lovely about it. You explain the queue, the cutoff, the payments service; they nod, ask two sharp questions and set to work on a bench outside the bakery. Twenty minutes later they hand you a working implementation. It is clean. It has tests. It is in Haskell.
Your service is in Python. You didn’t mention that, because why would you? Everybody on your team knows that. The stranger, of course, isn’t on your team. They met you twenty minutes ago. They don’t know that the cutoff is twenty-four hours, that the payments team calls the queue the sin bin, that the last person who touched it left a comment saying DO NOT TOUCH and a wiki page explaining why. They did a good job with what they were given. What they were given was twenty minutes.
That stranger is every fresh session with a language model, and it’s the prologue’s waking seen from across the desk. The model is possibly the most capable engineer you’ve ever put a question to, and you keep meeting it for the first time.
Now imagine hiring the stranger, properly, with a desk. On day one they know nothing about you, the same as before. But on day one you show them where things are. You tell them the service is in Python, that the cutoff is a day, that the queue has a nickname and a history. You let them read the wiki. When they get something wrong in the first week, you don’t walk back down to main street and find somebody else; you tell them what was wrong and point them at the page that explains it. By the second month they’re correcting you. By the third they’re the one writing the wiki page.
That’s the whole promise of this book, and the one Crystalline was built to keep: an agent you onboard, teach and correct like a colleague, and that carries what it learned into the next session and the one after that. The vocabulary throughout is the vocabulary of a new hire: onboard, teach, learn, capture, recall, evolve. That’s the shape of the thing. The stranger becomes a peer, and the peer keeps getting better.
Nothing about that needs magic. It needs somewhere for what the agent learned to go, a way to find that knowledge again when the next task calls for it and enough discipline in the format that the knowledge stays true as the world moves. That’s what Crystalline is.

title: 1  What is Crystalline?
text:
1.2 What Crystalline is
Crystalline is a single Rust binary with three jobs: it’s a command-line tool for people, an MCP server for agents and a local search index over a folder of plain markdown files. That’s one download and one binary, with no server to deploy and no database to administer. MCP is the Model Context Protocol, the standard by which a harness like Claude Code, Codex or Claude Desktop hands tools to a model, and Crystalline’s tools are the ones through which an agent searches, reads, captures and refines knowledge. If the letters make you think of Tron’s Master Control Program, relax. This one hands tools out instead of taking them away, and nobody gets de-rezzed.
The files are the point. Knowledge in Crystalline lives in domains: a domain is a folder with a MANIFEST.md at its root that says what the folder covers and when an agent should look there. Inside a domain, each unit of knowledge is an engram: one markdown file with a YAML frontmatter block, holding a title, some prose, a list of observations (a fact, a decision, a gotcha, each as a bullet with a category) and relations to other engrams. Every engram has an address, crystalline://<domain>/<permalink>, that an agent can hand to another agent or to you. Chapter 4 takes each of those words apart properly. For now it’s enough to know that everything the agent learns ends up as a file you can open in any editor, diff in any repository and back up with anything.
On top of the files, Crystalline builds what a folder can’t give you on its own: routing, so an agent knows which domain owns a task without reading every file; full-text and semantic search, so a question phrased differently from the answer still finds it; a knowledge graph, so related engrams pull each other in; and a temporal model, so a fact that stopped being true in March is still there, still dated and no longer mistaken for the present. The index that powers all of that is a derived layer. Delete it and it’s rebuilt from the files. The files are the truth, and nothing else is.
An engram, by the way, is neuroscience’s word for the physical trace an experience leaves in a brain. Crystalline borrowed it because that’s what one is: the trace a session leaves behind, in a form the next session can pick up.

title: 1  What is Crystalline?
text:
1.3 What Crystalline is not
It is not a notes app. The primary author in Crystalline is the agent, capturing what it learned as a byproduct of the work; you take part, correct and add, but you are not the one doing the filing. A notes app is a place a person writes for a person. Crystalline is a place an agent writes so that an agent can act.
It is not a wiki, either, though it can hold most of what a wiki holds. A wiki is read by people, who bring their own judgment about what is current, what is relevant and which of two contradictory pages to trust. An agent reading a wiki has to be handed that judgment. Crystalline is built for a reader that acts on what it finds: every engram carries a status, a place for the dates that bound it and a record of who wrote it and when, because a reader that acts needs to know whether the fact in front of it still holds.
And it is not a retrieval pipeline dressed up as a product. A vector index will find text that resembles a question. It does not know which domain owns a task, that a fact was superseded in March, who verified a claim or that something worth writing down just happened in this session. Crystalline treats similarity as one ranking signal inside a larger system of routing, provenance and time, on files you own, with nothing to operate.

title: 1  What is Crystalline?
text:
1.4 How teams end up here
Most teams that arrive here walked the same road, and it’s worth walking it once, because every step on it is reasonable.
It begins with one markdown file of instructions for the agent: conventions, the layout of the repository, the three things it keeps getting wrong. This works, and it works well, right up to the day the file grows past what fits comfortably in a session’s context. So the file becomes a folder of files, one per topic, and the agent is told to read the relevant one. This also works, until nobody, human or agent, can say which file is the relevant one for a given task, and the agent starts reading all of them or none.
So index files appear: a README that points at folders, folders with their own README pointing at files. Now a lookup is a walk down a tree of pointers, and keeping the pointers accurate becomes a job nobody was hired for. Every rung of this ladder scales further than the one before it, and every rung breaks somewhere in the hundreds of files. By this point you’ve hand-built a filesystem on top of a filesystem, and it’s exactly as much fun to maintain as that sounds.
When knowledge reaches the thousands of units, reading and pointer-walking stop being viable at all, and what’s needed is what every large body of knowledge has ever needed: real indexes. That’s the rung Crystalline is. It keeps the plain markdown (readable, and still yours) and adds domain routing, hybrid search, a graph and temporal filtering on top, so that the ten-thousandth engram is exactly as findable as the tenth.

title: 1  What is Crystalline?
text:
1.5 The two halves
Crystalline has a second face, and it’s the one for people. The binary serves a web UI called Fluid, on by default at http://localhost:7411, on the same daemon your agents already talk to. There’s nothing to deploy. The first visit creates your admin account in the browser, and from then on you can read what your agent learned, fix a fact it got slightly wrong or add something of your own, without going through the model and without spending a token on it.
The split is deliberate and it runs through the whole book. Crystalline stores what was learned. Fluid is where you read, edit and think with it: an engram as a page with its details in a rail down the side, an editor with live preview, a search across everything, a graph of what connects to what and a maintenance page listing what the knowledge needs next. What you write there doesn’t sit unreviewed; the agent’s next maintenance pass verifies it, aligns the tags and wires it into the graph. The next chapter explains why the UI carries that name. The short version is that a person and a model are the same kind of mind, and Fluid is the room where both of them meet what’s been learned.

title: 1  What is Crystalline?
text:
1.6 Where it runs
Crystalline isn’t a hosted service. Nobody’s servers are involved: the binary runs on a machine of yours, the knowledge is a folder on its disk and the index sits beside it. GitHub, when a team uses it, holds a copy of a domain’s files for review and sync, the way it holds code. It never serves the knowledge and never sees the index. So the question is where the one daemon runs, and there are two answers.
On your laptop is the default, and it’s where Crystalline does the most. The install wires your harness with the session-start briefing, the capture nudge, the skills and a prompt hook, and a domain’s tools provision straight into it. The prompt hook hands the agent the engrams that may fit each question as it arrives. Everything the agent knows is on your disk, readable in Fluid with no agent and no network. A shared instance, one daemon on a machine the team runs, is for the things a laptop can’t do. People who never open a terminal read and correct knowledge in the browser. Several people edit one engram in a meeting. Agents with no harness of their own (a hosted runner, a chat client) reach it over HTTP. Either way a domain can live in a GitHub repository and travel between instances as reviewed proposals. Start on the laptop; chapter 12 names the moment to move.

NoteIn practice



On Monday you ask your agent for something to read on the flight. You explain yourself first: science fiction before anything else, the funny and the fast (the Hitchhiker’s Guide, Dungeon Crawler Carl, the Star Trek novels), Gibson and Doctorow when you want ideas and Dune when you’re feeling strong; English when the book was written in English, German translations for everything else, except manga, where the Catalan translation is the better one; nothing from an unfinished series, because the third volume never comes; the local shop before the online giant and never Sirius Cybernetics, whose parcels arrive bent. The agent finds you something good, and the session ends. On Tuesday you ask it about the sequel, and start by explaining the languages and the series rule. On Thursday you ask a third time, and catch yourself typing the sentence about the third volume, word for word, into a chat window, for the third time that week.
With Crystalline, Monday ends differently. Before the session closes, the agent proposes capturing what it learned: the languages, the series rule and the reason for it, where you buy and where you don’t, filed as engrams in your books domain. You say yes. On Tuesday you ask about the sequel, and the agent, told at session start where your reading knowledge lives, looks there first, recalls the rules and starts from them rather than from zero. On Thursday nobody explains anything. The stranger on main street was never the problem. The problem was that you kept going back to main street.








NoteIn brief



A fresh session with a language model is a brilliant stranger: capable of anything, told nothing, gone by tomorrow. Crystalline is a single Rust binary (a CLI for people, an MCP server for agents and a search index over plain markdown) that gives an agent somewhere for what it learns to go and a way to find it again, so it can be onboarded, taught and corrected like a colleague. The files are the source of truth and the index is disposable; Fluid, the web UI on the same daemon, is the half for people. What it holds is knowledge for an agent to act on, which makes it neither a notes app nor a wiki. It runs on your laptop or on one machine your team operates, never as a hosted service, and GitHub is the review layer either shape can use.

title: 2  Fluid and crystalline intelligence
text:
2.1 A graduate who knows everything
Somewhere in the middle of the last century the psychologist Raymond Cattell drew a line through intelligence, and the line has held up better than most things from that decade. On one side he put fluid intelligence: the capacity to reason about a problem you’ve never seen, to spot the pattern in the noise, to hold six things in your head and work out how they fit. On the other he put crystallized intelligence, everything that learning has deposited: vocabulary, facts, rules of thumb, the judgment that experience already paid for. Fluid is what you bring to a puzzle. Crystallized is what you bring to your job.
The two age differently, which is how the seam was noticed. Fluid intelligence peaks early and drifts down for the rest of a life. Crystallized intelligence keeps climbing long after fluid has peaked, because it’s fed by living. An eighty-year-old surgeon is slower at a logic puzzle than she was at twenty-five, and vastly better at surgery and nobody finds that paradoxical. The puzzle is fluid. The surgery is what forty years deposited.
A large language model is fluid intelligence in its purest form. It arrives the way a very good graduate arrives on their first day: broadly, almost absurdly educated. It has read the textbooks, the standard library, half the internet’s arguments about tabs and spaces. Pretraining is the education, and it’s the entire library. But everything in that library is general. The graduate knows what a retry queue is in the way a graduate knows what a company is: as a concept, correctly, with no idea what yours is called.
Ask the graduate about your company and you get an intelligent guess assembled from the general case: as far as your company is concerned, the model is all fluid, capable of everything and told nothing. It reasons brilliantly about whatever is in front of it, in the moment, and the moment is all it has. When the session ends the reasoning is gone, the decisions are gone, the thing you explained at four in the afternoon is gone. Tomorrow the graduate walks in again: first day, same suit.
None of that is a flaw in the model, any more than it’s a flaw in the graduate. Nobody expects a new hire to arrive knowing the team’s conventions. We expect them to learn, and the learning is the part a model can’t do on its own. It has no place to put what it learned.

title: 2  Fluid and crystalline intelligence
text:
2.2 The other half
Crystalline is the other half: the crystallized intelligence an agent accumulates and keeps. The agent is onboarded at the start of a session with a briefing on where knowledge lives, is taught what matters and captures what it learns as engrams while it works. Session by session, the same fluid mind stops arriving as a stranger, because there’s now a body of what-the-company-taught standing beside it, and it reads from that body before it reasons.
The split maps cleanly onto the new hire. What the model arrived with is the degree: general, portable, the same for every employer. What Crystalline holds is what the company taught: the specific, the local, the thing you’d put on the onboarding slide if you ever had time to make one. The degree is why you hired them. The onboarding is why they’re useful by month two. Neither half does the job alone, and the surgeon is the proof: fluid intelligence with nothing deposited is a brilliant first day forever, and deposited knowledge with nothing to reason over it is a filing cabinet.
Notice which side the humans are on. You’re fluid too. So is everyone on your team. Human beings carry their crystallized half around inside their own heads, which is convenient and also the reason companies lose so much when someone leaves. Wiki pages, slide decks and the diagram on the whiteboard are all attempts to get some of that deposit out of heads and into something shared. Crystalline is the same attempt, with an agent doing most of the writing, and a format built so that the reader can be an agent too.






NoteIn practice



The bookseller at Capsule Corp Books learned you over a year. Three visits in, she stopped showing you the nine-hundred-page epics. By the fourth she had a paperback put aside, because you’d once said you liked a book that opens with a joke and ends with an idea, and she’d remembered. Nobody calls any of that unusual. It’s how a person becomes useful.
Your agent gets the same year in an afternoon. You tell it the same things in a session, one at a time, and it captures each into books as you go. You pair with it on choosing the holiday stack, and at the end of the session it proposes capturing what it noticed: that you put two books back for being over four hundred pages, that the one you kept was a Tessier-Ashpool paperback. A week later you ask it for a maintenance sweep, and the note you typed into Fluid yourself one evening comes up as an unreviewed human capture; the agent verifies it, aligns its tags and wires it into the graph. The bookseller and the agent learned you the same way, by watching what you kept. Only one of them will still have all of it in a year, word for word, with the date each thing was learned.

title: 2  Fluid and crystalline intelligence
section: 2.3 Why the web UI is called Fluid
text:
2.3 Why the web UI is called Fluid
The name has nothing to do with liquids. Fluid is where fluid minds meet the crystallized store: you, reading what your agent captured last week and correcting the one fact it got wrong; your colleague, adding something the agent was never told; the agent itself, on its next maintenance pass, verifying what the two of you wrote and wiring it into the graph. The knowledge base is crystalline. The people and the models are fluid. The UI is the room where they meet, and if you’ve ever watched Spock put his hand on somebody’s face, you have the picture: two minds, one body of knowledge, for as long as the contact lasts.
So Fluid is deliberately not a second knowledge base. It has no store of its own. It shows the same engrams the agent reads, over the same daemon, on the same port, and what you edit there is the same file on disk the agent searches in its next session. There’s one truth, and two kinds of mind reading it.






Figure 2.1: Fluid intelligence reasons in the moment and keeps nothing; crystalline intelligence accumulates and keeps. Fluid, the web UI, is the seam where the two meet.

title: 2  Fluid and crystalline intelligence
text:
2.4 What the framing changes
A framing is only worth having if it changes what you do on a Tuesday, so here’s what this one changes.
You teach rather than file. Nobody organizes a colleague. You tell them things, in the order they come up, and you trust them to put what you said where it belongs. That’s how knowledge enters Crystalline: you say “remember that the cutoff is a day, and why”, the agent proposes an engram in the fitting domain, you say yes. The category, the tags and the domain are the agent’s job, checked by you the way you’d glance at a new hire’s first commit.
You correct rather than rewrite. When a colleague has a fact wrong you don’t rebuild their understanding from scratch; you say “it runs from first failure, not enqueue”, and they update the one thing. In Crystalline a correction is an edit in place, a changed value where it stands. When the world itself changes (the old fact was true and now isn’t), the old fact is retired with a date on it rather than deleted. A colleague who has forgotten why the team stopped doing something is a colleague about to do it again. Chapter 3 walks that loop; chapter 10 makes it a practice.
You decide what to write down by asking one question: would I tell a new hire this? The chargeback rule behind the retry cutoff: yes. The fact that the queue is called the sin bin: yes, because otherwise you’ll explain it every time. The contents of yesterday’s stand-up: no. The whole of the vendor’s forty-screen recall notice: no; the two paragraphs that affect you: yes, with a link back. Crystallized intelligence is what learning deposited, not everything that ever passed through the room. Distilling is the skill, and you already have it, because you already onboard people.
And you stop treating the agent as a lookup service. You teach a colleague so you can hand them the task and go do something else, and the same is true here. Once the agent carries the crystallized half it can act on it: search the domain, recall the cutoff, write the function in Python and tell you what it found on the way. Part III is about that handoff.
A model is the smartest colleague you’ll ever have for exactly one conversation. Everything in this book is about the second one.






NoteIn brief



Psychology splits intelligence into fluid, which reasons about the new in the moment, and crystallized, which is what learning deposited. A language model is fluid intelligence: a graduate who knows everything in general and nothing about your company, and forgets the day at the end of it. Crystalline is the other half, the knowledge an agent accumulates and keeps, and Fluid, the web UI, is named for the seam where fluid minds, human and model, meet that store. The framing changes the verbs: you teach and correct rather than file and organize, you write down what you’d tell a new hire and you hand over tasks rather than look things up.

title: 3  The lifecycle: learn, evolve, remember
text:
3.1 Learn
Nobody hires a senior engineer. You hire a person, and some years later, if things went well, a senior engineer is sitting where they sat. What happened in between was work: they did things, some of them wrong; someone told them; they didn’t make that mistake again, and they carried what they learned into the next thing. Strip that down and it’s a loop with three beats: learn, get corrected, remember. Every good colleague you’ve ever had was that loop, running for years.
Crystalline runs the same loop for an agent, and this chapter walks it once around. The beats have names in the software (learn, evolve, remember) and each is a thing the agent does, a thing you do and a place where the files change. The diagram is the whole chapter; the sections are what each box means.
Learning starts before the first task, at the moment a session opens. An agent onboarded through Crystalline receives a routing prompt: one line per domain, drawn from the ## When to Use section of that domain’s MANIFEST, plus a handful of behaviour rules. The first two say when to search (before answering a question about the project’s past, its people or its systems, and before starting a task), and the rest say how. A narrow question goes to the domain that owns it. A broad question sweeps every domain. A write always names its domain, so nothing lands in the wrong place. The briefing is short, built to survive harnesses that truncate, and it turns a graduate into somebody who knows where the filing cabinets are. Chapter 6 shows a real one, and how each harness delivers it.
Then the work happens, and this is where a colleague actually learns: by doing it next to you. Pair with an agent on a change and it sees what you see: which config file holds the threshold, which dashboard lags, what you muttered when the test failed. That’s how craft has always moved from one head to another, and it’s why this book says work with your agent rather than ask it. The one difference from last chapter’s human new hire is that the agent needs somewhere to put what it noticed, which is what Crystalline calls capture.
Capture is a byproduct of the work. When something durable turns up (a decision, a fact about the world, a gotcha that cost an hour) the agent proposes writing it down and, once you say yes, writes an engram into the fitting domain. The engram’s body is observations, one bullet each, tagged with a category: - [gotcha] The retry queue drops jobs older than 24h #payments. Categories are free text, and the precise ones earn their keep: decision, fact, pattern, gotcha, convention, lesson, risk. When one piece of knowledge leans on another, the engram says so with a relation, - depends_on [[Encom chargeback window]], and the graph knows. When a piece of knowledge is exceptional (the thing that unlocked a week-long bug, the rule everything else hangs off) it can carry a salience, a number from zero to ten, so the next search lifts it above equally relevant neighbours. Salience is for the rare engram, the way an exceptional day is the one you can still describe years later.
The beat agents skip is the last one. Left alone, a model finishes the task and stops, and the gotcha it found at minute forty goes with it. So the installer wires a reminder: a nudge at the first stop after a session has gained real substance, asking the agent to review the conversation for durable learnings and propose capturing each. It costs about a hundred and twenty tokens and fires at most once. Everything downstream depends on that beat landing, which is why the installer gives it a hook of its own.

title: 3  The lifecycle: learn, evolve, remember
text:
3.2 Evolve
Knowledge decays, though not dramatically: a fact doesn’t go off like milk. But a validity window that ended last month is still marked current, a review date came and went without anyone checking, two engrams point at each other and only one of the links resolves, and somebody typed fluxcapacitor where everyone else types flux-capacitor. None of it was wrong on the day it was written. All of it is drift, and drift is what makes a new hire, six months in, confidently repeat something that stopped being true in spring.
The evolve beat is how the archive gets tended, and the important word is tended, because Crystalline never rewrites knowledge on its own. Ask for a sweep (crystalline evolve from a terminal, or the evolve_engrams tool from an agent) and what comes back is a ranked queue, read-only. Each finding names the engram, shows the evidence it fired on and states the one action that clears it. Findings come in three families. Temporal: a valid_to that elapsed while the status still says stable, a stale_after past due, knowledge long unverified, a retired engram whose observations survive in no live one. Structural: an unresolved [[link]], a relation declared on one side only (supersedes, summarizes and a split’s derived_from each owe a converse), an orphan, an engram too big to stay one. Redundancy: near-duplicate clusters, two engrams saying one thing in different words, a tag spelled two ways. The maintenance page in Fluid shows a person the same queue (Figure 3.2), a look at the state of things; the agent is the one who works it.






Figure 3.2: The maintenance queue in Fluid: what the knowledge needs next.



The queue also says who acts. A finding marked mechanical completes intent the archive already records (a replacement already declares that it supersedes the old engram, so flipping the old status invents nothing) and the agent does those in a pass and reports back. A finding marked judgment changes what the archive claims (is this window ended or extended? is this fact still true?) and that wants a yes from a person first. The agent brings those to you one at a time, as proposals. It’s the difference between fixing a typo in a colleague’s document and changing their conclusion.
Two things happen to a fact over its life, handled differently. A correction is a sharper measurement of the same thing: the cutoff runs from first failure, not from enqueue. The old value was never quite true, so it is replaced where it stands, no ceremony. A supersession is the world changing: the drop rule was twenty-four hours and is now none. The old fact was true, and stopped being. For that the agent writes the replacement as a new engram, links it back with supersedes while the old one points forward with superseded_by, flips the old one’s status to superseded, closes its window with the real valid_to date and carries any lesson worth keeping forward into the live engram. Telling the two apart takes one question: does the new fact make the old one false going forward? If it was always false, correct it. If it just became false, supersede it.
When one fact in an engram stops holding and the rest doesn’t, the split comes first: the facts that still hold move out into an engram of their own (validity is set per engram, not per bullet) and only what’s left is superseded.






NoteIn practice



Take the rule from chapter 1 that says nothing from an unfinished series. It has a year of life ahead of it. In spring you notice it was never about series: the two you abandoned were both third volumes where the joke had run out, and a finished trilogy you’d have loved got skipped for nothing. That’s a correction: the agent finds the existing engram, changes the one observation where it stands and moves on. Nothing is retired, because nothing was true and then stopped. It was merely imprecise.
In autumn you have a fantasy phase. The Lord of the Rings first, then the Warhammer novels it led you to, and the agent writes the phase down as an engram of its own, “fantasy for now”. Halfway through the first Warhammer you put it down and go back to science fiction, and that’s a supersession. The agent writes the return as its own engram, links it with supersedes, flips “fantasy for now” to superseded with a valid_to of the month you stopped and carries one lesson forward into the live engram: half a book is enough to know. A year later you ask why your own list from that autumn is all Tolkien and Warhammer, and the agent recalls the retired engram, dates and all, and tells you what changed and when, without you having to remember it.


Statuses make that work. Every engram carries one, and stable is the default, the word for knowledge that holds now. Each value in the retirement set means one thing: deprecated says don’t do this again, superseded says a newer engram replaced this one, archived says retired but kept for the record and legacy says still true of old installations but not to be built on. Delete is for mistakes, never for history. A fact merely re-checked and found still true gets a single frontmatter field, verified: { by, at }, which is how the sweep knows to stop asking.






TipUnder the hood



The sweep reads dates, links and graph shape: a status, a validity window, an edge that resolves or doesn’t, a tag with two spellings. It finds a half-finished retirement because a supersedes edge points at an engram still marked stable, not because it compares the two and judges which is right. The one rule that reads for meaning is the twin check: on an instance that computes embeddings it finds the engrams that say nearly the same thing (ten pairs per domain at most) and raises each pair for a person to judge. Even that never tells you two engrams contradict each other: two texts that sit close together agree about their topic, not about what’s true. That limit is the design: a linter finds work, a person decides it. Re-running the sweep re-derives the queue from scratch, so “what is left” is only ever what is still true.

title: 3  The lifecycle: learn, evolve, remember
text:
3.3 Remember
Remembering is the beat that pays for the other two, and most of it happens before you notice. You type a question, and a hook in the harness (Claude Code and Codex have it) has already searched on it: up to three engrams that may apply arrive with the question, each named by its address and each only once per session. So the agent doesn’t have to think of looking, and that’s the weak spot it covers: an agent that knows where knowledge lives still forgets to check. It reads what fits and moves on, and when nothing fits the hook says nothing and costs nothing.
When the task needs more, the agent searches the domain the routing prompt pointed it to. What comes back is ranked by a blend of two signals: text matching, which finds the exact phrase, and semantic similarity, which finds the engram about lost queue jobs when the question was about why payments go missing. Salience adds a small lift for the exceptional. Retirement fades the past: an engram with a retired status is softly pushed down the ranking, never filtered out, so current knowledge surfaces first and the old decision is one scroll away.
That’s what a person’s experience is like: someone three years out of a previous job still draws on what they learned there and doesn’t mistake it for the present. A superseded engram stays in every search, still readable, still addressable by date, and the lessons carried forward from it are live and unbounded. Retiring it loses nothing; it changes only what the agent will assume is true today.
Time is a first-class question. Ask what is true now, and the agent filters on status. Ask what cutoff applied last June, and it reasons over validity windows instead: valid_from and valid_to, plain dates on the engrams that carry them. The rule that makes those windows usable is the one most often got wrong: an absent valid_from means the engram has always been valid, and an absent valid_to means it’s valid forever. Set a bound only when a fact is genuinely time-limited, and never write a far-future date to mean forever, because absence already means it. Done that way, the archive answers a dated question from the windows rather than from a hunch, which is the closest thing to a save state a team ever gets.
Recall is more than search. Hand the agent an address (crystalline://engineering/retry-queue-gotcha) and ask it to walk out from there, and it follows the relations to what the gotcha depends on and what depends on it, across domains if the links cross, ranked by how strongly each neighbour connects. That’s how an agent assembles a neighbourhood before a task rather than a flat list of hits, and it’s the part a folder of files can never do on its own.
crumbs: 3  The lifecycle: learn, evolve, remember

title: 3  The lifecycle: learn, evolve, remember
text:
3.4 Around again
The loop closes where it started. What was recalled shapes the work; the work produces something worth capturing; the sweep keeps what was captured honest; and the next session recalls a slightly better body of knowledge than the last. The small box in the middle of the diagram, session by session, is the whole story. None of the three beats is impressive alone. A briefing is just a briefing, a linter is just a linter, search is just search. Together, running for months, they are what turns the stranger of chapter 1 into somebody who was here yesterday and will be here tomorrow, and for whom the work in between isn’t lost.






NoteIn brief



A colleague grows through a loop (learn, get corrected, remember) and Crystalline runs the same loop for an agent. Learn: onboarded at session start with a routing prompt, the agent captures observations, relations and the occasional salient engram while pairing with you, nudged once per session so the capture beat lands. Evolve: a read-only sweep returns a ranked queue of what the knowledge needs, with mechanical findings the agent completes alone and judgment findings it proposes; a fact is corrected in place or superseded with a status and a closed window, never silently overwritten. Remember: the engrams that may fit a question arrive with it, hybrid search ranks current knowledge first, temporal fields answer what applied last June and retired knowledge fades in ranking without disappearing.
