title: 4  Terminology
text:
4.1 Domains
Every word in this book has a file behind it. That’s the pleasant thing about Crystalline’s vocabulary: a domain is a folder you can list, an engram is a file you can print, an address is a string you can paste and a status is a line in that file you can change with whatever editor you already own. So this chapter doesn’t open with a table. It opens one engram, the retry-queue gotcha the screenshots in this book keep returning to, and reads it from the top, stopping at each term as it comes up. By the end you’ll have met every word the rest of the book leans on, and seen each one on disk.
Start with where the file lives: ~/knowledge/engineering/retry-queue-gotcha.md. The folder is a domain. A domain is a registered folder of knowledge with a MANIFEST.md at its root, and the manifest is what makes it more than a folder. It says what the domain covers and when an agent should look there, and those bullets are what the routing prompt is built from at the start of every session. Registering is one command, crystalline domain add engineering ~/knowledge/engineering, and the name you give it there is the name the agent uses from then on. Say your team has two domains: engineering for the payments service and everything around it, clients for the people it sells to. The line between them is who could vouch for a change (the engineers for one, the people who sell for the other), and chapter 13 makes that the rule for a shared domain. A domain can also be virtual, living in the database with no folder at all; it carries the same manifest and answers to the same tools.
Inside a domain, subfolders are topic prefixes. A singleton engram stays at the root; once a cluster forms, it gets a folder, and the folder becomes part of the engram’s address. The manifest’s ## Notes for Agents section is where the team writes down what it decided.

title: 4  Terminology
text:
4.2 Engrams
Below is the file itself, as it sits on disk, and everything in the rest of the chapter is a line of it:
---
type: engram
title: Retry queue gotcha
permalink: retry-queue-gotcha
tags:
- gotcha
- payments
status: stable
recorded_at: 2026-03-09
generated: { by: claude-code/2.1.233, at: 2026-03-09T16:42:10+00:00 }
---

The retry queue drops any job older than twenty-four hours instead of
retrying it. The team calls the queue the sin bin. The cutoff is not a
tuning choice: it mirrors the chargeback window at Encom, the bank
behind the card payments.

- [gotcha] The retry queue drops jobs older than 24h #payments
- [fact] The 24h cutoff mirrors Encom's chargeback window #payments
- depends_on [[Encom chargeback window]]
An engram is one markdown file holding one unit of knowledge, with a YAML frontmatter block on top. If the word sounds like something from a starship’s sickbay, that’s because Star Trek borrowed it from the same neuroscience textbook Crystalline did.






Figure 4.1: The anatomy of an engram: frontmatter, prose, an observation and a relation.



The frontmatter is identity and state. type says what kind of thing this is: engram by default, with guide, decision, architecture, runbook and reference as the recommended alternatives. title is the human name and the thing other engrams link to. permalink is derived from the title and is the half of the address that links point at; when the engram moves to another folder, the permalink moves with it unless somebody chose it by hand. tags are what a search or a filter narrows on. status says whether the knowledge holds, and it gets its own section below. recorded_at is the day it was captured; generated records who wrote it and when, and for an agent also which model. When the knowledge is time-bounded, valid_from and valid_to sit here too; this engram has neither, which means it has always held and holds until further notice. Both type and status are required and free form; the recommended values are guidance, never an enumeration a write is rejected for.
Then comes the prose, the explanation a colleague would give across a desk: what the thing is, what it’s called and why it is the way it is. The prose is what search matches on and what a reader reads first.
Then come the observations. A top-level bullet of the form - [category] text #tag is an observation, and observations are the atomic unit of an engram’s body: the fact, the decision, the gotcha, each indexed on its own line so a search hit can point at it. The category in brackets is free text, and the precise ones earn their keep: decision, fact, pattern, gotcha, convention, lesson, risk, idea. A trailing #tag attaches the tag to that observation.
Then comes the relation. A top-level bullet of the form - rel_type [[Target]] is an edge in the knowledge graph, typed by whatever word comes first: depends_on here, supersedes and superseded_by in chapter 3, derived_from and split_into between the two halves of a split, relates_to when nothing sharper fits or a quoted phrase for a multi-word type. The target is a title (resolved within the domain) or [[domain:Title]] across domains. The target’s page shows the edge back as a backlink, and a target that doesn’t exist yet is an unresolved link the sweep will mention.
One topic per engram is the rule that keeps all of this legible. When the topic grows, the engram is edited, not forked; when it splits, it splits by granularity or by validity. A large capture splits by granularity, a distilled summary beside a source engram holding the full text, linked both ways. An engram that bundles facts with different lifetimes splits by validity. Validity is set per engram, so when one fact expires while the rest holds, the still-valid observations move into an engram of their own first. The new engram carries the source’s tags and type, a stable status and no validity window, and points back with derived_from; the old one keeps what expired, points forward with split_into and retires.

title: 4  Terminology
text:
4.3 The open format underneath
None of that is a private format. The engram extends Google’s Open Knowledge Format, OKF, version 0.2: plain markdown with YAML frontmatter, readable by any OKF tooling, with Crystalline’s routing, temporal and graph conventions layered on top. Unknown frontmatter keys survive every write and edit, so an OKF document from somewhere else drops into a domain intact and comes back out intact. The generated block is the provenance record, and the index.md Crystalline writes at a domain’s root declares the format version for anything that browses the folder without Crystalline running. Your knowledge stays files in a folder that any editor opens and any diff tool diffs, whatever tools come next.

title: 4  Terminology
text:
4.4 Statuses
status is the field a reader that acts on knowledge needs most, because it answers the one question a page can’t answer about itself: does this still hold? stable is the default and the word for knowledge that holds now; the older spelling current means the same state, and a filter on either finds both. Before stability there are draft, proposed, idea and poc, for knowledge that’s on its way. implemented is on the recommended list too, and like any status outside the retirement set it ranks at full strength.
After stability there is the retirement set, four words that each mean one thing. deprecated says don’t do this again. superseded says a newer engram replaced this one, and the two are linked. archived says retired but kept for the record. legacy says still true of the old installation that’s somehow still running, like the terminals aboard the Nostromo, but not to be built on. A status in the retirement set fades the engram in search ranking, gently and never to zero, so current knowledge surfaces first and the past stays one scroll away, dated. Retiring is how a fact leaves the present without leaving the archive; deleting is for mistakes.

title: 4  Terminology
text:
4.5 Salience
Most engrams are ordinary, and that’s fine. A few are the ones everything else hangs from: the rule that explains a dozen other rules, the insight that ended a week-long bug. Those can carry a salience, a number from zero to ten in the frontmatter, and hybrid search adds a small, bounded lift for it, so a salient engram ranks above equally relevant neighbours while relevance keeps the upper hand and nothing is ever filtered out by it. It’s set sparingly at capture time, and raised later when an engram turns out to have been what a task hinged on. The retry-queue engram carries none, and most never will.

title: 4  Terminology
text:
4.6 Addresses
Every engram has an address, crystalline://engineering/retry-queue-gotcha: the scheme, the domain, the permalink. It’s the one absolute form. An agent hands it to another agent, build_context anchors on it, Fluid copies it to the clipboard in one click. It survives a commit message, a ticket or a chat. A folder prefix appears in the permalink (crystalline://engineering/queues/retry-queue-gotcha if the engram had been filed under queues/), and a trailing /* anchors the whole folder at once.
The rule that trips people up is the scheme-less one. An identifier without crystalline:// is domain-relative: retry-queue-gotcha, together with the domain named beside it, never engineering/retry-queue-gotcha, which would be read as a folder called engineering inside whatever domain you meant. The same holds for links: [[Retry queue gotcha]] resolves in the domain the linking engram lives in, and [[engineering:Retry queue gotcha]] reaches across. Either the address is absolute and carries its domain, or it’s relative and the domain comes from context. There’s no third form, and that strictness is what lets a permalink stay short.

title: 4  Terminology
text:
4.7 The MANIFEST, up close
The last term is the first file in every domain. MANIFEST.md is an engram of type: manifest with the permalink manifest, which means it’s read, indexed and edited with the same tools as everything else. Its job is routing, and two sections do it. ## Scope says what the domain covers. ## When to Use says when an agent should route a task here, and those bullets, one line per domain, are what become the session-start briefing. ## Notes for Agents, the third section the scaffold creates, holds the conventions the agent should follow inside this domain, the folder layout above all. Two optional sections come later. ## Tag Aliases folds an old tag name into its canonical one so old searches keep working. ## Provisioning names the folders of skills, slash commands, subagent definitions and MCP server configs a domain ships beside its knowledge. The tools that knowledge depends on travel with it, and install into a harness once a person says yes. That section gets a chapter of its own (Chapter 15). You don’t have to keep all of this in your head: the domain’s page in Fluid lays the manifest out section by section, with an example for every section still missing, and an edit that breaks routing says so as soon as it lands. An engineering manifest, a few months in:
---
type: manifest
title: engineering
permalink: manifest
tags:
  - manifest
status: stable
recorded_at: 2026-03-02
---

# engineering

## Scope

- The payments service, its retry queue and the services around it
- Deploy runbooks, team conventions and the decisions behind them

## When to Use

- Route questions about the payments service, the retry queue or a deploy here
- Check here before touching anything the team has already been burned by

## Notes for Agents

- Runbooks live under runbooks/, gotchas at the root
- One engram per gotcha; edit the existing one before writing a second
Write the When to Use bullets the way you’d brief a new hire on which drawer holds what. A machine reads them, but it reads them the way a person reads a label.






TipUnder the hood



The manifest being an engram is why routing needs no separate configuration: crystalline prompt system parses each registered domain’s MANIFEST.md, takes the ## When to Use bullets, or ## Scope when there are none, and emits one routing line per domain plus the behaviour rules. Two filenames in a domain are reserved and never engrams. index.md is the table of contents Crystalline regenerates after every write so the folder navigates itself without Crystalline running. Each machine builds its own, and a team share leaves it out unless the MANIFEST asks for it; log.md is reserved but never generated. A title that would slug to either is refused.








NoteIn practice



Say your books domain is a year old and you start a second one, shops, because where to buy is a different kind of knowledge from what to read: which shop orders from small presses, which one delivers by Friday if you ask on Monday, which one never again. Your first engram there is about Capsule Corp Books, and it needs to say that the paperback rule in books (wait for the Tessier-Ashpool paperback, the hardbacks fall apart) is why you order there. You type - relates_to [[Wait for the paperback]], and the sweep tells you the link doesn’t resolve, because shops has no engram by that title. You change it to [[books:Wait for the paperback]] and the edge appears, with a backlink on the books side that nobody had to write.
A week later a friend asks what to read and where to get it, and instead of typing the answer out you hand your agent the address, crystalline://shops/capsule-corp-books, and ask what you’d tell her. It picks up the address, walks one hop into books and comes back with the paperback rule, the small press and the two authors you’d tell anyone about. That’s two domains and one edge, and the string is still readable in a year.


You now speak the language. The rest of the book is conversation.






NoteIn brief



A domain is a registered folder with a MANIFEST.md whose When to Use bullets route an agent to it; an engram is one markdown file with YAML frontmatter, prose, observations of the form - [category] text #tag and relations of the form - rel_type [[Target]], all on Google’s Open Knowledge Format so nothing is locked in. status says whether knowledge holds: stable is the default, and deprecated, superseded, archived and legacy are the retirement set that fades in ranking without disappearing; salience is a rare, bounded lift. The absolute address is crystalline://domain/permalink, and anything without the scheme is domain-relative. The manifest is itself an engram, which is why routing needs no configuration of its own.

title: 5  Installing locally
text:
5.1 Install the binary
Everything in this chapter fits in one sitting, and the sitting ends with a test: you’ll ask your agent about something it learned an hour earlier, in a session that has never heard of it, and it will answer. Until that happens nothing is installed, whatever the package manager says. So the chapter is built backwards from that moment. Install the binary, wire the harness, give the agent a domain: three steps, the same three on every platform, and then the test.
If you skipped chapter 4, two words carry the chapter, and everything below makes one of each: a domain is a registered folder with a MANIFEST.md that says when an agent should look there (Section 4.1), and an engram is one markdown file of knowledge inside it (Section 4.2).
Crystalline is one binary, and it gets onto a machine the way that machine usually gets things.
Debian, Ubuntu and their relatives get a .deb for amd64 and arm64 from the releases page. It ships a systemd unit, installed disabled (chapter 12 turns it on). Windows gets an MSI that adds Crystalline to the PATH and upgrades in place. The Windows builds aren’t code signed yet, so expect a SmartScreen prompt and check the download against the SHA256SUMS file beside it. The bare binary ships for every platform too, and the macOS builds are signed and notarized. The permanent address for all of it is on the colophon page: https://github.com/jordiboehme/crystalline/releases/latest.
Claude Desktop is the pleasant exception: no binary, no terminal. Download crystalline-v<version>.mcpb from the same page, one universal bundle for Apple Silicon Macs and Windows, with per-arch bundles for Intel Macs, then in Claude Desktop open Settings > Extensions > Advanced settings > Install Extension… and pick the file. Upgrading is the same motion (Desktop has no in-app update for an extension): download the newer .mcpb and install it over the current one. Desktop users can skip the terminal parts of what follows: the agent creates its first domain itself.

title: 5  Installing locally
text:
TipUnder the hood



On a Mac with Homebrew the whole install is one line:
brew install jordiboehme/tap/crystalline

title: 5  Installing locally
text:
5.2 First run
Nothing needs starting: the first agent that connects starts a background daemon (the one process that holds the index open), and every later agent, terminal and browser tab attaches to it. The one exception is the daemon Claude Desktop’s extension starts: it stays tied to Desktop and exits five seconds after its last client disconnects, so on a machine with only Desktop, Fluid is there while Desktop is open. crystalline serve runs the same daemon in the foreground if you want to watch it, and crystalline serve --daemon in the background, but on a laptop most people never type either.
What you’ll type into is a browser: the daemon serves Fluid at http://localhost:7411 by default, however it was started. The first visit to an instance with no accounts yet is a short form, not a login page: pick a name and a password and you’re that instance’s admin, already signed in (Figure 5.1). You’re trusted to fill that form in because you’re on the machine: a connection from the machine itself needs no token, and a bind anyone else could reach gets a different treatment in chapter 12. Once any account exists the form is gone for good.






Figure 5.1: First visit: creating the admin account in the browser.



Semantic search wants one more download, the local embedding model (about 220 MB): the daemon fetches it in the background on its first start, and crystalline model download fetches it ahead of time. Until then search is plain text, which works, and finds only the words you searched for.

title: 5  Installing locally
text:
5.3 Onboarding a harness
This is the step that turns a binary into a colleague, and it’s one command per harness. Every part of what that command does is something a new hire gets on day one. It registers the MCP server with the harness, so the agent has the tools. It writes three hooks. A session-start hook delivers the briefing on a fresh start, after a /clear and after a compaction. A stop hook is the once-per-session nudge from chapter 3 that asks the agent to capture what it learned before the session ends. A prompt hook hands the agent up to three engrams that may fit each prompt, named by address and each once per session (Claude Code and Codex use it; Copilot gets the entry and stays quiet for now). It also copies the four skills into the harness’s skills folder, the playbook that says when to use which tool. Run it twice and the second run touches nothing.
Look at the briefing once with your own eyes: it’s the whole of what your agent knows about you at the start of a session. crystalline prompt system prints it (Figure 5.2): an intro, the behaviour rules and one line per registered domain, drawn from the ## When to Use bullets of that domain’s manifest. The rules open with when to search (before answering a question about the project’s past and before starting a task) and then say how: a narrow question goes to the domain that owns it, a broad one sweeps all of them and a write always names its domain. On a fresh install the domain lines are empty, and that’s correct: the desk is set up and nobody has shown the new hire the filing cabinets yet.
Claude Desktop runs no hooks and needs none: its server delivers the same routing block as part of the MCP server’s instructions on every connection, and the optional companion skill from the releases page, uploaded under Settings > Capabilities > Skills, adds the capture and collaboration playbook on top. A chat client with no hooks that never shows the model a server’s instructions gets a standing instruction instead: crystalline prompt connector prints the paragraph to paste into its custom instructions, and the agent fetches its own onboarding with one list_domains call at the start of every session.
Install a second harness and you’ve added a door, not a second colleague. Claude Code in a terminal, Codex, the Copilot CLI and Claude Desktop each spawn the same crystalline mcp over stdio. The first of them to connect starts the one daemon the rest attach to, so every one of them sees the same domains, the same index and the same briefing. Tell Desktop something over lunch and the terminal session knows it in the afternoon, with nothing copied and nothing configured twice. The one way to end up with a second colleague is a version gap: a Desktop bundle older than a binary Homebrew has since upgraded can neither reach that daemon nor take the index from it. The same happens when no daemon runs and a newer version has already upgraded the index: the old bundle refuses it rather than work on it. Instead of failing, it comes up degraded, with a single status tool whose instructions say to download the newer .mcpb and install it over the old one. Do that, and the door is open again; from then on, upgrade the extension together with the CLI.






Figure 5.2: The routing prompt an agent receives at session start.









TipUnder the hood



Claude Code takes one command:
crystalline install claude-code
Codex takes crystalline install codex and the Copilot CLI crystalline install copilot. The MCP server it registers is crystalline mcp --harness claude-code. --skip-mcp, --skip-hooks and --skip-skills leave a part out, --project writes into the current repository’s config instead of your global one, and crystalline uninstall claude-code reverses the lot while leaving anything that isn’t Crystalline’s own alone.
The install is recorded in a local receipt, and the receipt is what keeps a harness current: the first time a newer Crystalline runs, it refreshes the installed hooks and skills at session start (that’s how an older install picks up the prompt hook), updating changed skills (an edited copy is kept beside the new one as SKILL.md.bak) and removing any the new version no longer ships. The --harness flag in the MCP registration is the other half of the same idea. A crystalline mcp process started with it asks the receipt whether that harness has its hooks wired, and if so serves that session neither the skills over MCP nor a second copy of the routing block, since the harness already has both as files. Nothing in that decision comes from the connecting client: it’s settled before the session opens. A registration written by hand without the flag, or a remote client, is served the full surface, and skills.serve set explicitly to true or false makes every client identical.

title: 5  Installing locally
section: 5.4 The first domain and the first engram
text:
5.4 The first domain and the first engram
Now the filing cabinet. Before an agent can keep anything it needs a domain, and this section runs the whole loop in miniature: the domain is scaffolded and registered, one fact is written into it as an engram, and a question phrased nothing like the fact gets that fact back. The last one is the semantic ranking at work, on a model the daemon fetched in the background when it started.
Where that folder lives is up to you, and it doesn’t have to be where any other domain is: a domain is registered by its own path, and nothing ties one registration to the next. engineering can sit in a git checkout under ~/knowledge, reading under Documents where the agent put it, a third on a NAS mount that is already backed up. All three are served by the one daemon and named in the same briefing. Documents/Crystalline is only the default for a domain an agent creates when nobody names a path, and the domains_root setting moves that default without moving anything already registered. A network share changes two things. First, the index stays in the local state directory, and should: it’s a database, and a database on a share is how people learn about file locking the hard way. The share holds the markdown and nothing else. Second, the daemon’s file watcher hears the machine it runs on, not the network, so an engram written into that folder from another computer shows up at the next crystalline sync or the next daemon start, not the moment it lands. Written through Crystalline from any harness on this machine, it’s indexed as it lands, share or no share.
Open the manifest before you go any further and make sure the ## Scope and ## When to Use sections say what you would say, because those bullets are the one line your agent reads about this domain at the start of every session. Write them the way you’d label a drawer for a new hire: “route questions about the payments service, the retry queue or a deploy here”. The agent drafts them from what you say, and you check them once.
It takes three prompts and no terminal:
You:    Set up a Crystalline domain called engineering in
        ~/knowledge/engineering. Its scope is the payments service:
        route questions about the payments service, the retry queue
        or a deploy there.
Agent:  Created and registered engineering. The manifest's Scope and
        When to Use sections carry what you just said, so your next
        session will see the domain in its briefing.

You:    Remember in engineering: the retry queue drops jobs older
        than 24 hours. It is a gotcha, tagged payments.
Agent:  Captured "Retry queue gotcha" in engineering, at
        ~/knowledge/engineering/retry-queue-gotcha.md.

You:    Why does the payments queue lose jobs?
Agent:  The retry queue drops jobs older than 24 hours, from
        "Retry queue gotcha" in engineering.
A Desktop user’s path is exactly this, and it works even without the first prompt: an agent that finds nowhere to write creates a domain itself under Documents/Crystalline, and the first engram lands there. Open the manifest afterwards and make sure the two sections say what you’d say.






TipUnder the hood



The first prompt was three commands, the same three the manual’s terminal setup page starts with. domain init scaffolds the folder with a starter manifest and domain add registers it under the name the agent will use and indexes what is already there (there’s no separate sync step). The agent did the same through its own tools: add_domain to scaffold and register, then edit_engram on the manifest.
mkdir -p ~/knowledge/engineering
crystalline domain init ~/knowledge/engineering --name engineering
crystalline domain add engineering ~/knowledge/engineering
The second prompt was one command (the agent’s was one write_engram call), and running it by hand shows the file appear in the folder, retry-queue-gotcha.md, the file chapter 4 read line by line:
crystalline write engineering "Retry queue gotcha" \
  --content "- [gotcha] The retry queue drops jobs older than 24h #payments" \
  --tags gotcha,payments
The third prompt was a search, and crystalline search "retry queue" finds it as a plain text hit. On a machine where no daemon has fetched the model yet, fetch it, re-sync with embeddings and ask something the engram never says:
crystalline model download
crystalline sync --embed
crystalline search "why does the payments queue lose jobs"
crystalline sync is for files that arrive some other way (an editor, a git pull) when no daemon was watching, and crystalline status shows what got indexed.

title: 5  Installing locally
text:
5.5 Verifying the loop
Now the test. Start a session in your harness and ask about the retry queue without explaining anything. Watch what the agent does before it answers, because that’s the recall beat and it proves the wiring. In Claude Code or Codex the question arrives with the gotcha already attached by its address, and the agent reads it. Elsewhere it searches engineering, because the briefing told it that’s where the payments knowledge lives. Either way it answers from the engram, with the address in hand if you ask for it.
What that doesn’t prove yet is the capture beat, the one that matters over months. Tell the agent something it couldn’t have known, the way you did on chapter 1’s Monday:
You:    The cutoff is 24 hours because Encom's chargeback window is
        three days - the queue needs two days to notice a job. Remember
        that, and why.
Agent:  Captured: added the chargeback window as the reason to
        "Retry queue gotcha" in engineering, with a depends_on relation
        to a new "Encom chargeback window" engram. Want me to adjust
        the wording?
Close the session, open a new one (it has never heard of Encom) and ask why the cutoff is a day. If the answer names the chargeback window, you’re done: the agent looked something up that it learned in a conversation that no longer exists. It’s a Voight-Kampff test run in reverse: you’re not checking whether the thing across the desk is a replicant, you’re checking that it remembers.
Once the test passes, close the terminal. Nothing in daily use needs it: the agent recalls and captures through its tools, the daemon starts itself and the one place you’ll go on purpose is the browser tab. The commands in this chapter were the installation, and from here on what you type is addressed to a colleague.






TipUnder the hood



When it fails the fix is usually quick. If the agent answered from general knowledge, with no engram attached and no search, the session didn’t get the briefing: run crystalline prompt system yourself and check that engineering has a line (if it has none, the manifest’s ## When to Use section is empty). If the agent recalled the gotcha but not the reason, the capture never landed: look in ~/knowledge/engineering for the file and check that you said yes when it proposed writing. If nothing arrived with the question in Claude Code or Codex, check two things: the prompt hook stays quiet until the embedding model has loaded, and crystalline doctor says whether the hook is installed.








NoteIn practice



Your first afternoon is the five lines above. You run the brew line and the install line, domain init a books folder, and your agent’s first session opens with a briefing that names it and nothing else, because nothing has been taught yet. You tell it the series rule, the two shops and the press whose paperbacks you wait for, to see what happens, and close the session. In the next one you ask what to read, and it starts from your rules. In chapter 2 the bookseller took a year to learn you; the agent took a session. By Wednesday you have three doors open: Claude Code in the terminal, the Copilot CLI in a second terminal and Claude Desktop for the thinking you do away from the keyboard. Two crystalline install lines and one Desktop extension were the setup, and the daemon behind all three is the one that started that first afternoon. What you tell Desktop on Tuesday evening about the manga translations is what Copilot recalls on Wednesday morning, from the same file in the same folder, and nothing was copied between them.
Your sister, who has never opened a terminal on purpose, installs the Desktop extension the same week. She has no domains, and her agent makes one the first time it needs somewhere to write, a reading folder under Documents/Crystalline. By Friday it holds four engrams about the Dungeon Crawler Carl books she’s lining up for the holiday, and she opens localhost:7411 to read them while Desktop is running. Two installs, one with a keyboard and one without, and the same loop runs on both.


The desk is set up, the drawers are labelled and the new hire has remembered one thing overnight. Everything after this is a matter of what you choose to teach.






NoteIn brief



Installing is three steps on every platform: install the binary (Homebrew, a .deb, an MSI or the Claude Desktop .mcpb, which skips the terminal and upgrades by installing the newer bundle over the old), wire the harness with crystalline install <harness> and give the agent a domain with domain init and domain add. The install writes the MCP registration, the session-start hook that delivers the briefing, the stop hook that nudges capture, the prompt hook that brings matching engrams with each question and the four skills, and it’s safe to run again. Nothing needs starting: the first agent to connect starts the daemon, which serves Fluid at localhost:7411, where the first visit creates the admin account. Every harness on the machine shares that daemon, and a domain is registered by its own path. The install is finished when a fresh session recalls something a previous one learned.

title: 6  Onboarding an agent
text:
6.1 The briefing at session start
On a new colleague’s first morning somebody hands them the floor plan. Payments is on the second floor, the people who know about the bank sit by the window, the runbooks are in the cupboard that sticks. Which door leads where is the whole of day one, and it’s enough, because a person who knows where things are can find out everything else themselves.
That floor plan is what an agent receives at the start of every session with Crystalline. This chapter is about the day it arrives: what the briefing says, how the agent finds its way with it, what it means to hand a colleague a task instead of a question, and the reminder at the end of the day that turns a session into experience. Chapter 5 showed the wiring. This is what the wiring is for.
A session opens, and before the agent has read a word of your request, the session-start hook runs crystalline prompt system and puts its output in front of the model. Here is one a few months in, abridged:
Read it as the agent reads it. The opening says what this is and whose tools it governs, so an agent with four MCP servers connected knows which search_engrams is meant. Then there’s one line per domain, and every word of those lines came from a person: they’re the ## When to Use bullets of each manifest, joined with semicolons, exactly as the team wrote them (Section 4.1). On your own machine that’s every domain registered, since the CLI and a stdio session are the machine owner. On a shared instance the agent connects as an account, and the block lists every domain that account may see: a private domain it’s no member of is absent from the block, from list_domains and from every search, answered as if nobody had registered it (Chapter 14). Then come the behaviour rules, the same on every instance: the first two say when to search (before answering a question about the project’s past, its people or its systems, and before starting a task) and the rest name the exact tool each one reaches for. That’s the floor plan (Figure 6.1). It says where things are, nothing about what’s in them, and the agent goes and looks.

title: 6  Onboarding an agent
text:
CRYSTALLINE KNOWLEDGE ROUTING

You are being onboarded to the knowledge accumulated in this workspace.
It is served by the crystalline MCP server; these instructions govern
its tools. [...]

- engineering: Route questions about the payments service, the retry
  queue or a deploy here; Check here before touching anything the team
  has already been burned by
- clients: Route anything about a customer, a contract or a renewal
  here; Check here before preparing for a customer meeting
[...]

Behavior:
- Search before you answer: a question about this project's past
  decisions, its people, its systems or a name you do not recognise is
  answered from search_engrams first, never from memory or a guess.
- Search before you start: a task begins with search_engrams on its
  subject, so what an earlier session learned shapes the work instead
  of being rediscovered after the fact.
- Narrow question: search_engrams with domains=[that domain]; broad or
  unclear: no domains sweeps them all.
[...]
- Read a MANIFEST with read_engram only when the routing line is not
  enough; list_domains with include_routing=true re-fetches the index
  mid-session.







Figure 6.1: The same block unabridged, as crystalline prompt system prints it.









TipUnder the hood



How it reaches the desk depends on the harness, as chapter 5 said. Claude Code and Codex run the hook on a fresh start, after a /clear and after a compaction, and skip a resumed session; the Copilot CLI’s hook does the same on a fresh start and stays quiet on a resume; Claude Desktop gets the block inside the MCP server’s own instructions; a remote client fetches it with one list_domains call. Either way the agent starts out knowing which drawer holds what and nothing more, the state a good new hire is in at nine on Monday.
The block is built to survive being cut off. A harness in tool-search mode truncates a server’s instructions at roughly two kilobytes, so the MCP rendering keeps under a 1900-byte budget and degrades in fixed steps: every routing line drops to one bullet, then the list collapses to a count line pointing at the re-fetch call.
A remote client gets that count line on arrival whatever the block’s size. The MCP initialize handshake is answered before any request is in hand, so over HTTP there’s nobody to scope the block to and no way to leave a private domain’s name out of it. The handshake carries the behaviour rules, how many domains are registered and the pointer at list_domains, which does know who’s asking and filters.

title: 6  Onboarding an agent
section: 6.2 How the agent finds its way
text:
6.2 How the agent finds its way
A routing line is a targeting aid. The routing skill says so in as many words, and adds what every colleague knows about floor plans: the label on the door isn’t the inventory of the room.
The first decision is whether to look, and the rules settle it: before the agent answers a question about the project’s past or starts a task, it searches. In Claude Code and Codex the prompt hook has usually brought the first few engrams along with your message already. The second decision is scope. A narrow question, one that clearly belongs to one service, team or customer, goes to the domain whose line describes it, in a single search_engrams call with domains set. A broad or unclear question omits domains and sweeps everything, each hit labelled with its domain. The agent doesn’t stop to ask you which it is: a search is cheap and usually settles the ambiguity, and a clarifying question is for after it came back empty.
The third decision is when to widen. A scoped search can return plausible near-misses when the subject belongs to one domain and the question to another: who gets paged about refunds is a people question, not a payments one. When the obvious domain keeps missing after a rephrasing or two, the agent runs one unscoped sweep. Then it reads. A snippet is a short window around a match, and a colleague who answers from a snippet is guessing, so anything that summarizes or quotes an engram goes through read_engram first. A strong hit becomes an anchor for build_context, which pulls in what the engram depends on before the work starts.
The agent is given the doors and, with each prompt, at most three engrams that may fit it; what’s behind every other door is fetched when a task calls for it. A colleague with a floor plan beats one carrying the building around in a wheelbarrow.

title: 6  Onboarding an agent
text:
6.3 Assign, do not copy
You wouldn’t message a colleague a question, copy their answer into your editor and do the work yourself. You’d assign them the task, because doing it is how they get better at it. An agent with Crystalline’s tools is in the same position, and treating it as a lookup service wastes most of what you set up.
Give it the task. “Add a metric to the retry queue” lands better than “what do you know about the retry queue”, because the first sentence sends the agent through the whole loop on its own: it routes to engineering, recalls the gotcha and the bank rule, reads the engram in full, walks one hop to the deploy runbook, writes the change in Python and tells you what it found on the way. The floor plan only pays off when somebody walks the corridors, and the somebody should be the agent.
It follows the processes a person would, since it can be wrong in the same ways: review for its changes, a yes for its captures. A colleague you never delegate to never learns your work, and neither does an agent.






NoteIn practice



Here’s your first week with the agent, session by session. Monday is the afternoon from chapter 5: the briefing names books, and the agent knows your rules before you’ve typed one. On Tuesday you give it a real task (something for Saturday’s flight) and explain nothing. The agent routes to books, recalls the series rule and the translations, finds the note about the Tessier-Ashpool paperbacks you captured on Monday and comes back with three (a Doctorow you missed, the next Dungeon Crawler Carl and the Deep Space Nine novel that follows the one you finished last month), each with the shop that has it. On Wednesday it’s wrong for the first time: it recommends the new Vickers in hardback, and you tell it you don’t buy hardbacks, because you read outdoors and a hardback doesn’t survive the backpack. It asks whether to capture that in books as a [convention]. You say yes, and add the exception: a hardback is for collecting, bought after the ebook, when a book turns out to deserve a place on the shelf.
Thursday is a long session sorting the pile by the bed, and when it ends the reminder fires once: the agent proposes two captures (that you abandon anything with a map on page one, and a shelf engram per Star Trek series, classic, Next Generation, Deep Space Nine and the Destiny trilogy, saying which volumes you own and which is next) and raises the salience of the translations engram. On Friday you ask it to order the Vickers, and it answers, before you’ve said which edition, that the hardback is out by your own rule until you’ve read it, and the ebook is out today. On the first session it knew where the drawers were. On the fifth it told you something about yourself, unasked, that you’d taught it two days before. That’s the moment a stranger stops being one.

title: 6  Onboarding an agent
section: 6.4 The reminder at the end of the day
text:
6.4 The reminder at the end of the day
A first week only counts if what was learned survives the weekend, and that’s the beat agents skip. Left alone, a model finishes the task and stops, and the gotcha it met at minute forty goes with it. So crystalline install wires a reminder, the closest thing the loop has to a habit.
It’s a Stop hook. On the first stop after a session has gained real substance it asks the agent to review the conversation for durable learnings: facts, decisions, patterns, gotchas, corrections from you. It also names what doesn’t count: what the session did, temporary paths and outputs, a one-off bug’s error text, steps that won’t recur and anything any model already knows. For each one not yet captured the agent proposes an engram in the fitting domain and waits for a yes; a correction that makes an existing engram wrong becomes a proposed edit or supersession rather than a second engram. If a recalled engram proved to be the key to the task, the agent raises its salience. If nothing qualifies or everything is captured, it finishes normally. The reminder fires at most once per session, and costs about a hundred and twenty tokens. When maintenance is due, a paragraph rides along asking for a sweep; when a team domain holds unshared work, another asks the agent to propose sharing, still a proposal, because sharing puts somebody’s work in front of reviewers.
An agent that reaches a shared instance only over MCP has no hooks. Crystalline’s one reliable channel to a model mid-session is a tool result, so the reminder rides there: a write, edit, move, split or delete comes back with a single clearly prefixed line appended when something is due, never a search or a read, so recalled knowledge is never mixed with guidance. Sharing and maintenance travel this way. Capture doesn’t, because it’s a reflection at the end of a conversation and the server can’t tell when a conversation ends; the routing block keeps teaching capture as standing practice instead. Each person is nudged on their own cadence, a few hours apart:
---
[crystalline] 3 changes in the team domain engineering are not yet

NoteIn brief

Each harness delivers it the way chapter 5 wired it. The agent searches before it answers or starts a task, scopes a narrow question to one domain, sweeps for a broad one, widens when scoped hits keep missing and reads before it answers. title: 7  Teaching
text:
7.1 What to teach
The best onboarding you ever had was a walk. Somebody took you across the floor, stopped at a machine and said “that one lies”, and you never trusted it again. Nobody wrote that down. It was not on the slide. It was the kind of knowledge that only moves from one head to another when a person decides it matters enough to point at, and the pointing is what this chapter is about.
Day one, last chapter, was the floor plan. Now comes the proper onboarding: what you tell a colleague in the first month, how you tell an agent the same things, what a well-taught fact looks like on disk, and the two rooms where the teaching happens, a session and a browser tab. It ends with two people editing the same page at once, which is where teaching stops being a lecture.
Ask any good manager what a new hire needs and the list comes out in the same shape every time: what we value, and what we won’t do even when it would be faster. How things are done here (the review, the deploy, the meeting that actually decides) and what’s expected of the role. Which tools we use, and which we abandoned and why. And where information lives: which repository, which dashboard, which person. An agent needs the same list, in the same order of importance, and the last item is the one that makes the other four cheap.
A person’s knowledge doesn’t look like a source tree. No engineer on your team holds the payments service in their head by the letter. They know it’s in the payments repository, that the retry logic is under queue/, that the config nobody documented is in the deploy chart, who owns it and that Encom’s rule explains its strangest number. They know how to get access and which door to knock on. What they carry is a map of the territory plus the concepts to navigate it fast, and that’s exactly what to teach an agent. The source tree it can read with the tools its harness gives it whenever a task calls for it. What it needs from you is which repository holds the code for which purpose, how access is granted, the architecture and the vocabulary. Pointer knowledge, access knowledge and the mental model. Teach the map and the territory stays where it is, reachable.
So the engrams that earn their place in the first month are the ones a person would say across a desk: the chargeback rule behind the cutoff, the name the team uses for the queue, the fact that the wiki says gateway where the code says edge, and the rule about Fridays. Not one of them is on any page, and every one of them is what an experienced colleague knows.

title: 7  Teaching
text:
7.2 Teaching through the agent
In a session, the simplest way to teach is to say something worth keeping and watch what happens.
Tell the agent “the settlement job runs at six because Encom’s file lands at five, and it fails silently if the file is late”, and it doesn’t write. It searches first, in engineering, because the capture skill makes search-before-write a hard gate, and it checks whether an engram already owns the topic, in which case the new fact becomes an edit of that engram rather than a second one beside it. Finding nothing, it proposes: “Should I capture this in engineering as a [gotcha]?” A terse “store this” is already a complete instruction and skips the question; an aside you obviously didn’t mean to keep gets no question at all. It names the domain every time, since a write has no default, and when the owner isn’t obvious it asks rather than guesses. A rotation detail learned during a payments incident is people knowledge, and the agent sweeps every domain before filing it where the incident happened to be.
Then it writes a well-formed file: a title, tags drawn from the vocabulary already in use rather than a near-synonym, a folder matching the domain’s layout and a body of at least three lines, because verification rejects a lone bullet as too thin. Hand it one sentence and it pads honestly, one bullet for the fact in your words, one for how and when it was learned, one for the scope and never an invented specific. You glance at the result the way you glance at a new hire’s first commit, and say yes. The write answers with its nearest neighbours too: the receipt names the existing engrams closest in meaning to what just landed. The instruction beside them is to read the one that fits, then merge into it, supersede it or link it, never to pass over the list in silence. So the duplicate check runs twice, before the write on your sentence and after it on the engram as written.
Correction is the same conversation. “The file lands at half past five, not five” finds the engram and changes the value where it stands. “We moved settlement to the new broker in August” is a different thing, the world changing, and the agent supersedes rather than edits, as chapter 3 walked through. Teaching and correcting are one motion, which is why the framing in chapter 2 said teach, rather than file.

title: 7  Teaching
text:
7.3 Teaching through Fluid
The other room is the browser. Sometimes the fastest way to teach is to write it yourself, without a model in the loop and without spending a token: open the engram in Fluid, switch to edit and type (Figure 7.1). The editor previews live, the frontmatter is a form, and typing [[ completes titles across every domain, so a relation is two keystrokes and a pick. The file on disk is what changes; the page you were reading (Figure 11.4) is that file. Save a page you’re editing alone and you get the second look a session’s write gets, as a panel above the text with the same instruction.






Figure 7.1: Editing an engram in Fluid: live preview, the frontmatter form and wikilink completion.



What you write there doesn’t sit unreviewed. The engram records that a person wrote it, human: and your account name in its generated.by, and the next maintenance sweep raises it as a finding of its own: captured by a person and never reviewed. The finding is judgment class, so the agent doesn’t rewrite your words. It reads the engram, verifies the claim, aligns the tags with the vocabulary, wires relations both ways into the neighbourhood the engram belongs to and records a verified entry; any change to the wording it proposes and waits. In chapter 2 you typed a note into Fluid yourself, and that week’s sweep is where the agent tidied it into the graph. That’s the division of labour: you teach in whichever room is nearest, and the agent keeps the archive coherent.

title: 7  Teaching
section: 7.4 The anatomy of a good engram
text:
7.4 The anatomy of a good engram
Chapter 4 read an engram line by line. What makes one good deserves a page of its own, because the difference between a good engram and a page is the difference between a colleague who explains and one who forwards you a link.
An engram is one unit of knowledge, about one thing, and when the thing grows the engram is edited, not forked. One thing is one lifetime too: validity is set per engram rather than per bullet, so a fact that expires on its own schedule (a price, a deadline, an owner) gets an engram of its own. Where a bundle mixed them, split_engram moves the facts that still hold into a new engram before the rest retires. Prose comes first: the explanation you’d give across a desk, what the thing is and why it’s the way it is, because prose is what search matches and what a reader reads. Then the observations carry the facts, one bullet each with the most precise category you have, [fact] for verified state, [decision] for a choice, [gotcha] for the trap, [lesson] for what cost an hour, [risk] for the concern, never [fact] for a guess. Relations come next, for structure: depends_on, supersedes or a plain relates_to, so the graph can carry a reader to what the fact leans on. Tags stay within the vocabulary in use. A salience goes on only when the engram is genuinely exceptional (the rule a dozen other rules hang from), since most never need one. And an engram is what’s true now: a corrected value is replaced where it stands, never stapled on as a dated update, and the validity dates stay absent unless a fact is genuinely bounded. This one your agent wrote into books, after the exchange below:

NoteIn practice



You’ve had three duds in a row, and on Sunday you sit down with your agent:

Look at what you didn’t do. You didn’t tell the agent a fact. You handed it the source material and a question, the way you’d hand a friend the log and say “work out what I like”, and the agent derived the pattern, wrote it down with the log kept beside it as provenance, and six months later recalled it in a session that had never seen the log. That’s teaching at its most economical: you supply the material and the judgment about what matters, and the colleague does the learning.

title: 7  Teaching
text:
7.5 Attachments
Some teaching material is a file: the chargeback agreement, the deck a vendor sent, the diagram you drew at the whiteboard and photographed. In Fluid you paste, drag or upload it onto the engram it belongs to, and it lands under the domain’s assets/ folder with a reference in the engram’s body, an image ![...](assets/diagram.png) or a link [...](assets/deck.pdf). Images, PDFs, slide decks, office documents and data files are all accepted, up to ten megabytes each. Files enter through Fluid or a domain archive, never through an agent write, and an attachment always belongs to some engram’s teaching: a file nothing references comes up in the sweep as something to delete or to turn into knowledge.
They aren’t opaque to the agent. read_engram returns each attachment as a resource link, and the agent fetches the file itself over MCP before summarizing what it shows. The sweep closes the loop from the other side: an attachment nobody has analyzed is a finding, and working it means reading the file, capturing what it teaches and marking on the engram which file was analyzed at which version, so a changed deck comes back around. One small courtesy for images: a formatting fragment on the target, ![Chart](assets/chart.png#right,w=50%), floats and sizes the picture in Fluid, and every other markdown renderer ignores it.

title: 7  Teaching
text:
7.6 Editing together
Chapter 3 said the way a colleague really learns is by pairing, and Fluid makes pairing literal. Open an engram that somebody else has open and you see their cursor; type, and both sets of edits merge conflict-free and land as one save: two people, one page, the whiteboard version of a wiki. Review mode changes the room: everyone writes in a draft of their own, and a colleague joins yours through a draft share-link (chapter 13).
The third name in the strip can be the agent’s. When your agent reads or edits an engram somebody has open in the editor, it joins that page as a named peer: your account with an agent designation, a bot glyph beside the name and a colour from the same palette as everyone else’s. It has no cursor, so its sentences aren’t painted in that colour; the glyph in the strip is how you know an agent is writing. An edit it makes is computed against the page as it stands at that moment, so it composes with what you typed seconds ago instead of stomping it. When it reads, it sees your unsaved typing rather than a stale copy. Its write receipt says the change landed in a live page and names who is present, so it can tell you “I updated the section you’re looking at” and mean it. Only a wholesale overwrite of a page somebody has open asks first, and a client that can’t ask is refused. That’s the fluid and crystalline halves working on one page at once, human with human and human with agent.
What that is like is a napkin on the table between you. You write the line you’re sure of, the retention rule you want, and ask the agent in your session to fill in what you’re not. While you keep typing it goes and reads: the engram that holds Encom’s chargeback window, the vendor’s documentation for the retry limit. The window lands under your line, address and all, and the retry limit beside it with a link to the vendor’s page. The month you misremembered is corrected in the sentence you just typed. You say it should be clear enough for the new team, and a diagram of the retry flow appears under the text, drawn from what the two of you wrote. None of it waits for a save, and none of it happens unless you asked. It’s JARVIS in Tony Stark’s workshop: he builds, and the voice in the room has the schematic in the air before he asks for it and tells him, politely, when he’s wrong. On a shared instance anyone can pull up a chair. Chapter 13 puts a whole meeting in that room.






Figure 7.2: Your agent in the page with you: a named peer in the strip, writing while you write.



Teaching a colleague is pointing at the machine that lies. Teaching an agent is the same gesture, and this one writes it down.






NoteIn brief



Teach an agent what you’d teach a new hire: values, processes, expectations, tools and above all where information lives, taught as a map (which repository holds what, how access works, the architecture). In a session, say something worth keeping and the agent searches first, proposes a capture in the fitting domain, writes a well-formed engram once you say yes and reads the neighbours its receipt names, with corrections edited in place and changed facts superseded. In Fluid, write it yourself, and the next sweep verifies, tags and wires what a person captured without rewriting their words. A good engram is one unit of knowledge and one lifetime, with prose, categorized observations, typed relations and, rarely, a salience; attachments hand over files that agents read back. Co-editing merges live, and your agent can sit in that session as a named peer.

title: 8  Ingesting knowledge at scale
text:
8.1 What a briefing contains
Nobody has ever onboarded a colleague by pointing at four hundred wiki pages and walking away. Plenty of people have, and the colleague spent a month believing the architecture diagram from the year before the rewrite and calling the product by the name it had until the acquisition. The pages weren’t wrong when they were written. They were just handed over without the ten minutes at the whiteboard that tell a newcomer which of them to believe.
Those ten minutes are the subject of this chapter. Sooner or later the teaching of chapter 7, one fact at a time, meets the existing pile: the wiki, the shared drive, the decks. The agent can learn from it in an afternoon, and it wants to, like Johnny 5 flipping through pages of an encyclopedia: input, more input, need input. What it can’t do is bring the judgment a person brings to a wiki, the sense of what’s current, what was aspirational and which of two contradictory pages to trust. Chapter 1 said that judgment has to be handed over. This is how, and how you check what came back.
A briefing is the paragraph you’d say to a person before they opened the wiki, and the useful ones are concrete about the past. Names first: the product now called Settlement was called Ledger until the reorganization two years ago, so normalize to Settlement; the wiki says gateway where the code says edge, and edge is the word to keep. Then a rule for contradiction, since a wiki of any age contains them: trust the newer page, unless one of them is the runbook. Then what to skip: the archived spaces, the personal pages, anything under Drafts. Then the one everybody forgets because it’s obvious: the decks were written to persuade and the wiki is what we actually do, so where they disagree the page wins and the deck’s version goes in as an [idea] at most.
Add where things go: which domain, which folder layout, the tags in use. And the shape of the review you want: propose before writing, keep source links, ask about anything resembling a decision nobody wrote down. It fits in one message:
That message is the difference between an ingest that lands and one that produces a confident, well-formatted archive of things that stopped being true.

title: 8  Ingesting knowledge at scale
section: 8.2 The sources, and who reads them
text:
8.2 The sources, and who reads them
Crystalline ships no scraper, by design. The agent is the ingester, and it reads sources with whatever its harness gives it: the wiki over the MCP connector the harness provides, a folder of exported documents through its file tools, a repository through the code tools it already has. A repository, though, is a source the agent consults rather than one it ingests: the repository holds the code, and the engrams hold which repository holds the code for which purpose, how to get access and the architecture and concepts that make the right file findable in a minute. The division is precise: the harness supplies the reading, the agent supplies the distillation and Crystalline is the destination, where what was derived lands as engrams with provenance, and the review loop that checks it afterwards.
A wiki is the common source, read page by page through the connector. A folder of documents, PDFs and exports and the odd spreadsheet, is read the same way. Slide decks are the one source that usually comes in through Fluid instead: a person drops the deck onto the engram it belongs to, and the agent reads it back over MCP as an attachment, so the deck becomes teaching material rather than a file nobody opened (chapter 7). And a tree of markdown that already carries frontmatter, an old knowledge base that was nearly an archive already, doesn’t go through the agent at all: crystalline import <src> --domain <name> folds it into a domain as a pure file transformation, dry run first, normalizing legacy type values, backfilling status and dropping sentinel dates on the way.

title: 8  Ingesting knowledge at scale
text:
8.3 Distill, then propose
The cardinal sin of ingestion is mirroring: copying a source wholesale so that the archive looks complete, then filling the gaps with guesswork. A vendor recall notice is forty screens of marketing header, revision table, legalese and support matrix, with three paragraphs that matter. Distilled, it becomes two observations, a resource link back to the page and a source_date in the frontmatter: forty screens down to two facts and one link.
Distilling is also where the briefing does its work. The agent reads a page about Ledger and writes Settlement; it finds a deck slide claiming a feature and files it as an [idea] because you told it decks persuade; it meets two pages that disagree and applies the rule rather than picking one silently. And one shape earns verbatim retention, only ever beside its distillation: a document whose exact words you may need to quote. The summary stays an ordinary engram where its topic lives; the full text goes in as a type: source engram under sources/, linked both ways with summarizes and summarized_by. It’s split into parts only when it outgrows its budget, which is four times the size an ordinary engram gets. On recall the summary is what gets read, and the full text is pulled in only when the summary falls short.
Then, before anything lands, comes the list:
Proposed for engineering (23 engrams):
  runbooks/  Settlement deploy runbook
  runbooks/  Retry queue drain procedure
             Edge routing rules
             Encom file format, v3
  ...
Write these? (y / n)
You trim it. Proposing first is the rule for a whole space, not just a page, because the trimming is where your judgment enters the archive, and striking five lines off a list is cheaper than retiring five engrams next month.

title: 8  Ingesting knowledge at scale
text:
8.4 The review loop
What the agent writes is a proposal in a second sense: it carries provenance, and a person reviews it. Each engram names its source, a link, a date, an attachment, so the reviewer can open the page it came from and check the derivation. The review happens in Fluid, where an engram is a page and a fix is an edit, and a reviewer who knows the material corrects the one value the agent got wrong without going back through a session. A team domain sends the ingest out as a proposal (chapter 13).
Some duplicates never wait for the sweep. A write can come back naming the engrams it’s closest to, so a wiki page that repeats one the agent captured an hour earlier is merged on the receipt rather than an hour later. The agent says what it did with the list instead of moving on. Then run the sweep. The evolve tool is meant to be called after a large ingest, and its queue is built for this moment (Figure 3.2): links that don’t resolve because a page referred to a title nobody captured; near-duplicate clusters where two wiki pages became two engrams about one thing; a tag spelled two ways; an attachment nobody has analyzed; and the human captures that reviewers made in Fluid while correcting, each raised as a finding to verify, tag and wire into the graph. Work the mechanical findings in a pass, propose the judgment ones one at a time and sweep again until the number stops falling. That shrinking number is how you know the ingest settled.

title: 8  Ingesting knowledge at scale
text:
8.5 Temporal hygiene
An ingest is where dates go wrong, because a page written two years ago lands in an archive that treats everything as true today. Three fields keep it honest. source_date is when the source was written, and the agent sets it from the page’s last-edited date, so an engram derived from an old page says so. valid_from is for a fact that started on a known date, a policy that came in with the reorganization, and nothing else; absent means it has always held, and an absent valid_to means it still does, so neither is set to mean “we do not know”. stale_after is the one that buys you the most: put it on anything with a shelf life, a vendor’s terms, a pricing table, a contact name, and the sweep raises the engram when the date passes and nobody has re-checked it. A re-check that finds nothing changed is one verified entry, or a later stale_after, and the engram goes quiet.

title: 8  Ingesting knowledge at scale
text:
8.6 When not to bulk-ingest
Curation beats completeness, and the archive isn’t a mirror of the wiki. If a space is dead, leave it dead; if a page would not survive the “would I tell a new hire this” question from chapter 2, it does not become an engram because it existed. Four hundred pages distilled to nineteen engrams, worth more than the four hundred because every one is something the agent will act on.
The strongest case for not ingesting is the source tree. A person doesn’t remember the code by the letter. Well, Commander Data does, and yes, he’s a person, the court said so; but you didn’t hire Data. A person remembers where and how to find things, the map chapter 7 said to teach, and lets the territory stay where it is. Ingesting the source would give you a stale copy of something the agent can already read, and the map fits in a dozen engrams.






TipUnder the hood



Nothing about an ingest is special on disk. Each derived engram is one markdown file with frontmatter, the same format as a fact taught across a desk, with resource, source_date and generated as plain keys anyone can grep. A domain that lives in a repository shows the ingest as a diff: new files, nothing rewritten elsewhere, so a bad batch reverts with the version control the team already has. Attachments sit under the domain’s assets/ folder, referenced by relative path from the engrams that claim them. The index is derived from the files (crystalline reindex --full re-reads every file and keeps the embeddings), and crystalline verify in the repository’s CI refuses a malformed engram before the team pulls it.








NoteIn practice



Your reading log has four hundred and twelve entries, and a notes app holds a decade of half-sentences about them; you trust neither completely. You give your agent a briefing like the one above and let it read both over an afternoon. It comes back with a list of twenty-three engrams, each naming its source entry. You strike four: two are about a shop that closed, one is a wish list from 2019 dressed as taste, one is a note about a book you were given and never opened. The agent writes nineteen, every one with a link and a date, the shops among them with a stale_after for next year because opening hours change.
The sweep the next morning has eleven findings. Six are mechanical, links to titles the log spelled differently and the ingest renamed, and the agent fixes them in a pass. Three are judgment: a near-duplicate pair, two engrams about Dune from different years, which you have the agent fold into one; an orphan nothing links to yet, wired to the paperback rule; and a tag spelled two ways, which comes back as a crystalline tags merge command for you to run. The remaining two are your own: corrections you typed in Fluid while reviewing, which the agent verifies and wires into the graph. On Thursday you ask which Star Trek novels you already own, by series, and get the answer, the source entry for each and the date you wrote it, from a log you haven’t opened in a month.


Today the wiki is the source and the archive is derived from it. The last chapter turns that around: once the archive is what the team teaches and corrects, the wiki pages and the decks become views of it, which is no revolution at all, since every diagram and slide that exists today was already a reflection of somebody’s knowledge. The ingest is the last time the flow runs this way round.






NoteIn brief



Bulk ingestion needs the briefing a new colleague would get before opening the wiki: what was renamed and what to normalize to, which page wins a contradiction, what to skip and which sources persuade rather than describe. The agent reads the sources through its harness, distils rather than mirrors, keeps a source link and date on every engram, proposes the list before writing and lands the result in Crystalline, where a person reviews it in Fluid and the next sweep surfaces the unresolved links, duplicates and unreviewed captures an ingest leaves behind. Set source_date, reserve valid_from for genuinely bounded facts and put stale_after on anything with a shelf life. And don’t ingest what the agent can read for itself: teach the map of the source tree, not the tree.

title: 9  Finding
text:
9.1 Search as recall
Forty-two is a perfectly good answer. The trouble, as the mice discovered, is that nobody knew the question. Recall has the opposite trouble: you know the question, and the answer was written down by somebody who’d never heard it. The engram says the retry queue drops jobs older than twenty-four hours. The person on call at three in the morning types “why do payments go missing”. The two don’t share a single word, and the engram is the answer.
Closing that gap is what this chapter is about. Chapter 3 called the beat remember and chapter 6 watched the agent walk the corridors on its first day. What’s left is the craft: how a search ranks, how an agent gathers the neighbourhood around a hit before it starts work, how it asks what was true last June instead of what’s true now, and why a colleague who recalls costs less than one who reads everything. The retry-queue engram runs through every section.
A search in Crystalline blends two signals, and the blend is what makes the three-in-the-morning question land. Full-text matching finds the exact: the engram that says “retry queue” when you searched for “retry queue”. Semantic similarity finds the adjacent: the engram about dropped jobs when the question was about missing payments, because the two are about the same thing in different words. Each hit is scored on both and the ranking is the blend. Text alone would miss the on-call question. Similarity alone would rank a chatty engram that mentions payments above the terse one that explains them. Together they behave like a colleague who both remembers the phrase and understands the problem.
Meaning doesn’t stop at a language: the model behind the similarity reads more than two hundred of them, so an engram written in German answers a question asked in English. Your shelf note on translations, typed in German one evening (English when a book was written in English, German translations for everything else), is what comes back months later when you ask in English which edition of a French novel to buy.
Two small priors tilt the order, and both are bounded. Salience lifts the exceptional: an engram given a salience at capture, or raised later when it turned out to unlock a task, ranks above equally relevant neighbours, while relevance keeps the upper hand and nothing is ever excluded by it (Section 4.2). Retirement fades the past: an engram whose status is deprecated, superseded, archived or legacy is softly pushed down, never filtered out. So the cutoff that applied until September sits one scroll below the behaviour that applies now, still there and still dated (Section 4.4).
Around the ranking sit the filters. A search narrows by domain, by type, by tags, by status, by any frontmatter key or by a recorded-after date. A search with no query text at all is a legitimate way to ask for everything of one kind: every runbook in engineering, every engram tagged weyland-yutani. A tag filter also matches through a domain’s tag aliases, so an old spelling keeps finding what it always found. Every hit is labelled with its domain, and a hit inside an observation carries its line, so the agent can point at the fact rather than the file.
What comes back is a snippet, a short window around the match, often cut off, and it’s a targeting aid. A colleague who answers from a snippet is guessing, and the routing skill draws the line where it belongs: a single atomic fact completely visible in the snippet may be answered from it. Anything that summarizes, compares or quotes an engram goes through read_engram first. When several domains answer a broad question differently, the agent says so and names which domain each answer came from. Scope itself is chapter 6’s decision: narrow to the domain whose routing line fits, sweep for a broad question and widen when the obvious domain keeps returning near-misses.
The same ranking serves people. Fluid’s search page is faceted and backed by exactly the ranking an agent sees (Figure 11.2). Cmd+K is the other door: it jumps anywhere by name. The two answer different questions. Search is for when you know what it’s about. Cmd+K is for when you know what it’s called. When the agent has found something you’d rather read yourself, ask it for the link: every engram it reads or writes comes with the address of its page in Fluid, and the link can open that page at one heading.

title: 9  Finding
text:
9.2 Gathering the neighbourhood
A hit is a point, and a task usually needs the area around it: what the fact depends on, what depends on it, the runbook that mentions it. An experienced colleague does this without noticing. Ask them about the retry cutoff and they tell you about the bank unprompted, because in their head the two were never separate.
build_context is that reflex as a tool. Hand it an address, crystalline://engineering/retry-queue-gotcha, and it follows the relations and the prose links outward, one to three hops, crossing into other domains where an edge crosses, and returns the neighbours ranked by how strongly each connects to the anchor. What comes back is the shape of the neighbourhood (titles and typed relations, with an untyped prose link surfaced as links_to) and no content. The agent reads the nodes that matter with read_engram, which is the second half of the same motion. A /* suffix on the anchor globs a permalink prefix, and a permalink carries its folder, so that’s a whole folder: crystalline://engineering/runbooks/* (Section 4.6). max_related keeps the top-ranked, ten unless you say otherwise, so a densely linked engram doesn’t drown the task in its acquaintances.
The loop feeds itself. read_engram marks each relation and link as resolved or not, summarizes what links back and, when a neighbourhood exists, names the build_context anchor to run next. An edge that doesn’t resolve is a signal rather than an error: the target isn’t written yet, or lives in a domain this instance hasn’t registered. Fluid draws the same neighbourhood as an interactive graph (Figure 11.3), the quickest way to see whether an engram is wired in or standing alone.

title: 9  Finding
text:
9.3 What applied last June
Every fact in the archive is one of two kinds, and a good question knows which it’s asking for. “What is the cutoff?” wants the present. The present is a status question: filter on status: stable and the search returns what holds now, with the older spelling current folded in. “What cutoff applied in June?” wants a moment, and a moment is a window question, answered from valid_from and valid_to, the plain dates on the engrams that carry them. It’s the time circuits on the dashboard: set the destination time to June and the search returns the engram that was true when you land. Chapter 10 shows the window being closed with the real date.
Absent dates are unbounded, and that rule sets a trap in a filter. A strict comparison (valid_to greater than the first of June) skips every engram with no valid_to, which are exactly the unbounded ones the question meant to keep. The routing skill puts it plainly: reach for a window filter only for an explicit, bounded question about a date, and put it on the first search. For an ordinary present-day question, status: stable alone is both correct and sufficient. When a window filter isn’t getting traction, the supersedes chain and each hit’s status tell the same story a different way: search by topic, read which engram covers the period asked about and narrate the status of each rather than presenting a retired one as fact.
Time runs the other way too. A search takes a recorded-after date, and recent_activity answers “what changed while I was away” across every domain for the last week, day or fortnight, which is how a person back from leave starts current instead of starting over.

title: 9  Finding
text:
9.4 Recall is cheaper than reading
It’s worth stating the case as a mechanism, with no number attached, because the number depends on your archive and the mechanism doesn’t.
An agent that keeps its knowledge as a folder of markdown files has one way to use it: read it. The folder can’t say which file matters for today’s task, so the agent reads the folder, and reads it again in the next session, every file, whether or not the task touches it. That works while the folder is small, and it stops working at the scale where knowledge becomes worth having, the ladder chapter 1 climbed.
An agent working from Crystalline receives only the knowledge that applies. In Claude Code and Codex the prompt hook runs the first search before the agent has read the question and hands over at most three engrams. The routing prompt sends the task to one domain, or to a sweep, before a single engram is read.
