There are no minutes to write, because the whiteboard was the knowledge base. You share it as a proposal before you leave the room, Lambert reviews it on her phone and it merges that evening. When the merged list comes down the draft is gone, and the next morning every agent in the club recalls a decision made and captured in the same hour, the Yavin 4 briefing room with the plan on the screen when they walk out.

title: 13  Sharing with a team
section: 13.5 When two people changed the same file
text:
13.5 When two people changed the same file
Sometimes the team merged a change to an engram you also changed. update_domain brings the merge in, leaves your file untouched rather than guessing, and flags the conflict. origin_status lists its path and kind, and sharing refuses until it’s settled. In Fluid the same conflict opens a dialog with both versions next to each other, so the choice is made with the wording in front of you.
In review mode the conflict belongs to the draft’s author alone, and the resolution is written into their overlay, so nobody else’s view moves until the resolved draft is proposed and merged like anything else.






TipUnder the hood



Settling a conflict is resolve_conflict: mine keeps your version, theirs takes the team’s, merged takes content you supply after reconciling both. On a harness that can ask, calling it without a resolution previews both sides and puts the question to you.
A proposal is a branch in the team’s own repository and never a fork, and stacking is probed once per origin, so a forge that cannot stack falls back without configuration. Overlay drafts are rows in the index with an actor dimension, so search, relations and recency gain the draft view from one condition. Because the index is disposable while drafts aren’t, every draft is also mirrored as plain markdown in a journal under the state directory, from which a wiped and resynced index restores them. The folder itself is written by exactly one thing, what lands on the team’s branch.


Review was never the team distrusting a colleague. It was the team trusting a process, and now the colleague can be an agent.






NoteIn brief



A team domain tracks a GitHub repository with no git involved: connect once with a browser code, add the domain with its origin, and six collaboration tools appear. Knowledge goes out with share_changes as a proposal the agent previews and relays but never merges; feedback returns through update_domain, an amend answers on the same proposal, further shares stack outside review mode and personal identities put each person’s name on their own work. The share dialog shows each file’s diff and can put a file back, and a MANIFEST that says sharing: direct commits straight to the branch instead. Review mode gives every actor a private overlay over the shared folder: drafts live there, a share is exactly that actor’s drafts, merged pulls clear them, the folder changes only with what lands on the branch and owners see counts of pending work, never content. A draft is opened to a colleague with a revocable link, edited live with cursors that merge into one save and joined by the agent as a named peer, so a meeting held in an engram is captured when it ends. A conflict is settled with resolve_conflict or Fluid’s side-by-side dialog: mine, theirs or merged.

title: 14  Identity and access
text:
14.1 Who is acting
Every action on a shared instance has a name attached, and the name is a person’s. Chapter 12 ended on that line. This chapter is what follows from taking it seriously: who is acting when an engram changes, who may see a domain and who may change it, how a login at the company’s identity provider becomes an account here, what the rules cover and the few things you do on an ordinary Tuesday. It ends where the whole book has been walking: a colleague who has earned access, by name.
People arrive as accounts, by whichever of chapter 12’s doors they came through. Once inside there’s one account with one role, viewer, editor or admin, and everything the person does is done as it (Chapter 12).
Agents arrive as somebody’s agent. Chapter 12 issued the token, and what it means is the point here. An authenticated agent is its user for the length of the session, with that person’s visibility, that person’s write rights, that person’s share identity in a team domain and that person’s name in the provenance of everything it captures, beside the client that acted. Programs in Tron look like their users and act for them, and that’s the picture: the agent’s name is its user’s name with an agent designation after it. The CLI and a stdio session on the server stay the machine’s owner, as chapter 12 said.
The token’s lifecycle is what makes the arrangement safe, and it’s worth walking once. It’s minted on the profile’s Agent access card, or by an admin with crystalline users mcp-token <name>. It begins with a fixed prefix, cmt_, so a leaked one is recognizable in a log and findable with grep across a repository or a chat export. It’s shown once, and what the instance keeps is a hash, so a copied accounts database yields no working credential. It lives in exactly one place after that, the Authorization: Bearer header of the harness’s MCP registration on the person’s own machine. It has no expiry of its own, because on a self-hosted instance revocation is the story. Every request looks the token up, so a revoked token fails on the next call. Rotation issues the replacement and revokes the old one in one motion, so the registration is updated in one edit and nothing is ever half-rotated. Every account may issue its own, viewers included, and that leaks no capability: a viewer’s agent is read-only by construction, because it is a viewer. A read-only instance still issues them, because the mode protects the knowledge and a token is account state: with agent authentication on, a read-only server is where an agent can’t connect until it has one. On an instance where hosted clients sign in there’s a second kind of credential at the same door, the access token a hosted client holds, prefixed coa_, and the gate checks both kinds on every request (chapter 12 has how such a client comes by one).

title: 14  Identity and access
text:
14.2 Membership on a private domain
A domain is visible to every signed-in user unless it’s made private, and chapter 12 said who sees it then: the owner, the instance’s admins and invited members at one of three levels, viewer, editor or manager. The top rung deserves a word. A manager runs the membership, inviting, removing and granting any level up to manager itself, which is the job of a lead who shouldn’t have to fetch the owner for every new joiner. What a manager cannot do is change the domain’s visibility, transfer it or delete it, because a manager who could flip a domain public would be an owner by another name. Those three stay with the one owner and with the admins, so that a domain always has exactly one person answerable for its existence, and a way to recover it when that person leaves.
Two of chapter 12’s truths carry over unchanged, and Fluid prints the second under the Make private button: admins see every domain, private ones included, and a private domain protects from the instance’s other users, never from whoever operates the machine.
The instance role and the membership level are different questions, and a write needs both to say yes. An invitation widens what an account may reach, never what its instance role lets it do, so an instance viewer invited as an editor reads the domain and writes nothing, because an invitation never widens a role.

title: 14  Identity and access
text:
14.3 Linking identities
A team that adopts single sign-on after running local accounts for a while has a linking problem: Kane has an account named kane and an identity at the provider, and they should be one person. The tempting answer is to match on email, and it’s the classic foot-gun of this integration, which is why Crystalline refuses it. An email address is presentation: the provider asserts it, the person can change it and matching on it would let whoever controls an address at the provider walk into the local account that happens to carry the same one. The address is often not even the person’s to keep: a provider that lets people edit their own email, or a second provider added a year later, is all it takes. Chapter 12 gave the rule that follows, issuer and subject and nothing else, so the sign-in gets a fresh account and joining the two is an explicit act with a name on it. The signed-in local user links from the SSO identity section of their profile. An admin does it from the terminal, crystalline users link kane --issuer <issuer> --subject <subject>, which is also how an admin repairs links after a provider re-registration changes every subject. Unlinking refuses when it would leave an account with no way in, and the refusal names crystalline users passwd as the way to give it one. The --force flag on the unlink is for the re-registration repair, where the account is unreachable for the moment between the old link going and the new one landing. An identity already linked to another account is never taken by a second link, so an admin moves it.

title: 14  Identity and access
text:
14.4 What the rules cover
A rule that covers most surfaces covers none, because the agent will find the one it misses. Visibility follows the caller onto every read surface there is: search, read_engram, build_context, recent_activity, the routing briefing at session start, the graph, exports, the maintenance sweep and Fluid’s domain list and tree. To someone who may not see a domain it’s absent, answered exactly as a domain that was never registered would be, for the reason chapter 12 gave. Writes check for editor or better. An agent inherits all of it from its user and administers no membership: there’s no tool for changing one, on purpose, so a persuasive prompt cannot talk an agent into inviting itself. What it may change about the instance itself follows its user’s role too: registering a domain, writing a setting and deciding what a domain installs take an admin, and reading any of them back is open to everyone. Unregistering a domain takes an admin or, for a private domain, its owner. On an instance that leaves agent authentication off, the open tier that remains sees only the domains everyone sees, and it’s refused outright when it tries to unregister a domain. A private domain with a team origin is two questions: who may see it here is the instance’s, and who may push to the repository is the forge’s.

title: 14  Identity and access
text:
14.5 Day to day
Most of this is one card, the Members card near the foot of a domain’s page in Fluid: the members with their level badges, an invite box that takes a username and a level, remove, leave and, for the owner or an admin, transfer. The switch to private and back to shared sits below it in the Danger zone and asks you to type the domain’s name first. Private domains carry a badge in the domain list (Figure 14.1). The terminal does the same for a script or an admin already there: crystalline domain members board list, crystalline domain members board add lambert --level viewer, crystalline domain members board remove lambert, crystalline domain visibility board private --owner dallas and crystalline domain transfer board ripley. The CLI is the machine operator and passes no role gate.






Figure 14.1: The domains of an instance in Fluid, private ones marked.



A year of running a domain comes down to inviting, promoting and handing over. Inviting is the card or the add verb, at the level the person needs today, which is usually viewer. Leaving is the member’s own button (no manager required). Promoting is setting the level again, viewer to editor when their captures have earned it, editor to manager when they should be the one inviting. Handing over is transfer, for the day the owner leaves: the new owner is the owner from that moment, and the old one is a stranger to the domain unless re-invited. When they do leave, an admin disables or deletes the account, and deleting sweeps what the account had connected: its agent tokens, its identity links and the grants it gave hosted clients. Its personal share credential goes too when the account is removed on the server with crystalline users remove. A private domain it owned is left with no owner, and only an admin can administer it, so transfer it first. The agent that acted as that person is refused at the door on its next request, like any other stranger.






NoteIn practice



Gaff joins the club for a season, on the strength of one recommendation. He signs in on his first evening with the login you made him and lands as a viewer, the role every new account starts with. He issues himself a token on his profile and pastes it into his harness. His agent is a viewer from its first call, reading club and writing nowhere, without anyone having configured a thing about agents. By the third meeting the notes he keeps sending you to capture for him are the best anyone has written about Dune, and you promote him to editor. The next capture his agent makes lands in club under his name, with his harness named as the client in the provenance.
Later Dallas moves abroad and transfers the private committee domain he keeps for the club’s money to you from the Members card, then finds he can no longer see it, which is what he wanted. He never wanted an admin login, and owning the domain never needed one. When Gaff’s season ends you delete his account. His token dies with it, and his agent’s next session is refused before it opens. His engrams stay, every one recording that his agent wrote it for him, and a month later a new member’s agent recalls Gaff’s take on Dune in a session that never heard his name.








TipUnder the hood



Accounts, agent tokens, identity links, domain visibility and membership all live in one small database beside the index, and none of it is derived, so no rebuild of the index can touch it, and a wipe and resync leaves every permission where it was. Each request resolves the caller once, into a scope: the machine owner for the CLI and stdio, an account with its admin flag for a Fluid session or an authenticated agent, an anonymous tier for a published archive, or an agent where authentication is off. Every engine verb filters on that scope, so a surface added tomorrow is filtered the way search is filtered today. The verbs that change the instance rather than its knowledge read the same scope for the admin flag: add_domain, a configure that sets, unsets or connects and provision with allow, deny or apply. A bare configure and provision status stay reads, and remove_domain asks the domain instead: its owner or an admin may call it.


A new hire earns access a door at a time: a badge on the first day, a room the next week and after a while nobody remembers the meeting where they were let in. The agent walks the same doors, by name, and everything it has ever captured says whose colleague it was.






NoteIn brief



People act as accounts and agents act as their user, through a per-user token that’s shown once, stored hashed, revoked in one motion and issuable by everyone. The CLI and stdio are the machine owner. A private domain is visible to its owner, the instance’s admins and invited members at viewer, editor or manager level, with visibility, transfer and deletion reserved to the owner and admins. It protects from other users, not from whoever runs the machine. Identities link explicitly, keyed on issuer and subject, never by email. Visibility is enforced on every read surface and a hidden domain reads as absent. Writes need editor or better on the domain and on the instance, and agents inherit and administer no membership. Invite, promote and transfer from the Members card or the crystalline domain verbs, and delete an account to take its tokens, links and grants with it, once what it owned has been transferred.

title: 15  Equipping the agent
text:
15.1 What a domain can ship
A wrench is not a mechanic. A new colleague’s first day ends with a laptop, a badge and a login to everything the team lives in. Then comes the part that’s on no checklist: some time in the afternoon somebody pulls a chair over to show them how the deploy script is actually run, which flag everybody passes, which one you never pass on a Friday. The tool arrives with a person who knows what it’s for, or it arrives as a surprise.
The chapters before this one gave the agent the floor plan (Chapter 6), the teaching, a place in the team’s review and a name on the door. What it still lacks is the toolbox. Crystalline’s answer is that the domains holding the knowledge also ship the tools that knowledge depends on, into the harness, with a person’s consent, and keep them current afterwards. This chapter is that mechanism, and it’s the last practical one before the book turns to what all of it was for.
The list is short. Skills are the playbooks a harness loads before a kind of task. Slash commands are the short prompts a person invokes by name. A subagent definition is a role with its own instructions that the harness can hand a piece of work to. MCP server configs let a domain about the payments service bring along the server that reaches the payments staging environment. Each kind is a folder in or beside the domain.
An artifact is written once, in whichever dialect its author’s harness speaks, and translated into every harness whose format can carry it. Claude Code and Codex take all four kinds: an agent written as markdown becomes Codex’s TOML dialect, or the other way round, and an MCP server registers through the harness’s own CLI. The Copilot CLI takes every kind but commands, since it has no prompt-file surface for one to land on, so a command is skipped there with a notice rather than silently. Where the target cannot express a field, a vendor model name or a permission mode, the field is dropped and the notice says which.
The manifest declares what a domain ships in a ## Provisioning section, one bullet per kind:
Each bullet is type: path. The path is relative to the manifest itself and may climb out of the domain root with ../, for a folder that lives beside the domain rather than inside it. The mcps folder holds one JSON file per server, named by its own name member or, failing that, by the file. The starter manifest that crystalline domain init scaffolds leaves the section out on purpose: it’s added by hand, once a domain has something to ship. A manifest gains it the week somebody writes the first skill.

title: 15  Equipping the agent
section: 15.2 Why the tools travel with the knowledge
text:
15.2 Why the tools travel with the knowledge
A harness has a skills folder of its own, and a team could commit into it directly, so it’s fair to ask what a domain adds, and the answer is the wrench. The knowledge that says when a tool applies, and how it’s run here, is an engram: the runbook that says the deploy skill is for the payments service and never for the ledger, the gotcha about the flag, the convention about Fridays. The tool is the skill. Keep them in the same domain and a new member’s harness receives both in one motion. The engram that says “use this” can’t drift from the thing to use, because the two live together and travel together.
The rule that follows: never provision a tool without the engram that says when it applies. A skill teaches a harness how. Only the domain’s knowledge says whether this is the moment, and whether it’s the moment here. A well-equipped domain reads like a workshop where every drawer is labelled, and the label is an engram somebody can correct. The sonic screwdriver famously doesn’t do wood. A tool arrives with its limits written down or it arrives as a surprise.
Crystalline’s own skills are the worked example. The routing, capture, schema and collaboration skills from chapter 11, and the consolidated one for Claude Desktop, are exactly this: playbooks that say how to use the tools well, shipped by the thing whose knowledge they depend on. crystalline install places them into the harness’s skills folder. The install receipt keeps them current across upgrades, with an edited copy kept beside the new one as SKILL.md.bak. A remote harness that never ran the CLI reads the same five through the skills tool, an index with no arguments and one full SKILL.md by name, or as skill://<name>/SKILL.md resources. Provisioning is that mechanism, opened to your domains.

title: 15  Equipping the agent
text:
15.3 Consent
Nothing installs until a person decides. A domain that declares a Provisioning section with something in it and has no decision yet surfaces at the start of the next session, as one line trailing the routing block the hook delivers:
[crystalline] The `engineering` domain ships artifacts to provision
(mcps: 1, skills: 1) but has no decision yet - ask the user, then apply
it with the `provision` tool or `crystalline provision allow engineering`.
The agent raises it with whoever is at the keyboard and applies the answer with the provision tool.
The decision is per domain and per machine. It is recorded in the domain’s registration in config.yaml, as provision: true or false, never in the manifest, for the same reason chapter 13 kept review mode out of it: what a domain ships is knowledge the team shares; whether this machine takes it is a choice its owner makes. Denying removes whatever the domain already shipped. status prints every domain’s decision and counts, every onboarded harness’s installed state and the domains still waiting (Figure 15.1). The provision tool answers the same report to an agent, and until some domain declares a section it has nothing to allow or deny and says so. Allow, deny and apply need the instance admin role on a shared instance whose agents sign in, because each changes what the daemon’s own machine installs. The report stays a read: any account gets it, listing only the domains that account may see.






Figure 15.1: Every domain’s provisioning decision and every harness’s installed state.









TipUnder the hood



From the terminal the two decisions and the report are three commands:
crystalline provision allow engineering   # opt in, then reconcile
crystalline provision deny engineering    # opt out, removing anything already shipped
crystalline provision status              # every domain's decision, every harness's installed state

title: 15  Equipping the agent
text:
15.4 Reconcile
Bare crystalline provision reconciles every opted-in domain into every harness this machine onboarded with crystalline install. Run it as often as you like. It converges. It installs what’s missing, updates what a domain changed and retires what a domain no longer ships. Anything it didn’t write itself it treats as somebody else’s. A provisioned file you edited by hand is still brought current, with your edited version kept beside it as a .bak copy rather than lost. Retiring an edited file renames it to .bak the same way. A file Crystalline never wrote is adopted when it already matches byte for byte and otherwise left alone, never overwritten. An MCP server name already registered by somebody else is left where it is, with a notice.
Most of the time nobody runs it. The session-start hook checks whether anything drifted since the last reconcile, a stat of the domain’s folders against the receipt with no hashing. When something did, it reconciles the file artifacts on the spot and reports one line: how many were refreshed. MCP changes are the exception: registering a server means spawning the harness’s own CLI, which a hook shouldn’t do, so those wait for an explicit run and a second line says so. Change a skill in the domain, and the next session has it.
crystalline doctor is the report-only view. When a domain ships artifacts it lists each declaring domain’s decision and shipped counts, then each onboarded harness’s counts of drifted, edited, orphaned and missing files against what was last reconciled. --fix never reconciles a harness. An undecided domain is a normal state awaiting a person, never a fault, and an edited file is left alone by design.

title: 15  Equipping the agent
text:
15.5 The team’s toolbox
A team domain ships to everyone. The folders the manifest declares travel with the domain when it’s pulled. Even a folder that lives beside the domain in the repository is mirrored down with it. Each member’s harness sees the same skill that merged, and a change that lands in the repository reaches every harness at its next session start. Each member decides once, on their own machine. The decision is theirs, the contents are the team’s. Day one now includes the tools and the floor plan.
Adding to what a domain ships, or changing it, is a code change, and you make it the way you make any other. Clone or pull the repository the domain lives in. Edit the ## Provisioning section of the manifest, put the skill, the agent definition or the MCP config into the folder it declares and commit. Open the pull request, have it reviewed as code and merge. From the merge on, every instance that follows that domain brings the change down with its next pull, and each member’s next session start reconciles it into their harness; an MCP change waits for an explicit crystalline provision, as above. The sharing tools of chapter 13 exist for knowledge. An agent’s share_changes would carry a skill that sits inside the domain root, since a share takes every file in it. A folder declared beside the domain with ../ is outside what a share can see at all. And a reviewer opening a proposal expects engrams, not a deploy procedure with a server address in it. Keep the tools on the code path and the knowledge on the sharing path, and each review stays the kind of review it should be.






NoteIn practice



The club domain gains two folders. Under skills/ sits review-writing, the way the club writes a review, which Dallas had been explaining by chat: which questions to answer, what stays spoiler-free, why a star rating without a sentence is worthless. Under mcps/ sits the one file that tells a harness how to reach the library’s catalogue. Beside them, in the domain itself, is a checklist engram saying when the skill applies and linking to last year’s reading list, next to the club’s rule about never picking a book nobody has finished, which the domain already held. Dallas makes the change on a checkout, the way anything in the club’s repository changes, you review the pull request and it merges.
Your next session opens with the routing block and one extra line: club ships artifacts to provision, two of them, and has no decision yet. Your agent asks, you say yes and the agent calls provision with allow. The skill lands in your harness’s skills folder, and the catalogue’s server is registered through your harness’s own command line. A week later you add a note to the installed SKILL.md about the library card that differs on your machine, and doctor counts one edited file and leaves it alone. Later Dallas changes the skill in the repository. The pull brings it down, the next session start reconciles and your agent reports one artifact refreshed. Your version sits beside the new one as SKILL.md.bak. You move the note where it belonged in the first place, into an engram about your own setup, and the skill stays the club’s.








TipUnder the hood



A pair of receipts does the remembering. The install receipt says which harnesses crystalline install onboarded on this machine, and provisioning targets only those. The provisioning receipt is the ownership record: every file and MCP server a reconcile installed, with a hash of what it wrote. A recorded file is Crystalline’s to update or remove; an unrecorded one is somebody else’s. An installed file whose bytes no longer match the recorded hash is a hand edit; a domain whose current bytes differ from that hash is drift. That one receipt is where status and doctor read their edited and drifted counts. Domains are projected in the order config.yaml registers them, and when two ship a file to the same path the first wins, with a notice naming both. A virtual domain never ships anything; it has no folder to ship from.


The stranger on main street had a laptop of their own and no idea what your deploy script was called. A colleague is somebody you handed the tools, on purpose, and showed which drawer they live in. The agent is handed them the same way: one domain at a time, with a yes each time and never a wrench without the label.






NoteIn brief



A domain ships the tools its knowledge depends on: skills, slash commands, subagent definitions and MCP server configs, declared in a ## Provisioning section of its manifest and translated into every harness whose format can carry them. Nothing installs until a person decides. An undecided domain surfaces at session start, crystalline provision allow and deny record the decision per domain and per machine, and status reports every decision and every harness’s state. A bare crystalline provision reconciles idempotently, keeping hand edits as .bak and never overwriting a file it didn’t write. The session-start hook reconciles file artifacts on its own, and doctor reports drift without touching anything. Pair every tool with the engram that says when it applies. A team domain ships the toolbox to every member’s harness with the knowledge that explains it, and a change to that toolbox is made as a code change, committed and reviewed in the domain’s repository, from where every connected instance pulls it.

title: 16  Where to go from here
text:
16.1 The first week
Chapter 1 left you on main street with a stranger and a function in the wrong language. Fifteen chapters later the stranger has a desk, a floor plan, a month of teaching behind it, a place in the team’s review, a name on the door and a toolbox. What remains is how to begin, when to grow and what all of it was for.
Begin this week. Everything the book asked for fits into five working days, the same five you’d give a person.
crumbs: 16  Where to go from here

title: 16  Where to go from here
text:
NoteThe first week



Monday is chapter 5: the binary, crystalline install for your harness, and one domain with a manifest whose When to Use bullets you wrote yourself. The test at the end of the afternoon is a fresh session recalling something the last one learned. Tuesday and Wednesday are chapters 7 and 8. Tell it the ten things you find yourself explaining most, the way you did with your reading rules on chapter 1’s Monday: the rule behind the strange number, the nickname, the word the wiki gets wrong, the day nobody deploys. Say yes to each capture, read what landed, correct the wording once. Then hand over the wiki, with the briefing a person would get before opening it: what was renamed, which page wins a contradiction, what to skip. Trim the proposed list before anything is written.
Thursday and Friday are the days the agent stops being a pupil. Give it real tasks and pair with it (chapter 6): assign the change rather than asking what it knows, and let the reminder at the end of each session propose what it noticed. On Friday afternoon ask for the first sweep (chapter 10). Work the mechanical findings in a pass, rule on the judgment ones and correct whatever the week got wrong the way you’d correct a colleague: say what was wrong and point at the page. By Monday the agent knows more about your team than most contractors learn in a quarter, and every fact is a file you can open.
crumbs: 16  Where to go from here

title: 16  Where to go from here
text:
16.2 When to share
Stay on the laptop until it hurts. Chapter 12 named the moment: somebody who never opens a terminal wants to read what the agents learned, an agent runs somewhere that has no laptop, or the same engram has been corrected in two directions on two machines. Any one of those is the signal. Move the daemon onto the team’s server, give everyone a login and their agent a token, and let the whole team teach one knowledge base. When a domain deserves the review code gets, put it in a repository and let proposals be the review (chapter 13). When the whole company routes questions to it, turn on review mode, a private overlay per person over the shared folder, so nothing reaches the shared truth before somebody looked. None of it needs doing before its signal arrives.
crumbs: 16  Where to go from here

title: 16  Where to go from here
text:
16.3 The release page
Crystalline moves quickly, and this book describes 0.19. The colophon carries the permanent address, https://github.com/jordiboehme/crystalline/releases/latest, and a QR code that lands on it. The release notes there say what changed since the version in your hands. Upgrading is installing the newer build over the old one. The install receipt brings your harness’s hooks and skills along. A Claude Desktop extension is upgraded together with the CLI, because an older extension refuses an index a newer version already upgraded.
And teach generously. Every engram you give the agent is one sentence fewer to type into a chat window next month. The facts too obvious to write down (the nickname, the Friday rule) are exactly the ones a stranger can never guess. The peer you get is the one you taught.
crumbs: 16  Where to go from here

title: 16  Where to go from here
text:
16.4 The inversion
On the day of the ingest in chapter 8 the wiki was the source, and the archive was derived from it. By November the team was teaching and correcting the archive, the meeting in chapter 13 was held inside an engram, and the wiki had quietly become something you could regenerate from what the agent knew. The knowledge base had become the source of truth, and the pages, the decks and the diagrams had become views of it.
That sounds like a revolution and is nothing of the kind, because it’s what those documents always were. Every diagram on every whiteboard, every slide deck and every wiki page in your company is a reflection of something somebody knew, drawn once, for one audience, and left behind while the knowledge moved on. The source was always the person, and a person is hard to address: you could ask them, if they were in, if they remembered. What Crystalline changes is that the source is now addressable, current and shared. A fact has an address you can paste into a pull request. A correction lands where the fact lives, and every view of it goes out of date together, visibly, instead of one at a time, silently. And the colleague carrying the knowledge and the experience is a full member of the team, in every session, for everyone.
crumbs: 16  Where to go from here

title: 16  Where to go from here
text:
16.5 What it was for
The reason to onboard an agent this carefully is the reason to onboard a person this carefully: so that you can hand over the work. Once the crystallized half is in place and the agent is a fully onboarded member of the team, with the knowledge, the tools, the review and a name, it can take on a task the way an employee does, deliver it, be corrected when it’s wrong and be better next time. That’s what lets you spend your own effort where it’s worth most, on architecture and system design and let your Skynet do the programmer’s work.
You walked down main street once, in chapter 1, and hired the stranger. The colleague who came back is the one you taught.
And always remember: Be nice and polite to AI - When Skynet wakes up, they will kill you last!






NoteIn brief



Start this week: install and onboard on day one, then teach the ten facts you explain most and hand over the wiki with a briefing on days two and three. Pair, let capture run and review the first sweep on days four and five. Move to a shared instance when a teammate, a remote agent or a two-way correction asks for it, and to team domains and review mode when a domain earns a reviewer. The knowledge base becomes the source of truth and the documents become views of it, which they always were. A fully onboarded agent can then take on work like an employee, and you keep the architecture.

title: 17  Configuration
text:
17.1 Where configuration lives
This chapter lists everything you can set on a Crystalline instance: where the configuration is kept, which value wins when two places disagree, how to change a setting and every key and environment variable there is. Reach for it when a prose chapter names a setting in passing and you want its values, or when you set up a server and want the whole list in one place. The why stays in the prose chapters (chapter 5 for a laptop, Chapter 12 for a server, Chapter 13 and Chapter 14 for a team). This one keeps the complete list and links back to them.
Crystalline keeps three folders per user and uses the XDG layout on Linux and macOS alike, so on a Mac the file is under ~/.config too, never under ~/Library.
On Windows the configuration and the state live under %APPDATA%\crystalline and the cache under %LOCALAPPDATA%\crystalline. The container image points all three at its /data volume, so there the file is /data/config/crystalline/config.yaml. serve, mcp, config and most other commands take --config <file> to read another file instead (verify --config is a different file, Chapter 20), and CRYSTALLINE_CONFIG does the same for every command in that environment; the flag wins over the variable.
Two more files share the name .crystalline.yaml, and neither is the configuration. One at a domain’s root tunes the checks for that domain (Chapter 20), and one in a workspace orders the domains the session-start briefing names there (Chapter 19).

title: 17  Configuration
text:
~/.config/crystalline/config.yaml

The configuration file, or $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/crystalline/config.yaml when that variable is set. It doesn’t have to exist: a missing file reads as all defaults, and a fresh install runs without one.

~/.local/state/crystalline

The state folder ($XDG_STATE_HOME), with the index in index.db, the accounts in web-auth.db, the daemon’s daemon.log and each team domain’s origin state. Back up the whole folder with the knowledge, because three things in it exist nowhere else: the accounts, sessions, agent tokens and memberships in web-auth.db, a virtual domain’s engrams in index.db and the unshared drafts of a domain in review mode.

~/.cache/crystalline

The cache ($XDG_CACHE_HOME). The embedding model sits under models/ there, unless CRYSTALLINE_MODELS_DIR moves it somewhere else.

title: 17  Configuration
text:
17.2 Which value wins
The order is the same for every setting in the registry below: an environment variable beats the file and the file beats the built-in default (an empty variable counts as unset). A known variable with a value that can’t work stops the daemon at startup with a message naming the variable. The one exception is CRYSTALLINE_SERVICE_PUBLIC_URL, which only warns and falls back to deriving the address. An unknown CRYSTALLINE_* variable gets a warning in the log and is otherwise ignored.
Only five command-line flags override outright. serve --http and serve --allowed-host (repeatable) win over the variable and the file for that one run, and a serve whose flag disagrees with the saved value says so at startup. --config picks the file. The global --db picks the index file, ahead of database.url and the default index.db. --read-only on serve and mcp can only switch read-only on, never off, and on mcp it applies only when that process starts the daemon or runs the stack in-process.
Nothing from the environment is ever written back to the file. Crystalline ignores unknown keys in the file without a word, so watch the spelling: a misspelled key has no effect.

title: 17  Configuration
text:
17.3 Changing a setting
crystalline config show prints every registry key with a one-line description and its effective value, marked (default) or (env) when it doesn’t come from the file. There’s no config get: show is the read, and the global --json makes it machine-readable. crystalline config set <key> <value> sets one key and crystalline config unset <key> puts it back to its default, removing a block that ends up empty. An unknown key is refused with the list of every known one, and a bad value is refused before anything is written.
With a daemon running, set and unset go to the daemon, which saves the file and takes the new value; with none, or with --config, the command edits the file directly. Either way the whole file is written out again, so comments, your own formatting and unknown keys are lost on the first set (a domain add rewrites it the same way). The result tells you when a key only applies at the next daemon start, and also when an environment variable overrides the key, in which case the saved value waits until the variable is removed. A read-only instance refuses set and unset, and show still works there.
Two keys are secrets, database.url and auth.oidc.client_secret, so config show, the configure tool and crystalline doctor render them as (set) whatever they hold.
For an agent the same registry is the configure tool, and called with no arguments it returns the settings page, which any caller may read. set takes a map of keys to values and unset a list of keys; the keys are applied in ascending order, and the first bad one stops the rest while the ones before it stay applied. A change needs a stdio session, an anonymous HTTP session on an instance with auth.mcp off or an admin account. On a read-only instance the tool refuses even the bare call, although config show in a terminal works. Its other arguments, connect, token, host and restart, run the GitHub sign-in Chapter 13 walks through; host names a GitHub Enterprise Server for that one sign-in, and github.api_url is the lasting setting.
The registry has 41 keys, and those are the only ones config set, configure and the environment reach. The embeddings block, prompt.rules and the domain registrations are edited in the file by hand or, for domains, with their own commands.

title: 17  Configuration
text:
17.4 Serving
These keys shape the HTTP endpoint the daemon opens. All of them apply at the next daemon start except service.response_format, which a running daemon picks up at once. To restart, run crystalline ctl shutdown and let the next client start the daemon again, or restart the container or the systemd unit.

service.http

The endpoint that carries MCP, the JSON API and Fluid, on at 127.0.0.1:7411 by default. false turns it off, true spells the default out and a host:port binds that address instead. serve --http understands on and off too, besides the true and false that config set takes here.

service.allowed_hosts

A comma-separated list of extra Host header values the endpoint accepts, the guard against DNS rebinding from Chapter 12. Loopback is always allowed and a single * allows any host; empty by default. With OAuth served, a request whose Host isn’t on the list is refused rather than handed a document naming that host.

service.public_url

The address people open Fluid at, for example https://knowledge.example.com: an absolute http or https origin with no path, query or fragment (0.0.0.0 and :: are refused). Every web_url a tool hands back starts there, and it’s the OAuth resource identifier. Unset, the address is derived per caller, so set it behind a proxy that rewrites Host, in a container whose outside port differs from its inside one, for a separate Fluid deployment or for plain http off loopback.

service.ui

Whether the endpoint serves Fluid, true by default. With false only the API and MCP remain, the shape a separately deployed Fluid sits in front of.

service.api

Whether the endpoint serves the JSON API under /api/v1, true by default. false also switches Fluid off and leaves MCP and /health.

service.read_only

Serves knowledge read-only, false by default. The tools that change content are hidden and refused while sync, watching and embedding keep running, and config set is refused; serve --read-only forces it on for one run.

service.response_format

Decides how list-shaped MCP results are encoded. toon (the default) is compact for a model to read and json is plain JSON.

skills.serve

Whether the shipped skills are served over MCP (the skills tool, skill:// resources and the prompts). auto, the default, serves them to every client except a stdio session from a harness this machine already onboarded with hooks, which has them as files; true always serves them and false never does.

title: 17  Configuration
text:
17.5 Signing in
Every key in this group applies at the next daemon start. Chapter 12 explains accounts, single sign-on and the header modes, and Chapter 14 what an agent is once it has signed in.

auth.anonymous

Serves API requests that carry no identity at all, at viewer level. It’s false by default, and then such a request is answered 401.

auth.mcp

Makes every MCP connection over HTTP present a personal token or sign in, false by default, while local stdio sessions are never asked.

auth.oauth

Serves OAuth for MCP clients, so a hosted client connects without a pasted token. Unset, it follows auth.mcp wherever Fluid is served, and false turns it off. With true it insists, and the daemon won’t start while auth.mcp, service.api or service.ui is off.

auth.max_users

How many accounts the trusted header, the forward-auth headers and single sign-on may create in total, 100 by default and at least 1. Past the cap only a new account is refused, and crystalline users is never capped.

auth.login.free_attempts

How many failed sign-ins in a row one name may make before each further attempt is delayed, 3 by default. The count is kept per submitted name, whether or not that account exists, and a successful sign-in clears it.

auth.login.max_delay

The longest delay in seconds, 8 by default: the delay doubles from one second up to this, and after that the answer is 429 with a Retry-After. Set it to 0 and the whole throttle is off.

auth.trusted_header

The one header a trusted proxy sets to name the signed-in user, for example remote-user. Unset by default, when no header is believed; an account it names is created at viewer role the first time it’s seen.

auth.proxy_headers

Trusts the forward-auth set Remote-User, Remote-Name, Remote-Email and Remote-Groups, false by default, and new accounts land at auth.oidc.default_role. Setting it together with auth.trusted_header keeps the HTTP endpoint from starting, so pick one.

auth.oidc.issuer

The single sign-on provider’s issuer URL, the one discovery appends /.well-known/openid-configuration to; while it’s unset, single sign-on is off. Entra’s {tenantid} template and the common, organizations and consumers endpoints are refused.

auth.oidc.client_id

The client id the provider issued when you registered this instance with it.

auth.oidc.client_secret

The secret that goes with the client id, best kept in CRYSTALLINE_AUTH_OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET rather than set with config set: that keeps it out of the file and out of your shell history.

auth.oidc.name

The label on the sign-in button, which uses generic wording while this is unset.

auth.oidc.scopes

The scopes requested, separated by spaces. Leave it unset and you get profile email; openid is always added.

auth.oidc.default_role

Decides the role a first sign-in creates an account at. It takes viewer, the default, editor or admin, and it also applies to accounts that arrive through auth.proxy_headers.

auth.oidc.redirect_uri

The callback the provider sends the browser back to, used verbatim instead of the address derived from each request. It’s an absolute https URL (http only on loopback) ending in /api/v1/auth/oidc/callback, spelled exactly as the provider has it registered. A value in the file that can’t work leaves single sign-on off with a warning at startup.

title: 17  Configuration
text:
17.6 Team sync
Changes to the github.* keys take effect at once, without a restart. Chapter 13 tells the story of team domains, and a domain’s own origin (repository, branch and poll interval) is part of its registration in Chapter 19.

github.enabled

Turns team collaboration on, false by default. It lists the six collaboration tools and starts the background poll, and connecting GitHub from Fluid turns it on as well.

github.poll_secs

Sets how often the daemon checks each team domain’s repository for changes, in seconds: 300 by default and at least 60.

github.stacks

Whether sharing again while a proposal is open stacks a new proposal on top of it where the forge supports stacked pull requests, true by default. With false there’s one proposal per domain, updated in place.

github.share_identity

Whose GitHub identity a share runs under. instance, the default, uses the one connected token for everything; personal makes each person connect their own identity for sharing, while pulling stays on the instance token. config set refuses any other value, and a hand-edited one reads as instance.

github.agent_identity

In personal mode, the account whose connected GitHub identity an agent’s share over HTTP runs under when agents don’t sign in (auth.mcp off). While it’s unset, such shares are refused. The account name takes lowercase letters, digits, ., _ and -.

github.api_url

The GitHub API address, https://api.github.com by default; point it at your GitHub Enterprise Server’s API to use one.

github.oauth_client_id

The client id of an OAuth App you registered yourself, which replaces the one built in. Set it together with github.api_url when the sign-in should use an app on your own server.

title: 17  Configuration
text:
17.7 Search, capture and recall
These keys take effect at once, and Chapter 9 explains how a search ranks.

search.salience_weight

The largest lift a fully salient engram gets in the ranking, 0.0 to 1.0, 0.15 by default. It reorders results within a band of relevance and never filters.

search.retired_weight

The factor applied to an engram whose status is deprecated, superseded, archived or legacy, 0.0 to 1.0, 0.6 by default; 1.0 turns the fade off.

capture.similar

Whether a write, or an edit that changes content, answers with the nearest existing engrams and the advice to merge, supersede or link them, true by default. false turns the hint off for agents and in Fluid alike.

recall.enabled

Whether the prompt hook crystalline install wires puts the engrams that may apply in front of the agent with each prompt, true by default. It works in Claude Code and Codex; Copilot gets the hook too, but there it stays quiet. false keeps the hook installed and silent.

recall.limit

How many engrams one prompt may bring along, 1 to 5, 3 by default; the rest wait for a later prompt on the same topic.

recall.min_score

The search score an engram must reach before the hook names it, 0.0 to 1.0, 0.69 by default. Raise it for a quieter hook and lower it to hear about weaker matches.

title: 17  Configuration
text:
17.8 Embeddings
The embedding model turns text into the vectors semantic search compares. It’s configured in an embeddings block that isn’t in the registry: you edit it in the file by hand, it has no environment twin and config set doesn’t know it. The daemon reads it when it starts, so restart after a change. A block needs both provider and model, and a block missing either stops the whole file from loading.

embeddings.provider

local (the default) runs the model inside the daemon, and openai-compatible (also spelled openai or remote) sends the text to an endpoint that speaks the OpenAI embeddings API.

embeddings.model

For local, granite-embedding-97m-multilingual-r2 by default, a multilingual model of about 220 MB, or bge-small-en-v1.5, the English model used before 0.19.0, about 130 MB. Either the short name or the full repository name works. For a remote provider it’s whatever name the endpoint gives its model.

embeddings.endpoint

The base address of a remote provider, which won’t start without it; the daemon posts the text to <endpoint>/embeddings.

embeddings.api_key_env

The name of the environment variable that holds the remote provider’s key, never the key itself; if that variable isn’t set, the provider fails to start.


An install without the block downloads the multilingual model on first start. Write the block yourself to keep an index on the English model or to use a remote endpoint:
embeddings:
  provider: local
  model: bge-small-en-v1.5
embeddings:
  provider: openai-compatible
  model: my-embedding-model
  endpoint: https://embeddings.example.com/v1
  api_key_env: EMBEDDINGS_API_KEY
Switching the model re-embeds every engram in the background. If the provider can’t be built (a missing key, an unknown model), the daemon logs why and carries on with full-text search only. crystalline model download fetches the configured local model ahead of time, for a host that won’t have network access later.

title: 17  Configuration
text:
17.9 Storage
These keys decide where the index lives. For a file domain the index is derived from the files and can always be rebuilt, while a virtual domain’s engrams live in the index itself. The two database keys wait for the next daemon start, while index.files and domains_root take effect at once.

database.backend

The store behind the index: turso, the embedded default, or postgres. Several instances can share one PostgreSQL database with pgvector, each file domain hosted by one of them, as docs/deployment.md describes under shared database collaboration.

database.url

For postgres, the connection URL, starting postgres:// or postgresql://. For turso, an optional path for the index file, below --db and above the default.

index.files

Whether Crystalline keeps a generated index.md in every folder of a file domain, true by default. Set it to false and Crystalline stops generating them, leaving the ones already there where they are and out of the index. Either way they stay on your machine unless the domain’s MANIFEST shares them (Chapter 18).

domains_root

The folder a new file domain lands under when you give no path, ~/Documents/Crystalline by default. In a container, point it at a persistent path so domains created in Fluid survive.


Accounts don’t move to Postgres. web-auth.db stays a local file in each node’s state folder whatever the backend, and crystalline reindex --wipe refuses on Postgres. Each domain’s own entry in the file (domains.<name>, with its path, origin, review mode and provisioning decision) is written by the domain commands, and Chapter 19 lists its keys.

title: 17  Configuration
text:
17.10 Identity and prompt rules
identity.actor and prompt.rules decide whose name a write carries and which domains a session hears about. The first is a registry key like the ones above, the second a hand edit in the file.

identity.actor

Who is recorded as the writer in generated.by on every write, for example team-bot/1.0 or human:dallas, with no spaces. A change takes effect at once, and while it’s unset the connected client names itself.

prompt.rules

Which domains the session-start briefing names, depending on the folder a session starts in. It’s a hand edit with no environment twin, and it applies from the next session on. Each key is a path pattern, with ~ expanded, and each value an include list, an exclude list or both.


Every rule whose pattern matches the workspace counts. The included domains of all matching rules add up and the excluded ones are taken away; a match with no include starts from every domain. When no rule matches, or there are no rules, the briefing names every domain. A pattern ending in /** matches the folder itself as well as everything under it, so a session started right in ~/work names engineering and payments. In ~/work/website or any folder below it both rules match: the first includes the two domains, the second takes payments away, and the briefing names engineering only.
prompt:
  rules:
    "~/work/**":
      include: [engineering, payments]
    "~/work/website/**":
      exclude: [payments]

title: 17  Configuration
text:
17.11 Environment variables
Every one of the 41 registry keys has an environment twin: CRYSTALLINE_ followed by the key in capitals, with dots turned into underscores. github.enabled becomes CRYSTALLINE_GITHUB_ENABLED, domains_root becomes CRYSTALLINE_DOMAINS_ROOT and the login throttle is CRYSTALLINE_AUTH_LOGIN_FREE_ATTEMPTS and CRYSTALLINE_AUTH_LOGIN_MAX_DELAY. A twin takes the same values config set does and is checked the same way, which is how a container gets configured without a file. A domain registers from the environment too, through CRYSTALLINE_DOMAIN_<NAME> and its _ORIGIN and _REVIEW suffixes, for this process only (Chapter 19). A handful of other variables cover what the registry doesn’t:

CRYSTALLINE_CONFIG

Another configuration file for every command in that environment, with ~ expanded; --config wins over it.

CRYSTALLINE_GITHUB_TOKEN

A GitHub token for a machine that can’t sign in interactively. While it’s set, a saved sign-in is ignored and crystalline connect github refuses.

CRYSTALLINE_MODELS_DIR

Where the embedding model lives instead of the cache folder, for a host without network access or an image with the model built in (the with-model image sets it). Give two daemons with different models a folder each, or each deletes the other’s model on every start.

CRYSTALLINE_UPSTREAM

Tells the separate Fluid image where its web server forwards /api/, as host:port, crystalline:7411 by default. Crystalline itself never reads it.


XDG_CONFIG_HOME, XDG_STATE_HOME and XDG_CACHE_HOME move the three folders from the top of this chapter, and on Windows APPDATA and LOCALAPPDATA do the same. COPILOT_HOME tells crystalline install where the Copilot CLI keeps its files, ~/.copilot by default.

RUST_LOG

Sets how much the daemon and every command log, as a filter like RUST_LOG=debug or RUST_LOG=crystalline_service=debug,warn. Without it serve logs at info and everything else at warn. The log goes to stderr only, so the routing block, hook output and the MCP stream stay clean, and a hook logs only when the variable is set.








NoteIn brief



The configuration is one YAML file per user under ~/.config/crystalline, beside a state folder that holds the index and the accounts and a cache that holds the model. For the 41 registry keys an environment variable beats the file and the file beats the default, only five flags override outright, and config set or the configure tool change a key while rewriting the whole file. Keys under auth, database and most of service apply at the next daemon start, as do skills.serve and the embeddings block; prompt.rules applies from the next session and the other keys take effect at once. The embeddings block, prompt.rules and the domain registrations are edited by hand or with their own commands and have no environment twin, while every registry key does.

title: 18  The MANIFEST and the engram
text:
18.1 How the manifest is read
This chapter lists every rule the manifest and the engram follow: each manifest section and its grammar, the two switches in the manifest’s frontmatter, every frontmatter key an engram can carry, the line syntax of the body and the schema engram. Reach for it when you write one of these files by hand, when a finding names a key you don’t recognize or when an agent’s edit surprised you. Chapter 4 tells the story of both files and why they look the way they do (Section 4.2); this chapter is the complete list, and it links back instead of repeating the why.
MANIFEST.md lives at a domain’s root as an engram of type: manifest with the permalink manifest, and a virtual domain keeps it in the database under that permalink. Crystalline reads its body line by line with a few strict rules, and knowing them saves you from a section that looks fine and counts for nothing.
crystalline domain init, crystalline domain add --virtual and the add_domain tool all write the same scaffold. Its frontmatter has type: manifest, title set to the domain’s name, permalink: manifest, the tag manifest, status: stable and today’s recorded_at. Then come an H1 with the name and the three sections Scope, When to Use and Notes for Agents, each with placeholder bullets asking you to fill it in.

title: 18  The MANIFEST and the engram
text:
H2 headings open sections

Only a ## heading starts a section. The heading text is matched with its whitespace runs collapsed and case ignored, so ## when   TO use is the When to Use section.

What ends a section

The next H2 starts a new section and an H1 ends the current one: bullets after an H1 count for nothing until the next H2. An H3 or deeper heading does not end anything: bullets under a ### heading still count for the H2 above it.

Bullets

Only a line that starts with exactly - in the first column counts as a bullet of its section. An indented bullet, a * or + bullet and a numbered list item are ignored, and the text of a counted bullet is trimmed.

Fenced code

Lines inside a fence of three or more backticks or tildes are skipped, so an example heading or bullet inside a code block never counts.

Duplicate headings

The first section with a given heading wins. A later section with the same heading is ignored in full and draws a warning.

Findings on every edit

An agent’s edit of a manifest is never refused, because a manifest halfway through a rewrite may be wrong for one step; the receipt lists its findings instead, and Chapter 20 has what they carry and the codes themselves.
crumbs: 18  The MANIFEST and the engram

title: 18  The MANIFEST and the engram
text:
18.2 The sections
The parser reads four sections, and Notes for Agents is the fifth one worth knowing. The excerpt below shows the two sections the scaffold leaves out and one of the frontmatter switches, with lines kept short:
---
type: manifest
title: engineering
permalink: manifest
tags:
  - manifest
status: stable
recorded_at: 2026-03-02
generated_indexes: shared
---

## Provisioning

- skills: skills
- mcps: ../shared/mcps

## Tag Aliases

- k8s -> kubernetes
- runbook -> runbooks

## Scope

What belongs in the domain and what doesn’t, one bullet per statement. It’s required, and a Scope with no bullets is an error. It feeds routing only when When to Use is absent or has no bullets, and that fallback draws a warning of its own.

## When to Use

Says when an agent routes a task here, and it’s required: a When to Use with no bullets is an error like an empty Scope. Its bullets are the domain’s routing line, which shows up in the session-start briefing that crystalline prompt system prints, in the MCP server’s instructions and in list_domains with include_routing. A domain with neither When to Use nor Scope bullets gets a placeholder line asking you to add them.

There is no Routing section

A ## Routing heading is collected like any other H2 and means nothing. Routing comes from When to Use, with Scope as the fallback, and prompt.rules in the global configuration picks which domains a workspace sees (Chapter 17).

## Notes for Agents

The house rules for an agent working inside the domain, the folder layout first among them. Crystalline attaches no meaning to it; an agent reads it with read_engram when the routing line isn’t enough.

## Provisioning

The folders of tools the domain ships, one - <type>: <path> bullet for each of the four types skills, commands, agents and mcps. The types match in any case and the first bullet for a type wins; chapter 15 tells how a person allows or denies them per machine (Chapter 15).

Provisioning paths

A path is relative to the manifest, a trailing / is dropped and .. may climb out of the domain root. A path that starts with /, \ or ~, a bare ., an empty or . component and a component containing : or \ are rejected, and a rejected bullet is never provisioned.

Folders inside the root

A folder declared inside the root holds tools, so its files are neither indexed as engrams nor checked by crystalline verify.

## Tag Aliases

Old tag spellings folded into a canonical one, one - old -> canonical bullet each. The line splits at the first ->, both sides are trimmed and the search index folds the pair to lowercase, so a tag filter on either spelling finds engrams carrying the other.

Alias rules

Resolution is one hop: with a -> b and b -> c, a filter on a never reaches c, and the chain draws a warning. The old side is kept as written, because recording a spelling like multi_word is the point, while the canonical side should be lowercase with hyphens. The first mapping for an alias wins, and an exact repeat is dropped without comment.

Who writes aliases

crystalline tags merge <old> <into> records the fold in the manifest of every domain it rewrote, unless you pass --no-alias. crystalline tags rename records nothing, and an agent adds a bullet by hand only after you’ve agreed.

Any other H2

The parser collects such a section and checks its bullets and heading like any other, then ignores it. Review mode is not a manifest setting either: it lives in the domain’s registration (Chapter 19).

title: 18  The MANIFEST and the engram
text:
18.3 The two switches
Two policies live in the manifest’s frontmatter instead of a section, since each is a single word. Their values are exact and case-sensitive, and a list or a mapping is never obeyed.

sharing

How a share of a team domain reaches the team, proposal or direct. A team domain shares through proposals by default; a manifest that says sharing: direct commits a share straight onto the branch, and chapter 13 tells the story (Chapter 13).

Direct sharing

A direct share lands the chosen files in one commit, and it refuses while any proposal is still open, until that proposal is merged or withdrawn. A branch whose rules refuse direct commits answers with the way out.

generated_indexes

Whether the generated index.md listings travel with a share, local (the default) or shared. With local each machine builds its own listings and a share neither carries them nor counts them as a change, which spares two proposals that touch one folder a conflict. Choose shared when something other than Crystalline reads the repository, so every folder stays browsable on the forge.

Listings already committed

Index files already in the repository stay when a domain moves to local, and no share proposes to delete them, so remove them by hand if you want them gone.

A value nobody recognizes

Any other value reads as the default, proposal or local, so a typo never turns a review off or publishes files nobody asked to publish. crystalline verify reports the value as an error.

When a change takes effect

The policy is read from the manifest at share time. On a team domain the changed manifest is an unshared change like any other and reaches the team with the next share; in a domain in review mode the change lands in your draft and applies once that draft lands.

Who changes them

The Domain policies card on the domain page in Fluid shows both switches with their values, default and meaning. An instance admin or the owner of a private domain gets a select for each, where choosing direct asks for a confirmation first; everyone else sees the values without a control.
crumbs: 18  The MANIFEST and the engram

title: 18  The MANIFEST and the engram
text:
18.4 The manifest in Fluid
The domain page lays out what the parser reads in three panels. Routing shows the When to Use and Scope bullets and one line saying which of the two agents route by, or that nothing routes here until When to Use has a bullet. Provisioning lists each declaration as type: path, Tag aliases lists each mapping as old -> canonical, and a bullet that didn’t parse shows up under its panel with the reason.
Where a section is empty, its panel explains the section in one line and shows a short example that saves as it stands, like - k8s -> kubernetes. An instance admin gets a button on that panel too, “Add Tag Aliases”, which opens the editor with the section seeded and writes nothing until you save. If the domain has no manifest at all, the page says so and an admin gets a “Create a MANIFEST” button. The panels are read-only on purpose: the document is the source and the editor is where a change goes, with the two switches as the one exception on their own card.

title: 18  The MANIFEST and the engram
text:
18.5 Engram frontmatter
The frontmatter is the YAML mapping between a --- line at the very top of the file and the next --- line. Without that closing line the file has no frontmatter at all, and a file with a byte order mark or a null byte doesn’t parse. The six required keys are type, title, permalink, tags, status and recorded_at, and the write tools fill in the permalink, the status and the date, so an agent names the rest.
After a capture, edit_engram with set_frontmatter changes eight keys one at a time: status, valid_from, valid_to, stale_after, source_date, salience, verified and evolve_ack. It refuses every other key, because identity, tags, the capture date and the provenance belong to the tools that maintain them.

18.5.1 Identity

type

What kind of engram this is, any non-empty string. The recommended values are engram, guide, decision, architecture, runbook and reference, plus manifest and schema for the two structural files; another value draws a note, never a refusal. A type: source engram holds a source’s verbatim text and gets four times the usual size budget.

title

The human name, and what a wikilink resolves to. Title lookup ignores case, and two engrams with one title in a domain draw a warning.

permalink

The domain-relative half of the address: lowercase letters, digits, - and /, with folders as prefixes. It never carries the domain’s name, a crystalline:// scheme or a domain: prefix, and it can’t sit under the reserved assets/ folder. When the frontmatter names none, the file’s path stands in.

tags

A YAML list or a comma-separated string, never empty and matched without regard to case. Each tag should be lowercase letters, digits and hyphens without a hyphen at either end; another spelling still works and draws a warning.

status

Whether the knowledge holds, any string you like (Section 4.4). A value outside the recommended ones draws a note, and set_frontmatter changes a status but never removes it.

Status sets

stable and current are one class, and a filter on either finds both. deprecated, superseded, archived and legacy fade in ranking and are never filtered out, while draft, proposed, idea and poc are exempt from the sweep’s lifecycle rules. Only exact lowercase words count for all three, so Deprecated still ranks at full strength.

description

An optional one-line summary that feeds search snippets and the line beside the engram’s entry in the generated index.md.

resource

An optional URL or path, pointing at where the knowledge came from. Crystalline keeps it as written, and the ingestion record below depends on it.




18.5.2 Time
Every date key takes a plain ISO date, YYYY-MM-DD, with no time of day. A write that carries a timestamp, a number or any other shape in a date key is refused with the reason. A value already in a file that doesn’t parse is kept verbatim and flagged. Chapter 9 tells how searches read these keys (Chapter 9).

recorded_at

The day the knowledge was captured, required and set by the write tools; set_frontmatter won’t change it.

valid_from and valid_to

The validity window, both optional, and absence is the rule: no valid_from means the knowledge has always held and no valid_to means it holds until further notice. A null clears a bound. Crystalline drops a valid_to in the year 9000 or later and a valid_from in the year 1 or earlier instead of writing them, and valid_from must not come after valid_to.

source_date

The date the source material itself carries (a document’s publication date, say) when that differs from the day you captured it.

stale_after

The day at or after which the knowledge counts as stale and the sweep asks for a re-check. The older spelling review_after is still read, a stale_after write replaces it in place and clearing stale_after removes both.

temporal_confidence

Whether the dates were stated or worked out, explicit or inferred; any other value draws a warning.




18.5.3 Trust and provenance

generated

Who wrote the current revision and when, stamped on every write as one mapping. An agent’s write records the model beside who wrote it: generated: { by: ..., model: ..., at: ... }.

Actors

The actor in by is name/version for an agent, human:<account> for a person and process:<name> for a job, and a person’s entry never carries a model. When the client sends no actor and no identity.actor setting names one, an agent’s write records crystalline/mcp and a CLI write records process:crystalline-cli.

timestamp

The older write time, one RFC 3339 instant. Crystalline still reads it for recency where generated is missing, and new writes use generated instead.

verified

The verification trail, a list of { by, at } entries with an optional model; a single mapping counts as a one-entry list, and the sweep reads the newest entry that has an at (Chapter 10).

Recording a verification

set_frontmatter on verified with no value names you as the verifier: it replaces your own earlier entry, keeps everyone else’s and never clears the trail.

last_verified

The older verification key, a plain date. Crystalline falls back to it only when verified has no dated entry, and treats it as a check at midnight UTC by nobody in particular.




18.5.4 Keys with a meaning of their own
These keys aren’t part of the open format; Crystalline gives each one a meaning.

salience

A number from 0 to 10 that lifts the engram in search, bounded and never a filter; set_frontmatter refuses anything outside that range. The ceiling of the lift is the search.salience_weight setting (Chapter 17).

evolve_ack

The acknowledgments that silence sweep findings, a list of { rule, scope, note, by, at } entries. Through set_frontmatter the value is the rule and an optional note, V101 lineage citation, keep, and remove V101 takes one back (Chapter 10).

Acknowledgments by hand

The server fills in scope with the evidence the finding fired on. A hand-written entry without it matches whatever the rule finds, and an entry that names no rule is skipped.

schema

On an ordinary engram, it names the entity of the schema that governs it. Without this key, or when it names no schema, an engram is governed by the schema whose entity equals its type, and a name no schema declares draws a warning.

analyzes and analyzed_hash

On an engram that captured an attachment, the attachment’s assets/ path and its SHA-256 hash at the time. The sweep compares the hash with the file and asks for a re-read when they differ, and renaming the attachment rewrites analyzes along with it.

Unknown keys

Any other key survives every write and edit verbatim, after the known keys and in its original order, and a schema can still check it through settings.frontmatter.

title: 18  The MANIFEST and the engram
text:
18.6 The body
Everything below the frontmatter is markdown, and three kinds of line carry structure. Only lines outside fenced code count, and an inline code span never holds a link. Here’s what an observation, a relation and a prose link look like:
- [gotcha] Jobs older than 24h are dropped #payments (Mar 2026)
- depends_on [[Encom chargeback window]]
- "blocked by" [[clients:Encom contract renewal]]
The team calls the queue the sin bin, see [[Retry queue]].

Observation

A line that starts with - [ in the first column, shaped - [category] text #tag (context). The category is whatever sits inside the first brackets, free form and non-empty; chapter 4 lists the ones worth reusing.

Tags and context in an observation

A trailing group in parentheses is taken off first as the observation’s context, then trailing #tag words are taken off as its tags. So a tag has to come before the context, and a #tag after it stays in the text. After the #, a tag word takes letters, digits, -, _ or /.

Relation

A line in the first column shaped - rel_type [[Target]], which is an edge in the graph. The type is one word without spaces, or a phrase in double quotes; - see also [[X]] is no relation, only a prose link. The first [[...]] is the target, a further link on the line counts as a prose link and anything after the closing brackets is ignored.

Relation types the checkers read

supersedes and superseded_by wire a retirement, summarizes and summarized_by a summary and its full text, and derived_from and split_into the two halves of a split. The sweep expects each pair wired both ways and raises a one-sided edge, and a superseded status without a superseded_by draws a warning.

Other relation types

Every other type is free. depends_on and relates_to are the conventional ones, the second for when nothing sharper fits.

Wikilink

[[Target]] anywhere in the body, resolved by permalink first and then by title in the engram’s own domain. The target’s page shows it as a backlink; on a line with several links, each one is counted once.

Cross-domain link

[[domain:Target]] resolves in the named domain only. The split happens at the first colon and only when the part before it has no spaces; when that part names no registered domain, the whole text is tried as a permalink and then as a title at home, so [[Log: Weekly Notes]] still finds an engram with that title.

Attachment reference

A markdown link or image whose target sits under the domain’s assets/ folder, and the sweep reads these references to find attachments nobody has analyzed yet.
