title: 18  The MANIFEST and the engram
text:
18.7 Addresses and reserved names
The address and its one absolute form are explained in chapter 4 (Section 4.6); the entries below give every rule it follows.

crystalline://domain/permalink

The absolute address of one engram. A trailing /* anchors a whole folder for build_context, and a crystalline:// address you write in prose is checked by crystalline verify like a link.

Domain-relative identifiers

Anything without the scheme is relative to a domain given beside it, so retry-queue-gotcha together with the domain engineering is right, while engineering/retry-queue-gotcha names a folder called engineering.

Headings

An address names a whole engram, never a heading, and crystalline verify reports one with a # in it as broken. To open one section, use the engram’s web_url from a read or a write receipt and add # with the heading’s slug: lowercase, spaces as hyphens, letters, digits, hyphens and underscores kept and the rest dropped. A repeated heading gets -1, -2 and so on.

index.md and log.md

Both names are reserved at every folder level and never hold an engram. Crystalline regenerates index.md as the folder’s listing and never writes log.md, and a title that would slug to either is refused.

assets/

The folder attachments live in, and no permalink may point into it.
crumbs: 18  The MANIFEST and the engram

title: 18  The MANIFEST and the engram
text:
18.8 Schema engrams
A schema engram states what engrams of one type should contain, and validate_engrams checks them against it. It’s an engram of type: schema, and beside the usual engram keys its frontmatter carries the declaration in the Picoschema form:
type: schema
entity: runbook
version: 1
schema:
  service: string
  severity(enum): [low, high, critical]
  step(array): string
  owner?: Team
settings:
  validation: warn
  frontmatter:
    resource?: string

entity

The type the schema governs. An engram with that type, or with schema: naming it, is checked against it, and only schemas in the engram’s own domain count.

version

An integer that numbers the schema, kept as written.

schema

The field declarations for the body. A field with a lowercase type is an observation category of that name, so service: string asks for a - [service] ... line. A field with a capitalized type is a relation of that name, so owner?: Team names an optional - owner [[...]] relation.

Field names

A plain name is required and name? is optional. name(array) allows many lines, name(object) nests further declarations and name(enum) takes a YAML list of allowed values, one of which an observation’s text must match exactly.

Field types

string, integer, number, boolean, any or a capitalized entity name. A value of "string, what it holds" adds a description after the comma, and an unknown lowercase type counts as any while the definition draws an error.

settings.validation

How strict the check is: warn reports warnings, strict reports errors and off checks nothing. The default is warn, case doesn’t matter and any other value draws an error in the definition.

settings.frontmatter

Declarations for frontmatter keys, in the same syntax, including unknown ones. A finding names a nested key with a dot, as in review.owner.


infer_schema proposes a first schema from the engrams of a type that exist already. validate_engrams with drift lists the categories and relations in use that the schema doesn’t declare, and the declared ones nobody uses.

title: 18  The MANIFEST and the engram
text:
18.9 The ingestion record
The shipped skills add one convention on top of the format, and Crystalline doesn’t parse any of it. When an agent reads a source into a domain, a repository or a manual or a long document, it writes one record engram under sources/ with type: ingestion, titled after the source. The record carries resource for where the source lives, source_date where it has one, a verified entry and a source_version key holding a commit, a version, a revision or a content hash. Its body says what was extracted, which engrams received it as links and what was left out on purpose.
The next pass searches type: ingestion for the source’s resource, fetches only what changed since source_version, folds the change into the linked engrams, then moves source_version on and stamps verified. To Crystalline, source_version is an unknown key like any other, kept as written. Don’t mix the record up with a type: source engram, which holds a source’s own words (Chapter 8).






NoteIn brief



The manifest counts only H2 sections, matched without regard to case or spacing, and only - bullets in the first column, outside fences, with the first of two equal headings winning. Scope, When to Use, Notes for Agents, Provisioning and Tag Aliases are its sections, routing comes from When to Use with Scope as the fallback, and sharing and generated_indexes are its two frontmatter switches, reading as proposal and local whenever they say anything else. An engram needs type, title, permalink, tags, status and recorded_at, takes plain dates where it takes dates, treats an absent validity bound as unbounded and keeps every key it doesn’t know. Its body carries observations as - [category] text #tag (context), relations as - rel_type [[Target]] and links as [[Title]] or [[domain:Title]]. A type: schema engram declares in Picoschema what one type should contain, and the finding codes are in chapter 20.

title: 19  Domains
text:
19.1 Kinds of domain
This chapter is the lookup for everything you can set on a domain and every rule you run into while doing it: reach for it when a prompt to the agent isn’t enough (a script, a container or the question of why a command refused). The prose chapters keep the why (domains in Section 4.1, private domains in Chapter 12, team domains and review mode in Chapter 13, membership in Chapter 14, provisioning in Chapter 15). The MANIFEST’s own keys are in Chapter 18 and every other setting is in Chapter 17.
Every domain is one of three kinds, and the same tools read and write all of them. Whether a domain lives in files or in the database is fixed when you register it, and a file domain turns into a team domain once you connect an origin to it.

title: 19  Domains
text:
file domain

A folder of markdown files with a MANIFEST.md at its root, the default kind. The files are the source of truth and the index is derived from them, so a rebuild of the index loses nothing.

virtual domain

A domain that lives in the database with no folder on disk, for a container without a writable volume or a Postgres backend shared by several machines. Its engrams live only in the index, so removing it deletes them and crystalline reindex --wipe refuses while one is registered.

team domain

A file domain with an origin: a GitHub repository, an optional subfolder in it and a branch. It needs github.enabled and a GitHub connection, and it can’t be virtual, because a proposal needs files to carry.

title: 19  Domains
text:
19.2 The registration block
Each registered domain is one entry under domains: in the global config.yaml, keyed by its name, and the commands in this chapter write these entries for you. crystalline config set doesn’t reach them, so a key without a command is a hand edit.
domains:
  books:
    path: ~/Documents/Crystalline/books
    provision: true
  club:
    path: ~/Documents/Crystalline/club
    origin:
      repo: dallas/book-club
      path: knowledge
      branch: main
      poll_secs: 600
    review: overlay
  reading:
    kind: virtual

kind

Either file or virtual, and it only appears on a virtual domain, since a file domain leaves the key out.

path

The domain’s root folder, with a leading ~ expanded; a file domain registered without one lands at <domains_root>/<name>, and a virtual domain has none.

origin.repo

The GitHub repository of a team domain, as owner/name; its presence is what makes a file domain a team domain.

origin.path

The subfolder of the repository that is the domain root, for a repository that holds more than knowledge (absent means the repository root).

origin.branch

The branch the domain tracks. Adding a team domain without a branch writes the repository’s default branch here, asked from GitHub; an entry without the key, from before that or written by hand, tracks main.

origin.poll_secs

How often the daemon checks this origin for merged work, in seconds. Absent defers to the global github.poll_secs (300 unless set), and any value below 60 is raised to 60. No command sets it, so it’s a hand edit.

provision

This machine’s decision on the artifacts the domain ships: true installs them into every onboarded harness, false keeps them out and removes what was installed. Absent means undecided, and nothing installs.

review

overlay puts the domain in review mode; absent means the domain takes changes directly, which is how every domain starts.

title: 19  Domains
text:
19.3 Names
The name is the key in the config, the folder under the domains root, the first segment of every crystalline:// address and the word the agent routes by, so choose it once: no command renames a domain.

What a name may be

Letters and digits in any script, plus -, _ and ., up to 64 characters, with no dot at the start or the end. The Windows device names (CON, PRN, AUX, NUL, COM1 to COM9, LPT1 to LPT9) are refused on every platform. The command line, add_domain, Fluid and the API all run this check, and so does domain init --name, with the same message everywhere. A name registered before the check existed keeps working.

Names taken already

Adding a name that is already registered at the same folder, or as the same virtual domain, changes nothing and indexes it again, so every way of adding a domain is safe to repeat. The same name at another folder or as the other kind of domain is refused, and the message names what holds it. Every surface also refuses a name that an environment variable already defines, and the refusal names the variable, because that domain belongs to it.

Names given for you

add_domain without a name takes the folder’s name, with a suffix when that one is taken, and a team domain takes the repository’s name; a name made this way is always turned into a valid one (a folder called CON becomes con-2). Fluid does the same for a team domain whose name field is left empty.

title: 19  Domains
text:
19.4 Registering a domain
There are five ways in: the agent’s tool, the command line, Fluid, the JSON API behind it and environment variables. Each registers the domain, and all but --no-sync index it at once.

add_domain

The MCP tool, with domain, folder, virtual, repo, path and branch. The arguments pick the kind: repo makes a team domain, virtual: true a virtual one (it needs domain), anything else a file domain, and repo and virtual can’t be combined.

add_domain on a folder

A folder without a MANIFEST.md gets a starter one, and the files already there are kept and adopted in place. Without folder the domain lands at <domains_root>/<domain>.

Who may call add_domain

Any local session may. Over HTTP, on an instance where agents sign in, it takes the instance admin role, and a read-only instance refuses it.

crystalline domain add <name> [path]

Registers a domain and indexes it at once, in <domains_root>/<name> when no path is given. A file domain needs a MANIFEST.md in its folder already and refuses with the domain init line otherwise.

--virtual

Registers a virtual domain and scaffolds its MANIFEST into the index; it takes no path and can’t be combined with --origin.

--origin owner/repo[/subfolder]

Connects a team domain and downloads the repository, or the subfolder given after its name, into the domain’s folder; it needs github.enabled and a prior crystalline connect github. A folder that already holds knowledge, or a registered domain with no origin yet, is connected in place: nothing local is overwritten, and files that differ from the repository become local changes to share.

--branch

The branch to track, and it only works with --origin. Left out, Crystalline asks GitHub for the repository’s default branch and records it; when GitHub can’t answer, the add refuses and asks for --branch.

--no-sync

Registers a file domain without indexing it, for a script that runs crystalline sync later; a team domain is always indexed as it connects, so the flag refuses with --origin.

--private and --owner <account>

Registers the domain private from its first minute, owned by the named account. --private needs --owner, and before anything is registered the account has to exist and be enabled. A domain that is already registered is refused here; crystalline domain visibility makes that one private.

crystalline domain init <path>

Creates the folder if needed and writes a starter MANIFEST.md with the Scope, When to Use and Notes for Agents sections, then prints the domain add line to run, or says a MANIFEST is already there and leaves it alone. --name sets the name in the manifest, the folder’s name otherwise. It never touches the config.

crystalline domain list

Lists the registered domains, with engram counts when the index is there.

Fluid’s New domain dialog

Only admins get the dialog. Its Kind is Local folder, Virtual or GitHub team, and the fields follow it: a Name for the first two; a Repository, Branch, Folder in the repository and an optional Name for a team domain. A local domain always lands under the server’s domains root, since a browser can’t name a folder on the server, and the Private box makes the domain private with you as its owner.

POST /api/v1/domains

The request behind the dialog, for a script, with mode (local, virtual or github), name, repo, branch, path and private as its fields. A field that doesn’t belong to the mode is refused rather than ignored, and a team domain on an instance with no GitHub connection is refused with where to make one.

CRYSTALLINE_DOMAIN_<NAME>=<path>

Registers a file domain for as long as the variable is set, for a container that shouldn’t carry a config file. The domain’s name is <NAME> in lower case with _ turned into -, and the variable replaces a config.yaml entry of that name, with a warning at startup, without ever being written into the file.

CRYSTALLINE_DOMAIN_<NAME>_ORIGIN

Attaches an origin to that domain, as owner/repo[/subfolder][@branch], so a new node downloads the team domain on its first start; with CRYSTALLINE_GITHUB_ENABLED off the domain waits and says so, and without the matching CRYSTALLINE_DOMAIN_<NAME> the daemon refuses to start. Because the suffix is read first, no variable can define a domain whose name ends in -origin or -review, so register such a domain in the file, and look in Chapter 17 for the GitHub token variable that goes with the origin.

title: 19  Domains
text:
19.5 Moving knowledge in and out
These commands copy engrams between a domain and a folder or an archive, and none of them changes the domain’s registration.

crystalline domain import <path> --domain <name>

Loads engram files that are already well formed into a registered virtual domain, verbatim. A file domain is refused: for a folder of notes that still needs converting, crystalline import writes into the domain’s folder and crystalline sync indexes it.

--overwrite and --dry-run on domain import

An engram whose path or permalink already exists is skipped unless --overwrite says otherwise, and --dry-run reports what would land and writes nothing.

crystalline domain export <path> --domain <name>

Writes any domain’s engrams out as an ordinary markdown folder, which is how a virtual domain’s content gets checked with crystalline verify or turned back into files. --force writes into a folder that isn’t empty, and --dry-run only reports.

Fluid’s Backup card

The card sits above the Danger zone at the foot of the domain’s page and is drawn for admins. Download archive saves a zip of the whole domain, MANIFEST and attachments included, and works on a read-only instance too. An archive from a file domain restores into a virtual one and the other way round.

Import archive

Uploads such a zip into the domain, shows a preview of every entry first and imports only after you confirm. Skip existing, the default, leaves a path that’s already there alone, and Overwrite existing replaces it. A MANIFEST in the archive is never imported, and a broken or oversized archive is refused as a whole.

title: 19  Domains
text:
19.6 Removing a domain
Removing a domain unregisters it and clears its rows from the index. A file or team domain’s files stay on disk and the team’s repository is never touched: the only knowledge a removal can delete is a virtual domain’s, and that takes an explicit confirmation.

crystalline domain remove <name>

Unregisters the domain. Registering the same folder again adopts the files as they are, and a team domain is connected again with its repository, which keeps its origin. The visibility and membership records go too, so a later domain under the same name starts out shared.

--purge

Confirms that a virtual domain’s engrams are deleted with it, and nothing brings them back afterwards; a virtual domain that holds any refuses without it, so export first when you want a copy.

--end-drafts <actor>

Names one other person whose private drafts in a review-mode domain end with the removal; repeat it for each. The refusal says who is drafting and how many drafts each holds, and your own drafts need no naming.

remove_domain

The MCP tool, with domain, purge and end_drafts working as the flags do. On a harness that can ask, the first call removes nothing and puts a confirmation question to you naming the domain, its kind, its engram count and the drafts at stake.

Who may remove a domain

The machine operator, an instance admin or, for a private domain, its owner. An agent on an instance that leaves agent authentication off is refused. A domain defined by an environment variable can’t be removed at all: unset the variable instead.

Unregister domain

The button in the Danger zone at the foot of the domain’s page, drawn for admins and for a private domain’s owner. It asks you to type the domain’s name and says whether the files stay on disk or, for a virtual domain, are deleted.

title: 19  Domains
text:
19.7 Visibility and membership
Every domain starts shared, visible to every account on the instance. A private domain is visible only to its owner, the instance’s admins and the accounts invited into it, and to everyone else it answers as if it had never been registered (Chapter 12).

crystalline domain visibility <domain> private --owner <account>

Makes the domain private and hands it to that account, which has to exist and be enabled. Making a domain that is already private private again changes nothing, its owner included.

crystalline domain visibility <domain> default

Shares the domain with every account again and forgets its list of members, so making it private later starts from the owner alone.

Make private and Share with everyone

The same switch in Fluid’s Danger zone, confirmed by typing the domain’s name. Making a domain private is for admins, and the admin who does it becomes the owner; sharing it again is for the owner or an admin.

viewer

The membership level that reads and searches the domain and nothing more. It’s the level an invitation takes unless you name another.

editor

A viewer who also writes and edits engrams in the domain, as far as the account’s instance role allows.

manager

An editor who also runs the membership: inviting, removing and changing levels up to manager. A manager can’t change visibility, transfer the domain or remove it.

crystalline domain members <domain> list

Prints the owner and every member with their level, though a shared domain has no owner and no members, because membership only decides anything while a domain is private.

crystalline domain members <domain> add <user>

Invites an account, or moves a member to another level, with --level viewer, editor or manager; the owner can’t be added, because the owner already holds every level.

crystalline domain members <domain> remove <user>

Ends a membership, though the owner can’t be removed this way; hand the domain on first.

The Members card

The same list in Fluid, on the domain’s page: invite by username and level, change a level, remove, and a Leave button for a member’s own membership, which needs nobody’s permission.

crystalline domain transfer <domain> <new_owner>

Hands a private domain to another existing, enabled account, which becomes the owner at once. The old owner keeps nothing and is a stranger to the domain unless invited back. It’s for the owner or an admin, and Fluid offers it on the Members card.

A deleted owner

Deleting the owner’s account leaves the domain with no owner and only an admin can administer it after that, so transfer it before the account goes.

Instance role and membership level

On a shared domain an account does what its instance role allows: a viewer reads, an editor writes, an admin does everything. On a private domain the membership decides what the account may reach, and a write takes the lower of level and role. So an instance viewer invited as an editor writes nothing, and neither does an owner whose instance role is viewer.

The command line and a local stdio session are the machine operator and pass every gate in this table. An agent over HTTP on an instance where agents sign in is its user and gets exactly that user’s row, with no tool for membership at all. Where agent authentication is off, an agent is nobody in particular: it reads and writes the shared domains, registers and provisions without a role and is refused when it unregisters one.

title: 19  Domains
text:
19.8 Review mode
Review mode gives every writer a private overlay of drafts over a team domain’s folder, and the folder changes only with what lands on the team’s branch (Chapter 13). It lives in the registration as review: overlay, never in the MANIFEST, and no MCP tool turns it on.

crystalline domain review <domain> overlay

Turns review mode on. It needs a GitHub origin and a folder, so a virtual domain is refused, and it refuses while the folder holds unshared changes, listing their paths to share or revert first.

crystalline domain review <domain> direct

Turns review mode off, which ends every private draft in the domain. Run without answers it prints the plan (who holds drafts, how many and where two people drafted the same path), and then it needs one --fold or --discard per person the plan names.

--fold <actor>

Writes that person’s drafts into the domain’s folder as they are (your own drafts from the command line or a local session belong to the actor owner).

--discard <actor>

Ends that person’s drafts without touching the folder. Both flags repeat, one per person, and both refuse with overlay.

The Review mode card

The same switch near the foot of the domain’s page in Fluid. Turning it off shows the plan with a fold or discard choice per person, set to fold until you change it.

Who may switch review mode

The machine operator, an instance admin or a private domain’s owner; a domain an environment variable defines is refused, because its variable holds the setting.

CRYSTALLINE_DOMAIN_<NAME>_REVIEW=overlay

Puts a domain defined by CRYSTALLINE_DOMAIN_<NAME> in review mode, and any other value stops the daemon at startup, while an empty one counts as unset. The variable and a hand-edited review: key are taken as written, without the origin check the command makes, so pair them with an origin.

One proposal at a time

A domain in review mode keeps one open proposal, even with github.stacks on. A second share while one is open is refused: somebody else’s proposal is named with the choice to wait for the merge or ask for a withdrawal, and your own is withdrawn and shared again.

title: 19  Domains
text:
19.9 Sharing and sync
Whether a team domain shares through proposals or straight onto the branch is the MANIFEST’s sharing switch. That key and generated_indexes, which decides whether the folder listings travel with a share, are in Chapter 18. The per-domain part of sync is the origin block above.

github.enabled

The switch every team domain needs before it can be added or kept current, and Chapter 17 has it with the other github.* settings.

The background poll

The daemon checks each team domain’s origin on the interval above and brings merged work into the folder, and a read-only instance keeps polling, so it follows the team’s repository on its own.

title: 19  Domains
text:
19.10 The provisioning decision
A domain whose MANIFEST declares a Provisioning section ships skills, commands, subagent definitions and MCP server configs, and each machine decides per domain whether to take them (Chapter 15). The decision is the registration’s provision key.

crystalline provision allow <domain>

Sets provision: true and reconciles, installing the domain’s artifacts into every harness this machine onboarded.

crystalline provision deny <domain>

Sets provision: false and reconciles, which removes whatever the domain shipped before.

crystalline provision status

Prints every domain’s decision, the domains still waiting for one and each harness’s installed state.

provision

The MCP tool, with action set to status, allow, deny or apply and domain for the two decisions. On an instance where agents sign in, everything but status takes the admin role.

title: 19  Domains
section: 19.11 Where domains live and which ones an agent hears about
text:
19.11 Where domains live and which ones an agent hears about
Four more settings touch domains without belonging to one. Two sit in the global config and two are files named .crystalline.yaml, one in a workspace and one at a domain’s root.

domains_root

The folder a new file domain lands in when nobody names one; the setting is in Chapter 17.

prompt.rules

Narrows which domains the session-start briefing names for a workspace, by path pattern. The rule syntax and an example are in Chapter 17.

preferred_domains

A list in a .crystalline.yaml at a workspace’s root that puts those domains first in the briefing, in that order. It only reorders and never hides a domain.

Where the two routing hints apply

Both need a workspace path, so they shape the briefing the session-start hook prints with crystalline prompt system, while an agent connecting over MCP gets the server’s briefing, which covers every domain it may see and ignores both.

The domain’s own .crystalline.yaml

A file at a file domain’s root whose verify: block tunes the checker for that domain, with its keys and the codes they touch in Chapter 20; a virtual domain has no root, so it always takes the defaults.








NoteIn brief



A domain is a folder, a database-only virtual domain or a team domain with a GitHub origin, and each is one entry under domains: in config.yaml with path, origin, provision and review. You register one with add_domain, crystalline domain add, Fluid’s New domain dialog or an environment variable, and removing it leaves files on disk but deletes a virtual domain’s engrams, which is what --purge confirms. Every domain starts shared, and a private one belongs to one owner and admits members as viewer, editor or manager; a write there takes the lower of level and instance role. Review mode is switched with crystalline domain review or the Review mode card and needs a GitHub origin and a clean folder, and turning it off folds or discards each person’s drafts. prompt.rules and preferred_domains steer the hook’s briefing, and a domain’s own .crystalline.yaml tunes the checker of chapter 20.

title: 20  Every finding code
text:
20.1 Two checkers
Crystalline has two checkers, and this chapter lists every code either of them can put in front of you: what it means and what clears it. Come here when a code turns up in a verify report, a CI annotation or the maintenance queue and you want to know what it wants from you. The story behind the sweep and how the agent works its queue are in the chapter on evolving (Chapter 10); this one is just the lookup.
Verify asks whether the format holds. It reads files and needs no daemon, and its codes carry a letter for what they check: E for format, T for temporal metadata, L for links, Q for content quality, S for schemas and M for the MANIFEST. Each finding has a severity: error, warning or info (the report tags them E, W and I). The sweep asks whether the knowledge is still true and well organized. Its codes all start with V, and instead of a severity each finding carries a family, a priority and a class.
Verify codes show up in more than one place, and not every place runs every family:
crystalline verify scans folders, so a virtual domain is checked through validate_engrams, or with verify after an export (Chapter 19). That tool reports a schema finding under a name, not its number (the schema section below gives both). In Fluid’s editor the check runs whenever you pause typing, and a hard error holds the save back until you fix it. The sweep’s codes show in crystalline evolve, the evolve_engrams tool and Fluid’s maintenance page, all three reading the same queue.

title: 20  Every finding code
text:
20.2 Format: the E codes
An engram has to parse and carry a title, a permalink, a type and tags; the E codes tell you which part doesn’t hold.

E001 frontmatter doesn’t parse

The YAML between the --- lines is invalid or isn’t a mapping of keys to values (error). Fix the YAML first, because no other rule looks at a file that doesn’t parse.

E002 title or permalink missing

The engram lacks a title or a permalink (error); add the one that’s missing.

E003 type missing or unusual

Leaving out type is an error. A type outside the recommended set (manifest, schema, engram, guide, decision, architecture, runbook and reference) is only info and needs nothing, since Crystalline never enforces a closed list.

E004 no tags

The engram has no tags, or the list is empty (error). Add at least one, reusing what vocabulary shows is already in use.

E005 permalink isn’t a slug

The permalink holds capitals, spaces or other characters a lowercase slug path doesn’t (error). Use the slug the report’s fix line suggests.

E006 byte order mark or null byte

The file starts with a UTF-8 byte order mark or contains a null byte (error). Save it again as plain UTF-8.

E007 tag spelled oddly

A tag isn’t lowercase-with-hyphens (warning). crystalline tags rename changes it on every engram that carries it.

E008 permalink starts with the domain’s name

A permalink is relative to its domain and the domain’s name is each person’s own configuration, so a prefix that repeats it breaks under any other name (warning). Drop the prefix as the fix line shows; a real subfolder of the same name doesn’t count.

E009 paths differ only in case

Two paths in the domain differ only in upper and lower case (error). A checkout on macOS or Windows holds only one of them and loses the other without a word, so rename one.

title: 20  Every finding code
text:
20.3 Temporal metadata: the T codes
These check the lifecycle and provenance fields; a malformed date here (T003) is one the sweep’s V rules can’t read.

T001 status or recorded date missing

The engram has no status or no recorded_at (error); add whichever is missing.

T002 unusual status

The status is outside the recommended set: stable, current, implemented, draft, proposed, idea, poc, deprecated, superseded, archived and legacy (info). Status is free form, so there’s nothing you have to change.

T003 malformed date or provenance

A date field (recorded_at, valid_from, valid_to, source_date, stale_after or the older last_verified and review_after) isn’t a plain YYYY-MM-DD, a timestamp isn’t RFC 3339, generated isn’t a mapping with a by, or verified isn’t a { by, at } entry or a list of them (error). Write the value in that shape.

T004 window inverted

valid_from lies after valid_to (error). Correct whichever date is wrong.

T005 superseded without a successor field

The status says superseded and no superseded_by relation is present (warning). Add - superseded_by [[Successor]], or pick the retirement status that fits when nothing replaced it (Chapter 10). The sweep’s V004 also catches a relation that doesn’t resolve.

T006 no write provenance

The engram carries no generated block and no older timestamp (warning). Every write and edit through Crystalline stamps one, so a file written by hand clears on its first edit through the agent or Fluid.

T007 unknown temporal confidence

temporal_confidence is set to something other than explicit or inferred (warning); pick one of those two.

T008 placeholder end date

valid_to lies in the year 9000 or later, a stand-in for “forever” (warning). Remove the field; with no end date the window stays open, and that’s how an engram says it holds indefinitely.

title: 20  Every finding code
text:
20.4 Links: the L codes
These check that every link and relation reaches something, within the domains the run scanned.

L001 broken link

A [[wikilink]] or relation target resolves to nothing, in this domain or in another domain the same run scanned (warning). Fix the spelling or capture the engram the link expects.

L002 permalink used twice

Two files share one permalink, so one address names two engrams (error); change one of them.

L003 title used twice

Two files share one title, so a [[Title]] link can’t tell them apart (warning); retitle one or merge them.

L004 self-link

An engram links or relates to itself (warning); remove the link.

L005 broken crystalline:// address

A crystalline:// address in the body names an engram that doesn’t exist in a domain the run scanned (warning). Correct the address or remove it. Addresses inside code fences and backticks are skipped.

L006 link leaves the run

A link names a domain this run didn’t scan, so verify can’t check it (info). Pass that domain’s root to the same run when you want it checked.

title: 20  Every finding code
text:
20.5 Content quality: the Q codes
These look at the body: whether there is one, whether it fits and whether its bullets parse.

Q001 almost no content

The body has fewer than three non-blank lines outside code fences (error). Write the knowledge down, fold it into the engram that owns the topic or delete the file.

Q002 over the size budget

The body is over its token budget, counted roughly as characters divided by four: 2,500 by default and four times that for a type: source engram (error). Split it; the sweep’s V105 says which split fits, and the budget can be tuned per domain (see “Silencing and tuning” below).

Q003 duplicate heading

Two headings at the same level carry the same text (warning). Rename one or merge the two sections.

Q004 near-duplicate sections

Two ## sections of one engram carry nearly the same text, usually a paste nobody finished (warning); fold them into one.

Q005 near-miss bullet

A bullet almost matches the observation or relation grammar: -[category] without the space, an unclosed [category or an unclosed [[Target (info). Fix the typo, or the line never becomes an observation or a relation.

title: 20  Every finding code
text:
20.6 Schemas: the S codes
You’ll only meet these in a domain with schema engrams (the reference on the engram describes their format, Chapter 18). S001 to S004 are errors on the schema engram itself and S010 is a warning. S020 to S033 check an engram against its schema, and their severity comes from the schema’s settings.validation: warn makes them warnings, strict makes them errors and off silences them. In validate_engrams they carry the name in parentheses instead of the number.

S001 schema without an entity

The schema engram has no entity (error); add the type it governs.

S002 schema without declarations

There’s nothing under schema: (error), so declare the fields there.

S003 malformed declaration

A field declaration has an empty name, a modifier other than array, enum or object, an enum that isn’t a non-empty list, an object that isn’t a mapping, an unclosed parenthesis or a type other than string, integer, number, boolean, any or a capitalized entity name (error). Correct the declaration, in the body or under settings.frontmatter.

S004 unknown validation mode

settings.validation isn’t warn, strict or off (error); use one of the three.

S010 schema reference matches nothing

An engram’s schema: key names an entity no schema engram in the domain declares (warning); fix the name or write the schema.

S020 required relation missing (MissingRequiredRelation)

The engram lacks a relation its schema requires; add it.

S021 required observation missing (MissingRequiredObservation)

The engram lacks an observation category its schema requires; add one.

S022 observation value outside its list (ObservationEnumViolation)

An observation holds a value the schema’s enum doesn’t allow; use an allowed one or extend the enum.

S023 observation value of the wrong type (ObservationTypeMismatch)

An observation’s value doesn’t match the scalar type its schema declares; correct the value.

S030 required frontmatter field missing (MissingRequiredFrontmatter)

The engram lacks a frontmatter key its schema requires; add it.

S031 frontmatter value outside its list (FrontmatterEnumViolation)

A frontmatter value isn’t one the schema’s enum allows; use an allowed one.

S032 frontmatter field isn’t a list (FrontmatterNotArray)

The schema declares the key as an array and the engram holds a single value; write it as a list.

S033 frontmatter value of the wrong type (FrontmatterTypeMismatch)

A frontmatter value, or an item in a list, doesn’t match the declared scalar type; correct it.

title: 20  Every finding code
text:
20.7 The MANIFEST: the M codes
The MANIFEST is configuration as well as an engram: its When to Use bullets route every session to the domain (Chapter 18). M001 to M007 are errors and M101 to M108 warnings. You can put the same structural checks on any other file of a domain through the verify file described below.

M001 MANIFEST missing

The domain root has no MANIFEST.md, or a file the domain requires is missing. Create it; a MANIFEST carries type: manifest.

M002 wrong type

The MANIFEST’s type isn’t manifest, or a required file lacks the frontmatter the domain asks for. Correct the type or add the frontmatter.

M003 required section missing

## Scope or ## When to Use is absent, or a section the domain requires of another file; add it.

M004 section without bullets

Scope or When to Use has no top-level bullets (a - at the start of the line), or a configured section has fewer than its minimum; write the bullets.

M005 invalid provisioning path

A Provisioning path is absolute, home-relative, a bare . or contains a component that isn’t allowed, and nothing is provisioned from it. Give a relative path to the folder.

M006 unknown generated_indexes value

The key says neither local nor shared. It’s read as local, so the folder listings stay on your machine; fix the spelling.

M007 unknown sharing value

The key says neither proposal nor direct. It’s read as proposal, so shares still go through review; fix the spelling.

M101 When to Use empty

When to Use has no bullets and routing falls back to Scope. It comes along with M003 or M004 and says what sessions do in the meantime. Writing the bullets clears all of them. In a required file it means a configured fallback section stood in.

M102 bullet too long

A bullet in any ## section runs over 180 characters, or over a required file’s configured maximum; shorten it or split it into two.

M103 duplicate section heading

The same ## heading appears twice and the reader keeps only the first; merge the two sections.

M104 unknown provisioning type

A Provisioning bullet names a type other than skills, commands, agents or mcps, so pick one of those.

M105 provisioned folder missing

A folder the Provisioning section declares inside the domain doesn’t exist; create it or correct the path. Folders outside the domain root aren’t checked.

M106 malformed provisioning bullet

A Provisioning bullet has no colon or no path, or declares a type twice. Write one - type: path line per type.

M107 tag alias problem

A Tag Aliases bullet lacks the old -> canonical shape, maps a tag to itself, maps an alias a second time (the first wins), points at a target that isn’t lowercase-with-hyphens or points at another alias. Correct the bullet; an alias resolves in one hop.

M108 verify settings problem

The domain’s .crystalline.yaml holds a severity word verify doesn’t know (E007: of), or the file doesn’t parse at all, so the override you meant isn’t there. It’s reported against .crystalline.yaml in crystalline verify and in validate_engrams. Fix the word or the YAML; the rule keeps its default until you do.

title: 20  Every finding code
text:
20.8 Reading a V code
Every sweep finding carries a family, a priority and a class. The number beside each code here is the rule’s starting priority, what an unremarkable engram shows in brackets. The queue adds up to ten for salience, five for an engram three or more others link to and eight for one a person wrote, capped at 100, and min_priority (--min-priority in a terminal) drops what scores under a floor. The mechanical rules, which the agent completes without asking, are V005, V103 and V102 when the nearest title is a near-exact match in the domain the link named. The rest are judgment, which the agent brings to you one at a time. Engrams with the status draft, proposed, idea or poc are exempt from V002, V003 and V006, and retired engrams are never called old, unverified or unlinked.

title: 20  Every finding code
text:
20.9 Sweep, temporal: V001 to V010
The temporal family watches dates and the retirement lifecycle, plus attachments and unshared work that have waited too long.

V001 expired window still current (85)

The valid_to date is in the past and the status still says current. If the fact still holds, extend or remove valid_to; if it ended, retire the engram and wire the supersede pair when something replaced it.

V002 review date passed (70)

The stale_after date has passed and nobody has verified the engram since. Re-check the claim: record a verified entry and a later stale_after when it holds, correct or supersede it when it doesn’t.

V003 old and never verified (25)

A current engram is over 180 days old with no verification and no stale_after. Confirm it and record a verified entry, or set a stale_after so a later sweep has a real date to compare.

V004 superseded without a successor (65)

The status says superseded and no superseded_by relation resolves. Name the successor, or switch to deprecated, archived or legacy when nothing replaced it.

V005 replaced but still current (90, mechanical)

Another engram declares that it supersedes this one, and this one still reads current. Set the status to superseded, add superseded_by and set valid_to when the end date is known.

V006 human capture never reviewed (50)

A person captured this directly (its generated.by starts with human:) on an earlier day and nobody has recorded a verification. Verify the claim, align the tags, wire the relations both ways and record a verified entry; any change to the wording is proposed to its author first (Chapter 7).

V007 attachment never analyzed (50)

An engram shows an attachment and no engram claims it with analyzes. Read the attachment, capture what it teaches, and set analyzes and analyzed_hash on the engram that covers it.

V008 attachment changed since analysis (60)

The attachment’s current hash no longer matches the engram’s analyzed_hash. Re-read it, bring the engram in line, update analyzed_hash and record a verified entry.

V009 unshared work aging (40)

A team domain holds substantive local changes that have waited a week or more to be shared. The finding is about the domain rather than an engram, and regenerated folder listings never count. Share the changes after a yes (Chapter 13).

V010 carry-forward gap (55)

A retired engram holds observations that appear in no live engram of its domain. Move the ones that still hold into their own engram with split_engram, or acknowledge the finding when they expired too. Matching is by text, so a fact carried forward in other words takes an acknowledgment as well. A retired engram that already declares split_into stays quiet.

title: 20  Every finding code
text:
20.10 Sweep, structure: V101 to V109
The structure family watches the graph: links, relation pairs, size and where files and attachments sit.

V101 live link to retired knowledge (55)

A current engram links to a retired one. Repoint the link at the successor the evidence names, or keep it as a historical citation and acknowledge the finding.

V102 unresolved link (50, mechanical or judgment)

A link or relation points at nothing. Fix the spelling (the fix line names the nearest title), add a domain prefix or capture the engram the link expects; the target is never created automatically.

V103 one-sided relation pair (35, mechanical)

One half of supersedes/superseded_by, summarizes/summarized_by or derived_from/split_into is missing on the engram the finding names. Append the inverse there, as the fix line spells it out.

V104 orphan (30)

Nothing links to the engram and it links to nothing, 14 days after it was recorded. The rule runs only in a domain where at least a quarter of the engrams are linked, and it skips the MANIFEST and schemas. Link it into the neighbourhood its tags suggest, or acknowledge that it stands alone on purpose.

V105 oversized (60)

The body is over its token budget, the same size verify’s Q002 flags. The fix line picks the split: a distilled summary with the full text moved to a type: source engram under sources/, sequential parts when the engram is already a source or a split by topic when the observations alone are over.

V106 stub (45)

The body has fewer than three content lines, the shape verify’s Q001 flags. Enrich it, fold it into the engram that owns the topic or retire it.

V107 attachment reference to nothing (45)

The engram references an attachment path that holds no file. Restore the file (a Fluid upload or an archive import) or correct the reference, after asking, since either changes what readers see.

V108 orphaned attachment (55)

A file under assets/ is referenced or claimed by no engram. Delete it (delete_engram with the assets/ path, or Fluid’s Delete attachment button), or analyze it into an engram that claims it first. Deleting can’t be undone, so the agent asks.

V109 permalink off its folder (45)

The permalink names a different folder than the one the file sits in, usually after a move made by hand, so a build_context glob on the folder misses it. Files at the domain root never raise it. Repair it with move_engram, passing the file’s current path as destination and path as permalink, which rewrites every reference; ask first, since the new address breaks bookmarks outside Crystalline. A deliberate custom permalink is acknowledged instead, which holds until the permalink or the path changes.

title: 20  Every finding code
section: 20.11 Sweep, redundancy: V201 to V203 and V301
text:
20.11 Sweep, redundancy: V201 to V203 and V301
The redundancy family watches for knowledge written down twice, in the text, the titles, the tags or the meaning.

V201 near-duplicate content (80)

Several engrams carry nearly the same text. Merge into the richest one, then supersede or delete the others after repointing every inbound link. Detection compares wording, so a paraphrase can only show up as V301.

V202 near-duplicate titles (55)

Two engrams in one domain carry titles so close that links and search can’t tell them apart. Merge them or retitle one.

V203 tag drift (30)

One concept is spelled several ways in the domain’s tags, a finding about the domain rather than an engram. Run the crystalline tags merge command the fix line spells out; the agent hands it to you rather than rewriting tags itself.

V301 semantic twins (75)

Two current engrams say close to the same thing in different words, measured by their embeddings, so the rule runs only where the instance computes them. If one owns the topic, merge into it and supersede the other; if they disagree on a fact, reconcile them; if they are distinct, link them and acknowledge the pair. A pair already in a V201 cluster shows only there.

title: 20  Every finding code
text:
20.12 Silencing and tuning
A sweep finding is silenced where it stands, in the engram, and a verify code is tuned for a whole domain in a file at its root. Neither mechanism reaches the other’s codes.

20.12.1 Acknowledging a sweep finding
An acknowledgment is a note that a person looked at a finding and ruled it intentional. It lives in the engram’s evolve_ack frontmatter, names the V code with an optional note and holds while the evidence it was given for holds; when the evidence changes, the finding comes back marked stale. The agent writes it with edit_engram and set_frontmatter on evolve_ack, the value being the code and the note (V109 kept for the wiki's links), and takes it back with remove V109. On Fluid’s maintenance page anyone with write access gets an Acknowledge button with a note field on each row about an engram, Re-acknowledge once its evidence has moved and Unacknowledge on one already silenced. V009, V108 and V203 name no engram, so there is nowhere to put an acknowledgment and doing the work is the only way to clear them. How an acknowledgment differs from a verification is part of the evolving story (Chapter 10).


20.12.2 The domain’s verify file
A .crystalline.yaml at a domain’s root can carry a verify block. The workspace file of the same name is a different one (Chapter 19):
verify:
  rules:
    E007: "off"
    L003: info
    M102: error
  token_budget: 3000
  token_budgets:
    reference/api-catalogue.md: 8000
    changelog.md: 0
  required_files:
    - path: GLOSSARY.md
      require_frontmatter: true
      required_sections: [Terms]
      sections:
        Terms:
          min_top_level_bullets: 5
          max_bullet_length: 240
rules sets a code’s severity to off, error, warning or info (e, warn, w and i work too). An override wins over --strict, so a rule you set to warning stays a warning in a strict run. An unknown word keeps the rule’s default and a file that doesn’t parse is ignored whole, and each raises M108: a warning that fails a run only under --strict. The rule a typo was meant for still takes --strict like any other. The overrides apply in crystalline verify and on MANIFEST edit receipts; validate_engrams and Fluid’s editor report every code at its default.
token_budget sets the budget for every file of the domain and token_budgets for single files, keyed by their path from the domain root. A budget of 0 turns Q002 and V105 off for that file, and a type: source engram still gets four times whatever applies. The budget is the one part of the file the sweep reads.
required_files puts the MANIFEST’s structural checks on other files. A missing file raises M001, missing frontmatter M002 when require_frontmatter is set and a missing section M003. A section under its min_top_level_bullets raises M004, or M101 when its fallback_section has enough; a bullet over max_bullet_length (180 by default) raises M102, and a doubled ## heading M103.
With crystalline verify --config you load one such file for every domain in the run, in place of each domain’s own. A --config file that doesn’t load stops the run with a message and exit code 1.


20.12.3 MANIFEST edits answer at once
An edit of a MANIFEST, or a write that replaces one open in Fluid’s editor, returns its M findings on the receipt, as manifest_findings with code, severity, message and line, and an error among them comes with the guidance that routing for the domain is broken. The edit lands anyway, and the findings come at the severities the domain’s verify block sets (a virtual domain has none and gets the defaults), so the agent that just emptied When to Use can fix it in its next call. M001 is never on the receipt because the file exists. M105 isn’t either: it needs a full verify to look at the folders.

title: 20  Every finding code
text:
20.13 Verify in CI
crystalline verify takes one or more domain roots and defaults to the current directory. It exits with 0 when no error was found, 1 when at least one was and 2 when a path doesn’t exist, isn’t a directory or can’t be read. Warnings never fail a run unless --strict promotes them. --format chooses human, json (a stable report, version 1) or github, which writes annotations: errors and warnings as such, info as notices that never fail the job. Verify belongs on every proposal a team reviews (Chapter 8), and the bundled action does it in one step:
- uses: jordiboehme/crystalline/action@v0.19.5
  with:
    paths: knowledge/engineering knowledge/payments
    strict: 'false'
    version: v0.19.5
paths takes space-separated domain roots, strict promotes warnings, version pins the binary it downloads (latest by default) and comment (on by default) keeps one summary comment on the pull request up to date. The step’s exit-code output carries verify’s own exit code, and the step fails the job when it isn’t 0.






NoteIn brief



Verify’s E, T, L, Q, S and M codes say whether the files hold their format, and the sweep’s V codes say what the knowledge needs, in three families, each finding with a priority and a class. Each entry above names what the code means and the action that clears it. A sweep finding a person ruled intentional is acknowledged in the engram with evolve_ack or on Fluid’s maintenance page, except the three that name no engram. Verify codes are tuned per domain in the verify block of .crystalline.yaml: severities, token budgets and required files. In CI, crystalline verify exits 1 on any error and 2 on a bad path, and --strict makes warnings count.

title: Glossary
text:
These are the words the book uses without stopping, each as chapter 4 defined it. Terms in code are spelled the way they appear in a file or a command.

agent identity

What an authenticated agent is on a shared instance: its user, for the length of the session. It sees, writes and shares as that person, and the provenance of what it captures names the account and the client that acted for it.

attachment

A file a person adds to an engram in Fluid, stored under the domain’s assets/ folder and referenced from the engram’s body. Agents read attachments back over MCP, and the sweep notices one nobody has analyzed.

build_context

The tool that walks out from an address, following relations and links one to three hops, and returns the neighbourhood ranked by how strongly each engram connects to the anchor. A /* suffix anchors a whole folder.

crystalline:// address

The one absolute form of an engram’s address, crystalline://<domain>/<permalink>. Anything without the scheme is domain-relative and takes its domain from context.

daemon

The single process that holds the index open, watches the domain folders, embeds new engrams and answers every agent, terminal and browser tab. The first client to connect starts it; it stops only when told to.

domain

A registered folder of knowledge with a MANIFEST.md at its root, or a virtual domain that lives in the database with no folder. The manifest’s When to Use bullets are what route an agent to it.

engram

One markdown file holding one unit of knowledge: YAML frontmatter, prose, observations and relations. The word comes from neuroscience, where it names the trace an experience leaves.

evolve

The maintenance sweep, crystalline evolve or the evolve_engrams tool: a read-only, ranked queue of what the knowledge needs, in three families (temporal, structural and redundancy). Each finding is marked mechanical, for the agent to complete, or judgment, for a person to rule on.

Fluid

The web UI the daemon serves at localhost:7411, named for the seam where fluid minds, human and model, meet the crystallized store. It has no store of its own; it shows the same files the agent reads.

frontmatter

The YAML block at the top of an engram holding its identity and state: type, title, permalink, tags, status, recorded_at, generated and the temporal fields when a fact is bounded.

harness

The program that runs the model and hands it tools over MCP: Claude Code, the Codex CLI, the Copilot CLI, Claude Desktop or any other MCP client. crystalline install <harness> wires one up.

MANIFEST.md

The first file in every domain, itself an engram of type: manifest. Its Scope, When to Use and Notes for Agents sections describe the domain and route tasks to it.

MCP

The Model Context Protocol, the standard by which a harness hands tools to a model. Crystalline is an MCP server, and its tools are how an agent searches, reads, captures and refines knowledge.

mechanical and judgment findings

The two classes of sweep finding. A mechanical finding completes intent the archive already records, so the agent does it in a pass; a judgment finding would change what the archive claims, so it goes to a person as a proposal.

membership level

What an invited member of a private domain may do there: a viewer reads and searches, an editor also writes, a manager also runs the membership. Inside a private domain a write has to pass both the level and the instance role, and the lower of the two decides.

nudge

The once-per-session reminder the stop hook delivers, asking the agent to review the conversation for durable learnings and propose capturing each. It costs about a hundred and twenty tokens.

observation

A top-level bullet of the form - [category] text #tag in an engram’s body: the atomic unit of knowledge, a fact, decision, gotcha or lesson, indexed on its own line.

OKF

Google’s Open Knowledge Format, version 0.2, the markdown-plus-frontmatter format an engram extends. Unknown keys survive every write, so a document from any OKF tool drops in and comes back out intact.

overlay

A per-actor private layer of drafts above a team domain in review mode, where the on-disk folder changes only by pull. A draft is visible to its author alone until it is shared, reviewed and merged.

owner

The one person answerable for a private domain. Only the owner or an instance admin changes its visibility, transfers it or deletes it; a manager can do none of those.

permalink

The half of an address that links point at, derived from the title, with the folder prefix in front when the engram lives in a subfolder. A move carries it to the new folder unless it was chosen by hand.

private domain

A domain visible only to its owner, the instance’s admins and invited members. To everyone else it reads as absent rather than forbidden.

prompt hook

The hook crystalline install wires to run on every prompt: in Claude Code and Codex it puts up to three engrams that may fit the prompt in front of the agent, named by address and each once per session. Copilot gets the entry and stays quiet.

proposal

A unit of knowledge sent for review from a team domain with share_changes: a pull request in the team’s repository that a person reviews and merges, and that the agent never merges itself. It is how a team domain shares by default; a domain whose MANIFEST says sharing: direct commits a share straight onto the branch instead. Outside review mode proposals stack, and one is amended in place by sharing again with its number.

provisioning

The mechanism by which a domain ships skills, commands, subagent definitions and MCP server configs into a harness. It is declared in the manifest’s Provisioning section and installed only after a person allows it, per domain and per machine.

relation

A top-level bullet of the form - rel_type [[Target]]: a typed edge in the knowledge graph, shown back on the target’s page as a backlink. depends_on, supersedes and relates_to are common types, and a split links its two halves with derived_from and split_into.

review mode

A private overlay per actor over a team domain’s shared folder: every write lands in the writer’s own overlay and the folder changes only with what lands on the team’s branch. Set per domain in its registration as review: overlay. It needs a GitHub origin, so a virtual domain refuses it, and no tool turns it on: an agent does not decide how a team reviews.

routing prompt

The briefing an agent receives at session start: one line per domain from the manifests’ When to Use bullets, plus the behaviour rules. crystalline prompt system prints it.

salience

A number from zero to ten in an engram’s frontmatter that gives hybrid search a small, bounded lift for the rare engram everything else hangs from. Relevance keeps the upper hand and nothing is ever excluded by it.

share-link

A revocable link that opens one engram in one person’s overlay to one colleague, who reads it and, after joining the draft, edits it in the normal editor where the domain’s write right allows. It is the only way one person’s drafts are ever visible to another.

split

To move part of an engram into an engram of its own: by granularity, a distilled summary beside a source engram holding the full text, or by validity, when one fact expires while the rest holds. The new engram carries the source’s tags and type, a stable status and no validity window, and the pair is linked with derived_from and split_into.

status

The frontmatter field that says whether the knowledge holds. stable is the default; deprecated, superseded, archived and legacy are the retirement set, which fades an engram in ranking without removing it. The field is required and free form.

supersede

To retire a fact that was true and stopped being: write the replacement as a new engram with supersedes, set the old one to superseded with a real valid_to and a superseded_by, and carry any lesson forward. A fact that was never quite true is corrected in place instead. When only part of the engram has expired, first split out the facts that still hold, then retire what is left.

tag alias

A fold recorded in the manifest’s Tag Aliases section when crystalline tags merge unifies two spellings, so a filter on the old tag still finds what it always found.

team domain

A domain whose files also live in a GitHub repository, tracked through an origin, with knowledge travelling between members as proposals or as direct commits where the MANIFEST says so. It needs no git on any machine.

temporal validity

The window in which a fact holds, valid_from and valid_to, as plain dates. Absent valid_from means always valid, absent valid_to means valid forever. stale_after asks for a re-check by a date and source_date says when the source was written.

tombstone

The mark a deletion leaves in an actor’s overlay, hiding the file for that actor until a merged share removes it for everyone.

verification

The verified frontmatter entry, { by, at } plus the model when an agent verified, that records a re-check finding a fact still true, one entry per verifier. The sweep stops asking about a verified engram on age alone.

virtual domain

A domain that lives in the database with no folder on disk, for a container without a writable volume. It carries the same manifest and answers to the same tools.

title: Questions and answers
text:
These are the questions people ask in the first week, and a few that come up in the second, once somebody is onboarding agents for other people. Each answer points at the chapter that goes deeper.
Why not just a folder of markdown files?
It’s one. Every engram is a markdown file in a folder you chose, readable in any editor, diffable in any repository and backed up with whatever you already use. What a folder can’t do on its own is what Crystalline adds on top: routing, so an agent knows which domain owns a task without reading every file; search that blends the exact phrase with the meaning; a graph of relations and backlinks; and a temporal model, so a fact that stopped being true in March still carries its dates and is no longer mistaken for the present. Chapter 1 walks the ladder from one file of instructions to real indexes.
Why not a vector database or a retrieval pipeline?
Retrieval is the easy half. A vector index finds text that resembles a question. It doesn’t know which domain owns the task, that a fact was superseded, who verified a claim or that something worth writing down just happened in this session. Crystalline treats similarity as one ranking signal inside a larger system of routing, provenance and time, on files you own, with no pipeline to operate. A pipeline also swallows whatever it’s fed. Here knowledge is taught, and in a team it’s reviewed by default before it reaches anyone else’s agent, so what comes back is meant to make sense rather than merely to resemble the question. Chapters 9 and 11 cover the ranking, and chapter 13 the review.
Where does the name come from?
It comes from psychology. Crystallized intelligence is what learning deposits in a person; fluid intelligence is the reasoning applied to a problem never seen before. A model arrives with fluid intelligence in abundance and none of your crystallized kind, so every session starts as a brilliant stranger. Crystalline is the crystallized half, the store of what an agent has learned, and Fluid, the web UI, is named for the seam where fluid minds meet it. An engram is neuroscience’s word for the trace an experience leaves. Chapter 2 is the whole story.
Is Crystalline a hosted service?
No. It’s a binary that runs on a machine of yours, your laptop by default or a server your team operates, and the knowledge is a folder on that machine’s disk. Nothing runs on anyone else’s servers. GitHub, where a team uses it, holds a reviewed copy of a domain’s files, the way it holds code; it serves nothing and sees no index. Chapter 1 has the two shapes and chapter 12 the shared one.
Do I have to run a server?
No. The first agent that connects starts a background daemon on your machine, and every later agent, terminal and browser tab attaches to it. It stops only when told to, with crystalline ctl shutdown, Ctrl-C in a foreground run or the signal a container sends. It keeps running after the last agent disconnects, so the index stays warm for the next session. The one exception is the daemon that Claude Desktop’s extension starts, which exits five seconds after its last client. Keep that extension on the same version as the CLI, because an older one refuses an index a newer version already upgraded. If a crash ever leaves a stale lock or socket behind, crystalline doctor --fix clears it and a daemon that’s alive but no longer answering is replaced by the next client that connects.
How do I start the daemon myself?
crystalline serve runs it in the foreground, where you can watch it work, and crystalline serve --daemon puts it in the background. It’s the one process the machine shares: it serves Fluid at http://localhost:7411, answers MCP over HTTP on that same port and takes the agents and crystalline commands on the machine itself over a local socket. Starting it yourself is worth it when you want the browser open before any agent has connected. crystalline ctl status tells you whether one is already running, with its pid, its uptime and the sessions attached. On a server nobody types serve at all, because the systemd unit or the container starts the daemon at boot. Chapter 5 has the laptop and chapter 12 the server.
Do I need a terminal at all?
You need one only for the local install and the occasional maintenance command. Claude Desktop users install an extension from the releases page and never open one: the agent creates its first domain itself, and Fluid, in the browser, is where a person reads, edits and corrects. Chapter 5 has both paths.
Is the MCP endpoint over HTTP protected?
On a laptop it listens on loopback, 127.0.0.1:7411, and any process on that machine can reach it, which is the right trade for one person. crystalline config set service.http false turns the endpoint off. The daemon also checks the request’s Host header against a loopback allow-list to block DNS rebinding, so a hostname or a proxy name has to be added first. Fluid and its API on the same port have accounts of their own, and nothing there is readable without a session.
On a shared instance turn on auth.mcp, and from then on every agent that connects over HTTP identifies itself with a token that belongs to one person, with no anonymous tier beside it. Chapter 12 sets it up and chapter 14 says what the token means.
How does a hosted client connect, with nowhere to paste a token?
It signs you in instead. On a shared instance whose agents identify themselves (auth.mcp on), a chat website or the app on your phone connects by sending you to sign in through the instance, with the login the instance already has. From then on it holds a credential the same gate checks on every request, the way it checks a token. A harness that can send a header keeps working with a pasted token. Chapter 12 has the setup and chapter 14 the two credentials at one gate.
Where does my knowledge actually live?
In your domain folders, as plain markdown. By default those folders sit under ~/Documents/Crystalline, one per domain, which is where an agent creates a domain when nobody names a path. A folder you registered yourself lives where you put it, like chapter 5’s ~/knowledge/engineering, and the domains_root setting moves the default. Everything Crystalline derives from it is disposable: the search index lives in the state directory and crystalline reindex --full rebuilds it from the files at any time. The config file, the index and the embedding model live in the platform’s config, state and cache directories, ~/.config/crystalline, ~/.local/state/crystalline and ~/.cache/crystalline on Linux and macOS.
Is my knowledge locked in?
No. An engram extends Google’s Open Knowledge Format, OKF 0.2: markdown with YAML frontmatter, readable by any OKF tooling and by any text editor. Frontmatter keys Crystalline doesn’t know are preserved through every write, and an index.md at each domain’s root lets a folder navigate itself with nothing running. crystalline import brings an existing tree of frontmatter markdown in as a pure file transformation. If you stopped using Crystalline tomorrow, the folder would still be a readable knowledge base. Chapter 4 has the format.
What happens to wrong knowledge?
It depends on how it was wrong. A fact that was never quite true, a cutoff measured from the wrong event, is corrected where it stands. A fact that was true and stopped being is superseded: the replacement is written as its own engram with supersedes pointing back, the old one gets status: superseded and a real valid_to, and any lesson worth keeping moves forward. The past stays in every search, dated and gently below the present. The sweep finds the retirements nobody finished, the links that dangle and the tags spelled two ways, and hands each to the agent as a mechanical fix or to you as a judgment. Deleting is for mistakes, never for history. Chapter 3 has the lifecycle and chapter 10 the sweep.
What is GitHub, and what does Crystalline use it for?
GitHub is a website where teams keep files and every change ever made to them, above all source code. Its habit worth borrowing is the review: a change to something shared is proposed first, a colleague who knows the subject reads it, and only then does it land for everyone. Crystalline uses GitHub for exactly that, with knowledge in place of code. A team domain’s markdown lives in a GitHub repository. By default a change goes out as a proposal (a pull request, in GitHub’s own words) and reaches everyone’s agent once somebody has merged it. A small team can switch a domain to sharing straight onto the branch instead. You don’t need to learn GitHub’s tools to take part: a one-time sign-in through a code in the browser connects your machine. After that the agent, Fluid or the command line does the talking. Chapter 13 walks through it. A team that doesn’t use GitHub loses nothing else in this book; only sharing a domain between machines needs it.
Do I need git to share knowledge with a team?
No. A team domain talks to GitHub directly over its API: each person connects once with a browser code, and proposals open as pull requests that a person reviews and merges there, unless the domain shares straight onto the branch. There’s no local clone and no SSH key, and nobody types git. Chapter 13 has the detail.
Can the agent see my private domain?
Only if its user can. On a shared instance an agent authenticates with a token that belongs to one person and acts as that person for the length of the session: it sees what they see, writes where they may write and captures under their name. A private domain shows to its owner, to the instance’s admins and to the members the owner invited, and to everyone else it reads as absent, on every surface. There’s no tool for changing a membership, so an agent cannot talk itself in. The one thing an agent can do to a domain is unregister it: remove_domain is open to an instance admin or a private domain’s owner and refused outright on the open tier. With auth.mcp on, add_domain, a configure that writes and a provision that decides need the admin role behind the agent as well. Before you rely on it, know the limits: admins see every domain, and a private domain protects from the instance’s other users, never from whoever operates the machine. Chapters 12 and 14 have the rest.
What does the onboarding cost in tokens?
It costs little, and the same on the tenth session as on the thousandth. The routing block is one line per domain and a handful of rules. The reminder at the end of a session costs about a hundred and twenty tokens and fires once. Recall loads only the engrams that matter, routed by domain and narrowed by the indexes, instead of a folder read whole every session. Chapter 6 has the briefing and chapter 9 the recall.
What should I teach first?
Whatever you’d tell a new hire in the first week, and the test is that sentence. Think of the rule behind the strange number, the nickname, the word the wiki gets wrong, the day nobody deploys. Teach where information lives rather than the information itself: which repository holds what, how access is granted, the architecture, so the agent can reach the territory with the tools its harness already gives it. Chapter 7 has the list, and chapter 8 says what to do when the first week meets the wiki.
